signals.title: [Bug]: usage is all zeros (and inputs are fused) for gemini-embedding-2 multimodal embeddings via /v1/embeddings
signals.text: ## What happens Calling the proxy's OpenAI-compatible `/v1/embeddings` with `model=gemini/gemini-embedding-2` and an `input` array containing a media data URI (e.g. `data:image/png;base64,…`), optionally mixed with text strings: 1. The response `usage` is all zeros (`prompt_tokens: 0, total_tokens: 0`), even though the upstream native `embedContent` response includes `usageMetadata.promptTokenCount` and per-modality `promptTokenDetails` (e.g. `{"modality":"IMAGE","tokenCount":258}`). 2. The whole `input` array is fused into a single `content` and returns **one** embedding vector, whereas text-only arrays return one vector per input. The single-vector semantics may be intentional for multimodal fusion, but the asymmetry deserves a docs note. ## Why it matters Google bills gemini-embedding-2 media input at modality-specific token rates (IMAGE 258 tokens/image, AUDIO 25 tokens/s, VIDEO 66 tokens/s — verifiable via `usageMetadata`). With `usage` zeroed, any cost tracking / spend logging / budget enforcement built on the proxy's usage fields silently sees zero cost for media embeddings. ## Expected Propagate `usageMetadata.promptTokenCount` into `usage.prompt_tokens` / `total_tokens`, and ideally expose the per-modality breakdown (e.g. `prompt_tokens_details`) so cost tracking can price modalities separately. ## Repro ```bash curl -s http://localhost:4000/v1/embeddings \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $LITELLM_MASTER_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"model": "gemini/gemini-embedding-2", "input": ["hello", "data:image/png;base64,iVBORw0KGgoAAAANSUhEUgAAAAEAAAABCAYAAAAfFcSJAAAADUlEQVR42mP8z8BQDwAEhQGAhKmMIQAAAABJRU5ErkJggg=="]}' # → data has 1 embedding (not 2), usage.prompt_tokens == 0 ``` Native comparison (same key): `POST …/v1beta/models/gemini-embedding-2:embedContent` returns `usageMetadata: {"promptTokenCount": 262, "promptTokenDetails": [{"modality":"TEXT","tokenCount":4},{"modality":"IMAGE","tokenCount":258}]}`. Observed on litellm-proxy 1.83.7 and 1.83.10 (Gemini API key path, `gemini/` prefix).
signals.author: huangdawei

signals.title: [Bug]: vertex_ai region-based cost tracking not supported (works for bedrock & azure)
signals.text: ### What happened? Region-based cost tracking works for **bedrock** and **azure** but **not** for **vertex_ai**. All vertex_ai regions are billed at the same model-name price, even though Google charges different rates for the global endpoint vs. non-global (regional) endpoints such as `eu`. `cost_calculator.py` supports region-scoped pricing keys of the form `"{provider}/{region_name}/{model}"` and uses them when present in `litellm.model_cost` (verified at v1.95.0-dev.1, `cost_calculator.py:454`): ```python model_with_provider_and_region = f"{custom_llm_provider}/{region_name}/{model}" if model_with_provider_and_region in model_cost_ref: # use region based pricing, if it's available model_with_provider = model_with_provider_and_region ``` `region_name` is read from the response's `_hidden_params` (`cost_calculator.py:1291`): ```python region_name = hidden_params.get("region_name", region_name) ``` But `region_name` is only ever **populated for bedrock** — it is hardcoded from `aws_region_name` in `main.py:5174`: ```python if model_response is not None and hasattr(model_response, "_hidden_params"): model_response._hidden_params["custom_llm_provider"] = custom_llm_provider model_response._hidden_params["region_name"] = kwargs.get( "aws_region_name", None ) # support region-based pricing for bedrock ``` For **vertex_ai**, the region is supplied via `vertex_location`, and it is mapped internally to `region_name` **for auth only** (`llms/vertex_ai/gemini/vertex_and_google_ai_studio_gemini.py:128`): ```python def get_mapped_special_auth_params(self) -> dict: return {"project": "vertex_project", "region_name": "vertex_location"} ``` That value is **never written into `_hidden_params["region_name"]`**. As a result, on the cost path: 1. `region_name` stays `None` for every vertex_ai request. 2. The region-scoped key `vertex_ai/{region}/{model}` is never constructed or looked up. 3. All vertex_ai regions (`global`, `eu`, `us`, …) are costed identically. Additionally, no region-scoped `vertex_ai/{region}/...` entries ship in `model_prices_and_context_window.json` (unlike the existing `azure/eu/...` and bedrock `bedrock/{region}/...` entries), so even if `region_name` were populated there would be nothing to match yet. ### Expected behavior Same as bedrock/azure: when a vertex_ai request specifies `vertex_location`, LiteLLM should propagate it as `region_name` into `_hidden_params` so a region-scoped cost key like `vertex_ai/eu/gemini-2.5-flash-lite` (when present in `model_cost`) is used for cost calculation. This also enables contributing region-scoped vertex pricing entries the way `azure/eu/...` and bedrock region entries already exist. ### Suggested fix In `main.py`, populate `region_name` from `vertex_location` for vertex_ai in addition to `aws_region_name` for bedrock: ```python if model_response is not None and hasattr(model_response, "_hidden_params"): model_response._hidden_params["custom_llm_provider"] = custom_llm_provider model_response._hidden_params["region_name"] = ( kwargs.get("aws_region_name") # bedrock or kwargs.get("vertex_location") # vertex_ai (sdk) or litellm_params.get("vertex_location") # vertex_ai (proxy/router deployments) ) ``` Region-scoped `vertex_ai/{region}/{model}` entries could then be added to `model_prices_and_context_window.json`, mirroring the existing `azure/eu/...` and bedrock region entries. ### Current workaround Define a **separate deployment per region** in the proxy config, each with its own inline `model_info` pricing block: ```yaml - model_name: gemini-flash-lite # global endpoint -> built-in price litellm_params: model: vertex_ai/gemini-2.5-flash-lite vertex_project: os.environ/VERTEX_PROJECT vertex_location: global - model_name: gemini-flash-lite-eu # regional endpoint -> overridden price litellm_params: model: vertex_ai/gemini-2.5-flash-lite vertex_project: os.environ/VERTEX_PROJECT vertex_location: eu model_info: input_cost_per_token: 3.3e-07 output_cost_per_token: 2.75e-06 cache_read_input_token_cost: 3.3e-08 ``` This works but is verbose and easy to get out of sync, and it doesn't help the plain SDK path where two `completion()` calls to the same model differing only by `vertex_location` are always costed identically. ### Relevant log output _No response_ ### Are you a ML Ops Team? No ### What LiteLLM version are you on ? v1.95.0-dev.1 (also confirmed on v1.89.3) ### Twitter / LinkedIn details _No response_

signals.title: [Bug]: Microservice images (litellm-gateway / litellm-backend) never initialise the secret manager, so os.environ/<KEY> config references silently resolve to None
signals.text: ### Check for existing issues - [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate. ### What happened? ### What happened? With the split/microservice images (`ghcr.io/berriai/litellm-gateway`, `ghcr.io/berriai/litellm-backend`), a config that resolves the master key and provider keys from AWS Secrets Manager does not work. The proxy starts, logs `LITELLM_MASTER_KEY is not set!`, and the Admin UI rejects the correct master key with *"Master Key not set for Proxy"*. Provider keys in `model_list` are nulled the same way, so model calls fail authentication. The identical config, secret, and IAM role work on the monolithic image (`ghcr.io/berriai/litellm-database`) at the same versions, which isolates this to the deployment topology rather than the release. Config used (trimmed): ```yaml model_list: - model_name: gpt-4.1 litellm_params: model: azure/gpt-4.1 api_base: "https://example.openai.azure.com/" api_version: "2024-10-21" api_key: os.environ/MY_AZURE_KEY general_settings: master_key: os.environ/LITELLM_MASTER_KEY key_management_system: aws_secret_manager key_management_settings: aws_region_name: "us-east-2" access_mode: "read_only" hosted_keys: - LITELLM_MASTER_KEY - MY_AZURE_KEY primary_secret_name: "my-app/litellm-secrets" ``` `LITELLM_MASTER_KEY` is **not** set as an environment variable — it is expected to come from Secrets Manager, as it does on the monolith. ### Root cause Two things combine. **1. The split images bypass the CLI, which is where the secret manager gets initialised.** ``` litellm-database (monolith): docker/prod_entrypoint.sh -> litellm CLI litellm-backend: ENTRYPOINT ["uvicorn","backend.main:app"] litellm-gateway: ENTRYPOINT ["sh","-c","exec uvicorn gateway.main:app --workers \"${NUM_WORKERS:-1}\" \"$@\"","--"] ``` `litellm/proxy/proxy_cli.py` calls `proxy_config.initialize_secret_manager(...)` before the app reads its config. `gateway/main.py` and `backend/main.py` contain no equivalent call (0 matches for `initialize_secret_manager` / `load_aws_secret_manager` in both, v1.93.0 through v1.94.0), so nothing initialises the manager ahead of config load. **2. `_check_for_os_environ_vars` resolves and writes back before the manager exists.** Call stack captured on v1.94.0: ``` litellm/proxy/proxy_server.py:4306 in load_config -> config = await self.get_config(config_file_path=...) litellm/proxy/proxy_server.py:4127 in get_config -> config = self._check_for_os_environ_vars(config=config) litellm/proxy/proxy_server.py:3954 in _check_for_os_environ_vars -> config[key] = get_secret(value) ``` `get_config()` walks the whole config and **replaces** every `os.environ/...` string with the result of `get_secret()`. At that point `litellm.secret_manager_client` is still `None` (`initialize_secret_manager` is called later, in `load_config`'s `general_settings` block), so every key that lives only in Secrets Manager resolves to `None` — and that `None` is written into the parsed config. This is what makes it unrecoverable rather than merely mistimed. Later in `load_config`: ```python master_key = general_settings.get("master_key", get_secret("LITELLM_MASTER_KEY", None)) if master_key and master_key.startswith("os.environ/"): master_key = get_secret(master_key) ``` The default argument **does** resolve correctly (the manager is up by then), but `general_settings["master_key"]` now exists with value `None`, so `.get()` returns `None` and the working default is discarded. The `startswith` branch then short-circuits, so no second attempt is made. Instrumenting `get_secret` during startup in the running container shows exactly this: ``` get_secret('os.environ/MY_AZURE_KEY') manager_ready=False -> None get_secret('os.environ/LITELLM_MASTER_KEY') manager_ready=False -> None get_secret('os.environ/DATABASE_URL') manager_ready=True -> SET # only because it is also a real env var get_secret('LITELLM_MASTER_KEY') manager_ready=True -> SET # resolves fine, result discarded CRITICAL proxy_server.py - LITELLM_MASTER_KEY is not set! ... ``` AWS access itself is fine — from the same pod, `boto3` reads the secret and a direct `get_secret("os.environ/LITELLM_MASTER_KEY")` after startup returns the key. Nothing is logged to indicate a secret lookup failed; the only signal is the `LITELLM_MASTER_KEY is not set!` line, which points users at environment variables when the config and credentials are both correct. (The `Unable to locate credentials` error in local output is expected without AWS credentials and is not the point — the `manager_ready=False` ordering and the `None` write-back are.) ### Suggested fix Either would resolve it; the second also hardens the monolith path: 1. Initialise the secret manager before config resolution in the split entrypoints — have `gateway/main.py` and `backend/main.py` do what `proxy_cli.py` does, or move `initialize_secret_manager()` ahead of `get_config()` inside `load_config`. 2. Make `_check_for_os_environ_vars` leave the original `os.environ/<KEY>` string in place when `get_secret()` returns `None`, so downstream fallbacks still see a resolvable reference instead of a null. A warning when a `os.environ/<KEY>` reference resolves to `None` while `key_management_system` is configured would also have turned a two-day investigation into a one-line log read. ### Impact On the microservice deployment, any key sourced solely from a secret manager is unavailable: - Admin UI login is impossible (`master_key` is `None`, so `/v2/login` rejects the correct key). - Every `model_list` entry using `os.environ/<KEY>` loses its credential, so model calls fail auth. - No error is logged for the failed lookups. Workaround: supply the keys as real environment variables (they are read before the secret manager is consulted), or run the monolithic `litellm-database` image, whose CLI entrypoint initialises the manager first. ### Related - #13076 — same family: AWS `get_secret` returns `None` silently instead of raising, unlike Google Secret Manager / Hashicorp Vault, so failures are invisible. - #26151 — custom secret manager not invoked at request time (different lifecycle, noting for context). - #28619 — two Helm charts now exist; the microservice path is the one affected here. ### What LiteLLM version are you on? - Affected: `ghcr.io/berriai/litellm-gateway` and `ghcr.io/berriai/litellm-backend` at `v1.93.0`, `v1.93.1`, `v1.94.0` - Not affected: `ghcr.io/berriai/litellm-database` (monolith) at `v1.93.0` and `v1.94.0` ### Environment - Kubernetes (EKS), credentials via IRSA; `sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity` verified working from inside the pod - AWS Secrets Manager, consolidated JSON secret via `primary_secret_name` + `hosted_keys` - Python 3.13 (image default) ### Steps to Reproduce ### Minimal reproduction (no AWS account or cluster required) The write-back happens before any secret manager exists, so the defect is observable without credentials — only the image is needed. `ordercheck.py`: ```python import asyncio, litellm, pathlib from litellm.proxy import proxy_server as ps pathlib.Path("/tmp/cfg.yaml").write_text(""" general_settings: master_key: "os.environ/LITELLM_MASTER_KEY" key_management_system: aws_secret_manager key_management_settings: aws_region_name: "us-east-2" access_mode: "read_only" hosted_keys: [LITELLM_MASTER_KEY] primary_secret_name: "some/secret" """) orig = ps.get_secret def traced(secret_name, default_value=None): ready = litellm.secret_manager_client is not None v = orig(secret_name, default_value) print("get_secret(%r) manager_ready=%s -> %s" % (secret_name, ready, "SET" if v is not None else None)) return v ps.get_secret = traced try: asyncio.run(ps.ProxyConfig().load_config(router=None, config_file_path="/tmp/cfg.yaml")) except Exception as e: print("load_config raised:", type(e).__name__) print("general_settings['master_key'] =", repr((ps.general_settings or {}).get("master_key"))) ``` ```bash docker run --rm -v "$PWD/ordercheck.py:/w/ordercheck.py:ro" \ --entrypoint python ghcr.io/berriai/litellm-backend:v1.94.0 /w/ordercheck.py ``` **Actual** (v1.93.0, v1.93.1, v1.94.0 — identical): ``` get_secret('os.environ/LITELLM_MASTER_KEY') manager_ready=False -> None general_settings['master_key'] = None ``` **Expected:** either the lookup happens with the secret manager already initialised, or the unresolved reference is left intact so the later fallback can resolve it. (The `Unable to locate credentials` error in local output is expected without AWS credentials and is not the point — the `manager_ready=False` ordering and the `None` write-back are.) ### Relevant log output ```shell 09:06:58 - LiteLLM Proxy:CRITICAL: proxy_server.py:4538 - LITELLM_MASTER_KEY is not set! All requests will be treated as INTERNAL_USER with no admin access. Set LITELLM_MASTER_KEY for production use. 10:29:28 - LiteLLM Proxy:ERROR: proxy_server.py:13328 - litellm.proxy.proxy_server.login_v2(): Exception occurred - Master Key not set for Proxy. Please set Master Key to use Admin UI. Set `LITELLM_MASTER_KEY` in .env or set general_settings:master_key in config.yaml. https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/proxy/virtual_keys. If set, use `--detailed_debug` to debug issue. litellm.proxy._types.ProxyException: Master Key not set for Proxy. Please set Master Key to use Admin UI. Set `LITELLM_MASTER_KEY` in .env or set general_settings:master_key in config.yaml. https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/proxy/virtual_keys. If set, use `--detailed_debug` to debug issue. ``` ### What part of LiteLLM is this about? Proxy ### What LiteLLM version are you on ? v1.93.0 ### Twitter / LinkedIn details https://www.linkedin.com/in/dinkey-mahawar-13ab67125/

signals.title: [Bug]: A single malformed tool_calls[].function.arguments DoSes a proxy replica — pre-network transformation error is mapped to retryable APIConnectionError, and the cyclic fallback graph is walked without cycle detection (79,858 attempts against num_retries=2, ~2.3 GB of logs in ~7 min, event loop starved, pod killed with exit 137)
signals.text: ### Check for existing issues - [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate. ### What happened? > **Title (paste into the GitHub issue title field):** > > `[Bug]: A single malformed tool_calls[].function.arguments DoSes a proxy replica — pre-network transformation error is mapped to retryable APIConnectionError, and the cyclic fallback graph is walked without cycle detection (79,858 attempts against num_retries=2, ~2.3 GB of logs in ~7 min, event loop starved, pod killed with exit 137)` > > Suggested labels: `bug`, `bedrock`, `router`, `availability` --- ## What happened? A client replayed a conversation history in which one assistant message contained a **truncated** `tool_calls[].function.arguments` JSON string. LiteLLM's Bedrock Converse transformation tried to `json.loads()` that string, failed, and raised a **bare `Exception`**. `exception_mapping_utils.exception_type()` classified it as **`litellm.APIConnectionError`** — a *retryable* class. Because the failure occurs inside `_async_transform_request()`, i.e. **before any network I/O**, each retry costs ~0.56 ms of pure CPU. The router's retry + fallback machinery therefore degenerated into a **CPU-speed busy loop**. Each iteration wrote a ~30-line, ~3 KB chained traceback synchronously to stdout, on the **same thread that runs the asyncio event loop**. Measured result for **one single client request**: - **79,858** transformation failures in **45.05 s** (≈ **1,773 failures/s**, one every **0.56 ms**) - …against a configured budget of `num_retries: 2`, i.e. **at most ~9 attempts** for the model group involved. The observed count overshoots the configured bound by **≈8,900×**, because the `fallbacks` graph contains a 4-node **cycle** that the router walks without cycle detection (§5.10) - the configured `retry_after: 2.0` was **not applied** — measured interval between attempts was **0.564 ms**, not 2 s - **53,202 log lines/s**, ≈ **5.5 MB/s** to stdout, **~2.3 GB** of logs for the ~7-minute event - **4 container-log rotations in 50 seconds** - one CPU core saturated, **asyncio event loop starved** - Redis client reads started timing out (the Redis *server* was provably idle and healthy) - `/health/readiness` and `/health/liveliness` stopped answering within their timeouts - **12 consecutive liveness failures → kubelet killed the container → SIGTERM (8 s grace, the frozen process could not handle it) → SIGKILL → `exitCode: 137`, `reason: Error`** So: **an unprivileged client can take down a LiteLLM proxy replica with one HTTP request**, without any large payload, high request rate, or misconfiguration on the operator's side. This is why I'm filing it as an availability issue and not only as a transformation bug. This is not a hypothetical — it happened in production on 2026-07-30 and it is reproducible from the request body alone. ## Impact / severity | Dimension | Assessment | | --- | --- | | Trigger cost to attacker | One HTTP request, a few hundred bytes, any valid API key | | Effect | Replica becomes unresponsive on **all** endpoints (health, other tenants' traffic) for minutes, then is killed by the orchestrator | | Blast radius | Not limited to the offending request: the event loop is shared, so every in-flight request on that replica is affected and lost on SIGKILL | | Self-amplifying | Killing the replica pushes its traffic to peers; after restart the same client retried and the fresh container was starved again within 65 s (see §5.9) | | Secondary | ~2.3 GB of logs per incident — real risk of filling the node disk and of blowing up log-ingest cost | | Detectability | Very poor: `exitCode 137` with `reason: Error` looks exactly like an OOM kill, but `memory.events oom_kill` is `0`. Node-level CPU/memory metrics look completely healthy (see §5.7) | ## Environment | Item | Value | | --- | --- | | LiteLLM version | **v1.93.0** | | Image | `ghcr.io/berriai/litellm-database:1.93.0` | | Deployment | `litellm-helm` chart 1.93.0, 6 replicas, namespace `ai-gateway` | | Python | 3.13 (`/app/.venv/lib/python3.13/site-packages/litellm/...`) | | Provider | AWS Bedrock **Converse**, streaming (`converse_handler.py::async_streaming`), `ap-southeast-1` | | Platform | Amazon EKS, Amazon Linux 2023, kernel `6.12.92-122.166.amzn2023.x86_64`, 16 vCPU / 63 GB nodes | | Container limits | 8 CPU / 16 Gi | | Backing services | PostgreSQL (Bitnami) and Redis (Bitnami), both off-pod, both healthy throughout | | Are you an ML Ops team? | Yes | Relevant configuration (managed through the Admin UI, therefore stored in the `LiteLLM_Config` table; secrets removed): ```yaml # router_settings num_retries: 2 retry_after: 2.0 allowed_fails: 3 cooldown_time: 60.0 timeout: 300.0 routing_strategy: simple-shuffle model_group_alias: {} fallbacks: [ 11 entries — full graph in §5.10 ] # litellm_settings num_retries: 2 request_timeout: 600 drop_params: true modify_params: true cache: true cache_params: { type: redis, ttl: 300, supported_call_types: [acompletion, completion] } success_callback: [langfuse] failure_callback: [langfuse] callbacks: [custom_callbacks.proxy_handler_instance, prometheus] store_audit_logs: true # general_settings store_model_in_db: true store_prompts_in_spend_logs: true database_connection_pool_limit: 10 database_connection_timeout: 60 health_check_interval: 300 maximum_spend_logs_retention_period: 7d maximum_spend_logs_retention_interval: 1h ``` Note `drop_params: true` and `modify_params: true` are both enabled — we have already opted into LiteLLM's message-fixup leniency, and it does not cover this case. Probe configuration at the time of the incident (already **relaxed** relative to the chart defaults, and still not enough): ```yaml livenessProbe: { path: /health/liveliness, periodSeconds: 30, timeoutSeconds: 10, failureThreshold: 12 } # ≈6 min tolerance readinessProbe: { path: /health/readiness, periodSeconds: 15, timeoutSeconds: 10, failureThreshold: 3 } startupProbe: { path: /health/readiness, periodSeconds: 10, timeoutSeconds: 5, failureThreshold: 30 } terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 8 ``` Note the replica was killed **despite a ~6-minute liveness tolerance**. The loop had been running for longer than that. ## Root cause: three separate defects ### Defect 1 — a client input error is raised as a bare `Exception` and mapped to a *retryable* class `litellm/litellm_core_utils/prompt_templates/factory.py::_convert_to_bedrock_tool_call_invoke` 1. line 3682 — `json.loads(function_arguments)` → `json.decoder.JSONDecodeError` 2. line 3695 — fallback `split_concatenated_json_objects()` (`common_utils.py:1711`) also fails, because it handles *concatenated* JSON but not *truncated* JSON 3. line 3731 — `raise Exception(f"Unable to convert openai tool calls={tool_calls} to bedrock tool calls. Received error={e}")` `litellm/litellm_core_utils/exception_mapping_utils.py:2482 / 2505` then wraps that bare `Exception` into `litellm.APIConnectionError`. `APIConnectionError` means "the network or the upstream provider hiccuped, try again". Here nothing has been sent anywhere — the request never reaches Bedrock. This is a **400-class client input error** and must be non-retryable. The `split_concatenated_json_objects` helper is itself evidence that upstream already added leniency for malformed model-emitted tool arguments; truncation was simply not covered. ### Defect 2 — the fallback graph is walked without cycle detection, so retries are effectively unbounded Frames observed in the traceback: ``` router.py:6235 async_function_with_fallbacks (log site) router.py:6286 async_function_with_fallbacks router.py:6387 async_function_with_retries router.py:6465 async_function_with_retries router.py:6532 async_function_with_retries router.py:6541 make_call router.py:2802 / 2753 _acompletion utils.py:1870 / 1689 wrapper_async main.py:696 / 643 acompletion ``` Retrying a *deterministic* failure can never succeed. Worse, because the failure is raised before any socket is opened, there is **no natural rate limit**: retry-after / backoff logic that keys off provider latency or `retry_after` headers has nothing to slow it down. The loop runs at CPU speed (measured 0.564 ms per attempt). **Our configured budget is small, and cannot account for what happened.** `num_retries: 2` (set in both `router_settings` and `litellm_settings`) means at most 3 attempts per model group; the group involved has 2 fallback groups, bounding the work at roughly **9 attempts**. We measured **79,858** — an overshoot of ≈8,900×. The reason is that our `fallbacks` graph contains a cycle (full graph and derivation in §5.10): ``` claude-sonnet-5 ⇄ claude-sonnet-4-6 claude-sonnet-4-6 → claude-haiku-4-5 → GLM-5.2 → claude-sonnet-4-6 ``` `{claude-sonnet-5, claude-sonnet-4-6, claude-haiku-4-5, GLM-5.2}` form a strongly connected component. Every group in it fails *identically* on this input, so the traversal never terminates. Nothing in the logs suggests the router noticed it was revisiting a model group it had already tried. I'd argue a cyclic fallback graph should not be able to hang the proxy regardless of whether the config is "correct" — it is trivially easy to create by accident (each of the 11 entries above looks locally reasonable), the UI accepts it without warning, and there is no startup validation or runtime guard. Two further mechanisms that should have stopped this did not fire. I'd like maintainers to confirm whether that is expected: - **`retry_after: 2.0` was not honoured.** Measured inter-attempt interval: 0.564 ms. Backoff appears not to apply to `APIConnectionError` on this path, which is what allows CPU-speed spinning. - **`allowed_fails: 3` + `cooldown_time: 60.0` never cooled anything out of the loop.** If cooldown bookkeeping is written to Redis, and Redis calls were themselves timing out because the loop was starved (§5.6), then the circuit breaker cannot engage precisely when it is most needed. That feedback loop deserves an explicit guard — cooldown state that depends on the resource being starved is not a circuit breaker. ### Defect 3 — the error path logs the entire message history, once per retry, synchronously Two problems in one: - The exception message embeds the **full `tool_calls` repr**, and the `verbose_logger.exception()` call emits a multi-level chained traceback. Measured: **exactly 30.0 log lines and 3,089 bytes per failure** (constant across three independently rotated log files — see §5.3). Multiply by the retry loop and you get GB-scale log volume. - The logger format string is **never interpolated**. The log contains the literal: ``` Unable to convert openai tool calls={} to bedrock tool calls. Received error={} ``` i.e. a `str.format`-style template passed to a `%`-style logger (or emitted without arguments), so the operator-facing log line carries **no information at all**. The useful text only appears in the exception message. Also worth noting: because the tool-call repr is logged, **user conversation content is written to stdout at ERROR level** — a data-handling concern independent of the volume issue. ## Evidence All commands below were run against the live cluster. Times are UTC unless suffixed "local" (local = UTC+8). ### 5.1 The traceback (verbatim frames, from `/var/log/pods/.../litellm/2.log.20260730-071804.gz`) ``` LiteLLM Router:ERROR: router.py:6235 - litellm.router.py::async_function_with_fallbacks() - Error occurred while trying to do fallbacks - litellm.APIConnectionError: litellm.APIConnectionError: Unable to convert openai tool calls=[{'id': 'tooluse_MAh2QLVjBRkvi5QJkLQ08V', 'type': 'function', 'function': {'name': 'replace_note_content', 'arguments': '{"note_id": "999af35c-4061-4ece-8581-7d43fc988ba4", "title": "WG-全站内容版图坐标表"'}}] to bedrock tool calls. Received error=Expecting ',' delimiter: line 1 column 76 (char 75) Traceback (most recent call last): File ".../litellm/litellm_core_utils/prompt_templates/factory.py", line 3682, in _convert_to_bedrock_tool_call_invoke File "/usr/lib/python3.13/json/__init__.py", line 352, in loads File "/usr/lib/python3.13/json/decoder.py", line 345, in decode File "/usr/lib/python3.13/json/decoder.py", line 361, in raw_decode json.decoder.JSONDecodeError: Expecting ',' delimiter: line 1 column 76 (char 75) During handling of the above exception, another exception occurred: File ".../litellm/litellm_core_utils/prompt_templates/factory.py", line 3695, in _convert_to_bedrock_tool_call_invoke File ".../litellm/litellm_core_utils/prompt_templates/common_utils.py", line 1711, in split_concatenated_json_objects File "/usr/lib/python3.13/json/decoder.py", line 361, in raw_decode json.decoder.JSONDecodeError: Expecting ',' delimiter: line 1 column 76 (char 75) During handling of the above exception, another exception occurred: File ".../litellm/main.py", line 643, in acompletion File ".../litellm/llms/bedrock/chat/converse_handler.py", line 105, in async_streaming File ".../litellm/llms/bedrock/chat/converse_transformation.py", line 1604, in _async_transform_request File ".../litellm/litellm_core_utils/prompt_templates/factory.py", line 4549, in _bedrock_converse_messages_pt_async File ".../litellm/litellm_core_utils/prompt_templates/factory.py", line 3731, in _convert_to_bedrock_tool_call_invoke Exception: Unable to convert openai tool calls={} to bedrock tool calls. Received error={} ^^^^ ^^^^ unformatted placeholders (Defect 3) File ".../litellm/router.py", line 6286, in async_function_with_fallbacks File ".../litellm/router.py", line 6532, in async_function_with_retries File ".../litellm/router.py", line 6465, in async_function_with_retries File ".../litellm/router.py", line 6541, in make_call File ".../litellm/router.py", line 2802, in _acompletion File ".../litellm/router.py", line 2753, in _acompletion File ".../litellm/utils.py", line 1870, in wrapper_async File ".../litellm/utils.py", line 1689, in wrapper_async File ".../litellm/main.py", line 696, in acompletion File ".../litellm/litellm_core_utils/exception_mapping_utils.py", line 2505, in exception_type File ".../litellm/litellm_core_utils/exception_mapping_utils.py", line 2482, in exception_type litellm.exceptions.APIConnectionError: litellm.APIConnectionError: Unable to convert openai tool calls=[...] ``` ### 5.2 The offending input ``` "arguments": "{\"note_id\": \"999af35c-4061-4ece-8581-7d43fc988ba4\", \"title\": \"WG-全站内容版图坐标表\"" ``` Exactly 75 characters long, with **no closing `}`** — `raw_decode` reports `Expecting ',' delimiter: line 1 column 76 (char 75)`, i.e. it ran off the end of the string right after the `title` value. A partially-streamed / truncated tool call that a client then replayed back into the message history. ### 5.3 Amplification measurements (three independently rotated log files) Counted with `zcat/wc -l` and `grep -c 'Unable to convert openai tool calls'`; the time span is the delta between the first and last `kubectl logs --timestamps` RFC3339 timestamps inside each file. | Log file | Bytes | Lines | `Unable to convert` count | Lines / failure | Bytes / failure | Timestamp span | Lines/s | Failures/s | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `2.log.20260730-071804.gz` | 17.6 MB gz (~247 MB raw) | 2,396,900 | 79,858 | **30.0** | — | `07:17:16.342308096Z` → `07:18:01.395021768Z` = **45.05 s** | **53,202** | **1,773** | | `2.log.20260730-071854` | 41,086,647 | 399,041 | 13,302 | **30.0** | **3,089** | 7.046 s | 56,634 | 1,888 | | `2.log` (current file at SIGKILL) | 61,634,348 | 598,651 | 19,954 | **30.0** | **3,089** | 0.845 s | — (buffer flush after SIGTERM, not a steady-state rate) | — | The three files independently agree on **30.0 log lines** and **3,089 bytes per failure** and **~103 bytes per line**, which is what makes the per-second figures trustworthy. Derived: `45.05 s / 79,858 = 0.564 ms` per retry iteration. Sustained stdout write rate `1,773 × 3,089 B ≈ 5.5 MB/s`. Over the ~7-minute event that is **~2.3 GB**. ### 5.4 Container log rotation — four times in fifty seconds ``` /var/log/pods/ai-gateway_<pod>_<uid>/litellm/ 2.log.20260730-071804.gz 2.log.20260730-071835.gz 2.log.20260730-071844.gz 2.log.20260730-071854 2.log ``` Rotations at `07:18:04`, `07:18:35`, `07:18:44`, `07:18:54`. Node-side confirmation from `sar -d -p` on the node running the pod (10-minute samples, 15:00 and 15:20 local): ``` nvme1n1 wkB/s 7478.35 %util 1.86 # 15:00 local nvme1n1 wkB/s 5582.55 %util 1.18 # 15:20 local ``` The sustained ~5.5–7.3 MB/s write rate matches the computed log volume — the flood was running *before* the pod froze, not only during the death throes. > **Operator warning worth adding to the docs:** `kubectl logs` only reads the *current* CRI log file. During this incident that made it look as though the process had emitted **zero** logs for 11 minutes, when in fact the opposite was true — the earlier content had been rotated away. I initially drew exactly the wrong conclusion from `kubectl logs --previous`. Anyone debugging this must look directly at `/var/log/pods/<ns>_<pod>_<uid>/<container>/`. ### 5.5 Proof that this is ONE request, not a client retry storm ```bash zcat 2.log.20260730-071804.gz | grep -o "tooluse_[A-Za-z0-9]*" | sort -u | wc -l # -> 1 zcat 2.log.20260730-071804.gz | grep -o '"note_id": "[^"]*"' | sort -u | wc -l # -> 1 ``` **Exactly one** distinct `tool_call.id` (`tooluse_MAh2QLVjBRkvi5QJkLQ08V`) and **one** distinct `note_id` across all **79,858** failures. The loop is entirely internal to LiteLLM. A client hammering the proxy would have produced many distinct tool-call ids. ### 5.6 Event loop starvation, shown by Redis client timeouts against a healthy Redis The pod logged `redis.exceptions.TimeoutError` (client-side read timeout) via `/usr/lib/python3.13/asyncio/timeouts.py:117 __aexit__`. Server side, at the same moment: | Redis metric | Value | | --- | --- | | `dbsize` | 470 keys | | `used_memory_human` | 2.40 MB | | largest key (`redis-cli --bigkeys`) | string, 10,779 bytes | | `slowlog get` | **empty** | | `latency history` | **empty** | | `blocked_clients` | 0 | | `evicted_keys` | 0 | | AOF status | `ok` | | `connected_clients` | 171 | | Redis node CPU idle | 97.4 – 97.5 % | | Redis node disk `%util` | < 2 %, `await` < 1.4 ms | A perfectly idle server plus a client-side read timeout inverts the usual reading: **LiteLLM's own event loop was too starved to drain the socket.** Redis is the victim here, not the cause. (Equally: the fact that `asyncio.timeout` fired at all proves the loop was still *cycling*, just hopelessly behind — this was CPU starvation, not a hard block.) ### 5.7 Every infrastructure explanation is excluded `sar` on the node running the pod, 10-minute samples at 15:10 / 15:20 local: | Metric | 15:10 | 15:20 | Verdict | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `%memused` | 17.24 % | 15.54 % | ~51 GB available (`free -m`: 49,105 MB) → not memory pressure | | `%user` (16 vCPU) | 6.91 % | 10.73 % | **one saturated core ≈ 6.25 %** → consistent with exactly one hot thread | | `%idle` | 91.5 % | 87.7 % | node looks perfectly healthy — this is the trap | | `%iowait` | 0.12 % | 0.10 % | not I/O bound | | `%steal` | 0 | 0 | no hypervisor contention | | `ldavg-1` | 0.97 | 2.06 | fine for 16 cores | | `runq-sz` / `blocked` | 4 / 0 | 1 / 0 | nothing blocked in D-state | Container cgroup v2: ``` /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.events -> oom 0 oom_kill 0 # NOT an OOM kill /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.stat -> nr_throttled 1 throttled_usec 303009 # 0.3 s total, irrelevant journalctl -k | grep -i oom -> (no output) ``` Network/kernel: ``` net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_count = 1760 net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max = 524288 journalctl -k | grep -Ei 'conntrack|neighbour|net_ratelimit' -> (no output) ``` PostgreSQL was not implicated: it runs off-pod, showed no slow queries or lock waits, and the only relevant proxy config was spend-log retention (`maximum_spend_logs_retention_period: 7d`, `store_audit_logs: true`). The one readiness `503` (15:18:21 local) is consistent with LiteLLM's *internal* DB health check timing out under loop starvation, not with PostgreSQL being unhealthy. **No debug logging was enabled.** Grepping the proxy ConfigMap for `verbose`/`debug`/`json_logs`/`log` returned only the two spend-log retention keys. The entire ~2.3 GB was error-path output at default log level. ### 5.8 Kill timeline (`journalctl -u kubelet -u containerd`) Local time = UTC+8; the klog `I0730 07:xx` stamps in the same lines are UTC. | Time (local) | Event | | --- | --- | | ≤ 15:10 | readiness probe already timing out; pod flaps Ready/NotReady (brief recoveries 15:11:27, 15:15:33) | | 15:12:00 | liveness probe begins failing, **every 30 s, 12 consecutive times** | | 15:17:30 | `Container litellm failed liveness probe, will be restarted` | | 15:18:21 | readiness probe returns `statuscode: 503` (process answers but self-check fails) | | 15:18:52.983 | containerd `StopContainer ... with timeout 8 (s)`; `signal terminated` (SIGTERM) | | 15:19:00.990 | `Kill container` (SIGKILL — the frozen process never handled SIGTERM) | | 15:19:01.179 | `exit_status:137` → this is where `exitCode 137 / reason: Error` comes from | | 15:19:02.309 | new container started, `attempt:3` | `137 = 128 + 9` (SIGKILL). Crucially `reason: Error`, **not** `OOMKilled` — but almost every operator, and much of the existing tooling, reads 137 as "out of memory". Combined with §5.7 this misdirection cost us a full day of investigation. ### 5.9 The restart does not help — the fresh container was re-starved in 65 seconds | Time (local) | Event | | --- | --- | | 15:19:30 | new container reports Ready | | 15:20:35 | readiness probe **already** timing out again | | 15:22:00 – 15:24:00 | liveness probe failing again | | after 15:24 | recovered on its own, without being killed | Two conclusions. First, this is not a slow resource leak — it is instantaneous re-poisoning by the same retried request. Second, **the liveness kill is net-negative here**: the process demonstrably recovers by itself, while the kill drops every in-flight request and shifts load onto peer replicas, spreading the failure. ### 5.10 The configured retry budget vs. the observed iteration count — and the fallback cycle Full `fallbacks` graph, verbatim from `LiteLLM_Config.router_settings`: ```yaml fallbacks: - gemini-3.1-flash-image: [gemini-3.1-flash-image-preview] - gpt-5.6-sol: [gpt-5.6-luna, gpt-5.6-terra] - gpt-5.5: [bedrock_mantle/gpt-5.5, bedrock_mantle/gpt-5.4, gpt-5.4, gpt-5.4-mini, gpt-5.4-nano] - gemini-3-pro-image: [gemini-3-pro-image-preview, gpt-image-2] - GLM-5.2: [claude-sonnet-4-6, bedrock/claude-sonnet-4-6, claude-sonnet-5] - claude-opus-4-8: [claude-opus-4-7, claude-opus-4-6] - claude-sonnet-5: [claude-sonnet-4-6, claude-haiku-4-5] - claude-opus-4-7: [claude-opus-4-6] - claude-opus-4-6: [claude-sonnet-5, claude-sonnet-4-6] - claude-sonnet-4-6: [claude-sonnet-5, claude-haiku-4-5] - claude-haiku-4-5: [gpt-5.5, GLM-5.2] ``` Cycles present: | Cycle | Length | | --- | --- | | `claude-sonnet-5 → claude-sonnet-4-6 → claude-sonnet-5` | 2 | | `claude-sonnet-4-6 → claude-haiku-4-5 → GLM-5.2 → claude-sonnet-4-6` | 3 | | `claude-sonnet-5 → claude-haiku-4-5 → GLM-5.2 → claude-sonnet-5` | 3 | Strongly connected component: `{claude-sonnet-5, claude-sonnet-4-6, claude-haiku-4-5, GLM-5.2}`. Additional entry points that funnel *into* the SCC without being part of it: `claude-opus-4-8 → claude-opus-4-7 → claude-opus-4-6 → claude-sonnet-5`. In other words, **six of our Claude/GLM model groups can all reach a non-terminating fallback walk.** Arithmetic: | Quantity | Value | | --- | --- | | `num_retries` | 2 → **3 attempts** per model group | | fallback groups for the group involved | 2 | | Expected upper bound if the graph were acyclic | 3 × (1 primary + 2 fallbacks) = **9 attempts** | | **Observed** | **79,858 attempts** | | Overshoot vs. configured bound | **≈8,873×** | | Measured interval between attempts | **0.564 ms** (configured `retry_after: 2.0` s) | | `allowed_fails` / `cooldown_time` | 3 / 60.0 s — no deployment observably cooled out of the loop | Side observation, possibly a separate usability bug: one fallback target, `bedrock/claude-sonnet-4-6`, looks like a deployment / `litellm_params.model` string rather than a model-group name. If that silently never resolves, a clear startup warning would help — as would rejecting (or at least warning about) a cyclic fallback graph at config-load time. ### 5.11 Secondary amplifiers — per-request side effects also ran ~80,000 times Because each retry re-enters the full call wrapper (`utils.py::wrapper_async` appears in every iteration of the traceback), the per-request side effects were multiplied by the loop as well. Flagging these as **mechanism inference** — they follow from our config plus the traceback frames, and maintainers are better placed to confirm which of them actually fire per attempt: | Setting | Value | Consequence at ~80,000 attempts | | --- | --- | --- | | `failure_callback` | `[langfuse]` | ~80,000 Langfuse failure events, each carrying the full request payload. We have separately had a single oversized Langfuse report block this event loop, so this path is known-sensitive in our deployment. | | `cache` / `cache_params` | `true`, redis, `supported_call_types: [acompletion, completion]` | a cache lookup per attempt → ~80,000 Redis round-trips issued *from the very loop that was starving*. This is plausibly the direct source of the `redis.exceptions.TimeoutError` in §5.6, and of the failure of `cooldown_time` to engage. | | `store_prompts_in_spend_logs` / `store_audit_logs` | `true` / `true` | error + spend rows per attempt, **including prompts**, against `database_connection_pool_limit: 10` — consistent with the single readiness `503` at 15:18:21 in §5.8. | | `callbacks` | `[..., prometheus]` | metric updates per attempt. | The general point: **an unbounded retry loop does not just burn CPU — it multiplies every observability and persistence side effect the operator has configured**, and several of those write to the exact dependencies (Redis, PostgreSQL) whose health the proxy reports on. ## Minimal reproduction Any model group backed by Bedrock Converse. The essential ingredient is an assistant message whose `tool_calls[].function.arguments` is a **truncated** JSON string. ```bash curl -sS http://<litellm-proxy>:4000/v1/chat/completions \ -H 'Authorization: Bearer sk-<key>' \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{ "model": "<any bedrock converse model group>", "stream": true, "messages": [ { "role": "user", "content": "rename that note" }, { "role": "assistant", "content": null, "tool_calls": [ { "id": "tooluse_MAh2QLVjBRkvi5QJkLQ08V", "type": "function", "function": { "name": "replace_note_content", "arguments": "{\"note_id\": \"999af35c-4061-4ece-8581-7d43fc988ba4\", \"title\": \"WG-example\"" } } ] }, { "role": "tool", "tool_call_id": "tooluse_MAh2QLVjBRkvi5QJkLQ08V", "content": "ok" } ] }' ``` Note the missing `}` at the end of the `arguments` string — that is the whole payload. **Observed:** `APIConnectionError`, then the router retries the transformation. With `num_retries: 2` alone you get ~9 attempts and a few hundred log lines. With a **cyclic** `fallbacks` graph the walk never terminates — in our case ~80,000 attempts, tens of thousands of log lines per second, and a starved event loop. **Expected:** HTTP `400` with a message identifying the offending message index and `tool_call_id`, no retry, one log line. To reproduce the full replica takedown, add a cycle to `fallbacks` — two lines is enough: ```yaml router_settings: num_retries: 2 fallbacks: - model-a: [model-b] - model-b: [model-a] # ← cycle; both groups must be Bedrock Converse ``` Then send the request above at `model-a` and watch log lines per second and `/health/liveliness` latency while it is in flight. Note that neither `retry_after` nor `allowed_fails`/`cooldown_time` stops it. ## Expected behaviour 1. Invalid `tool_calls[].function.arguments` is a **client input error** → `BadRequestError` / HTTP 400, **not** `APIConnectionError`. 2. Errors raised during request transformation (before any network I/O) must be **non-retryable** and must not enter the fallback chain. 3. A fallback walk must never revisit a model group it has already attempted for the same request, and a cyclic `fallbacks` graph should be rejected or warned about at config-load time. 4. Configured backoff (`retry_after`) should apply to every retryable class, so that a zero-latency failure cannot spin at CPU speed. 5. The error should be logged **once per request**, not once per retry attempt, and the log line must not contain the full message history at ERROR level. 6. Per-request side effects (`failure_callback`, cache lookups, spend/audit log writes) should fire once per request, not once per attempt. 7. Log format placeholders must actually be interpolated. ## Suggested fix **a) Raise a non-retryable, typed exception in the transformation layer** — `factory.py::_convert_to_bedrock_tool_call_invoke`, around line 3731: ```python except Exception as e: raise litellm.BadRequestError( # instead of: raise Exception(...) message=( f"Invalid tool_calls[{idx}].function.arguments: not valid JSON. " f"tool_call_id={tool_call.get('id')!r}, error={e}" ), model=model, llm_provider="bedrock", ) ``` This alone fixes most of the problem, because `BadRequestError` (400) is already excluded from the router's retry set — Defect 2 stops being reachable via this path. **b) Do not sweep bare transformation exceptions into `APIConnectionError`** — in `exception_mapping_utils.py::exception_type` (lines ~2482/2505), the "unknown exception → `APIConnectionError`" catch-all is what makes any future transformation bug retryable in the same way. Consider a distinct non-retryable class for errors raised before the HTTP request is issued. **c) Track visited model groups in the fallback walk** — this is the fix that would have prevented the outage even without (a) and (b). Carry a `visited: set[str]` through `async_function_with_fallbacks` and skip (or terminate on) any model group already attempted for this request. Additionally, validate the `fallbacks` graph when config is loaded and refuse/warn on cycles — the Admin UI currently accepts a cyclic graph silently, and each individual entry looks locally reasonable, so this is very easy to create by accident. **d) Guard the router against zero-latency failure loops** — even with (a)–(c), a deterministic pre-network failure should be structurally incapable of becoming a busy loop. Suggestions: enforce a minimum backoff floor (even a few ms) per retry and apply the configured `retry_after` to all retryable classes, not only rate limits; add a per-request wall-clock budget in addition to the retry count; break the loop when N consecutive attempts fail with an identical exception type *and* message hash. Also consider that cooldown state which lives in Redis cannot act as a circuit breaker when the loop being broken is what is starving the Redis client — a purely in-process failure counter would be more robust for this case. **e) Bound the error-path log volume and per-attempt side effects** — truncate the request/tool-call repr in exception messages (e.g. first 512 chars), demote the full repr to `verbose_logger.debug`, keep a short one-line summary at ERROR, and log the traceback only on the first attempt of a request rather than on every retry. The same applies to `failure_callback`, cache lookups and spend/audit-log writes (§5.11): firing them per *attempt* rather than per *request* multiplies the blast radius into Redis and PostgreSQL. **f) Fix the format string** so `Unable to convert openai tool calls={} to bedrock tool calls. Received error={}` actually interpolates its arguments. **g) Optionally, be lenient like `split_concatenated_json_objects` already is** — that helper exists because models emit malformed tool arguments in practice. Extending it to attempt recovery of *truncated* JSON (or to surface a clear 400) would close the original trigger. Leniency is optional; **non-retryability is not**. ## Workaround we deployed Since we cannot patch the image, we added a validation gate in a `CustomLogger.async_pre_call_hook`, which runs **before** the router and can therefore reject the request with a real 400 instead of letting it into the retry loop: ```python import json for i, msg in enumerate(data.get("messages") or []): if not isinstance(msg, dict): continue for tc in (msg.get("tool_calls") or []): args = ((tc or {}).get("function") or {}).get("arguments") if not isinstance(args, str) or not args.strip(): continue try: json.loads(args) except (ValueError, TypeError): raise HTTPException( status_code=400, detail={ "error": "malformed_tool_call_arguments", "message": "tool_calls[].function.arguments is not valid JSON " "(truncated tool call in message history)", "message_index": i, "tool_call_id": (tc or {}).get("id"), }, ) ``` For other operators hitting this before a fix lands, the mitigations that actually helped, in order of effect: (1) the pre-call validation hook above; (2) **break the cycles in `fallbacks`** — check your graph for strongly connected components; ours had a 4-node one and `num_retries: 2` was already as low as it usefully goes; (3) raise the log level of the router logger to `CRITICAL` in an emergency to stop the flood; (4) switch the liveness probe to `tcpSocket` (or raise `failureThreshold` a lot) so a temporarily starved-but-recovering replica is not killed; (5) set kubelet `containerLogMaxSize` / `containerLogMaxFiles` so a flood cannot fill the node disk. ## Questions for maintainers The configuration is included above (§Environment and §5.10), so the "is this just a huge `num_retries`?" question is settled: it is not — `num_retries: 2` bounds the work at ~9 attempts and we observed 79,858. What I cannot determine from outside the codebase: 1. **Is the fallback walk cycle-guarded at all?** If `async_function_with_fallbacks` re-enters itself for a fallback group that has its own `fallbacks` entry, a cyclic graph is unbounded by construction. Our data is consistent with that; please confirm. 2. **Should `retry_after: 2.0` have applied here?** Measured 0.564 ms between attempts. If backoff is deliberately limited to rate-limit errors, then any zero-latency retryable error can spin at CPU speed, which seems worth changing independently of this bug. 3. **Why did `allowed_fails: 3` / `cooldown_time: 60.0` not cool the deployments out of the loop?** Is cooldown state written to Redis on the request path — and if so, is it expected to fail open when Redis times out? 4. **Do `failure_callback`, cache lookups and spend/audit-log writes fire per attempt or per request?** (§5.11) If per attempt, the loop also generated ~80,000 Langfuse events and ~80,000 Redis and PostgreSQL operations, which changes the recommended mitigation. 5. **Is a cyclic `fallbacks` graph considered invalid configuration?** If so, validation at config-load time would turn a production outage into a startup error. If not, cycle-tracking during the walk becomes mandatory. Happy to provide on request: the first N lines of a rotated log file at full verbosity, the complete `kubectl describe pod`, the raw `journalctl` extracts, `sar` output for other windows, further Redis/PostgreSQL statistics, or a `grep -c` across the other five replicas to confirm blast radius. ## Checklist - [x] Reproduced on the latest version we run (v1.93.0) - [x] Searched existing issues for `_convert_to_bedrock_tool_call_invoke`, `split_concatenated_json_objects`, `Unable to convert openai tool calls` - [x] Included the full traceback with file/line references - [x] Included a minimal reproduction request body - [x] Included the full `router_settings` / `litellm_settings` / `general_settings` (secrets removed) - [x] Ruled out OOM, CPU throttling, node resource pressure, conntrack exhaustion, Redis, PostgreSQL, and network as causes ### Steps to Reproduce 1. 2. 3. ### Relevant log output ```shell ``` ### What part of LiteLLM is this about? Other ### What LiteLLM version are you on ? v1.93.0 ### Twitter / LinkedIn details _No response_

signals.title: Anthropic /v1/messages bridge for Responses-API models drops cache accounting (cache_read_input_tokens always 0)
signals.text: ## What happens When the Anthropic `/v1/messages` endpoint is served by a model whose upstream is the **OpenAI Responses API** (e.g. `openai/gpt-5.x` reasoning models), the returned Anthropic-format `usage` never contains `cache_read_input_tokens`, even when the upstream cache hit covers ~100% of the prompt. Clients consuming the Anthropic shape (e.g. the Claude Agent SDK / Claude Code as a client of the proxy) therefore see zero caching and compute wildly overstated costs, while OpenAI is in fact caching and discounting upstream. Verified on `v1.94.0`; the same code is present on `main` as of 2026-08-06. ## Repro 1. Proxy config routes `gpt-5.6-luna` (any Responses-API model) to `openai/gpt-5.6-luna`. 2. Send the same `/v1/messages` request twice (system prompt >1024 tokens, identical prefix): ``` call 1 usage: {"input_tokens": 25616, "output_tokens": 5} call 2 usage: {"input_tokens": 25616, "output_tokens": 5} <-- no cache fields, ever ``` 3. Same prompt via the proxy's OpenAI-format `/v1/chat/completions` shows the upstream cache working: ``` call 2: prompt_tokens=25616 cached_tokens=25613 ``` ## Where it's lost `litellm/llms/anthropic/experimental_pass_through/responses_adapters/`: **`streaming_iterator.py`** — the lookup fetches the details objects into the wrong variables, then unconditionally overwrites both with Anthropic-named attributes that don't exist on a Responses usage object, so both counts are always 0: ```python cache_creation_tokens = getattr(usage, "input_tokens_details", None) # type: ignore[assignment] cache_read_tokens = getattr(usage, "output_tokens_details", None) # type: ignore[assignment] # Prefer direct cache fields if present cache_creation_tokens = int(getattr(usage, "cache_creation_input_tokens", 0) or 0) # always 0 cache_read_tokens = int(getattr(usage, "cache_read_input_tokens", 0) or 0) # always 0 ``` **`transformation.py`** (non-streaming) — builds `AnthropicUsage(input_tokens=..., output_tokens=...)` and never maps cache fields at all. ## Expected OpenAI Responses usage reports cached prompt tokens at `usage.input_tokens_details.cached_tokens`, *included* in `input_tokens`. Anthropic usage reports cache reads separately and *excludes* them from `input_tokens`. The bridge should split accordingly: ```python _itd = getattr(usage, "input_tokens_details", None) cache_read_tokens = int(getattr(_itd, "cached_tokens", 0) or 0) input_tokens = max(0, int(input_tokens) - cache_read_tokens) # ... emit cache_read_input_tokens when nonzero ``` With that change (both paths), the same repro returns: ``` call 2 usage: {"input_tokens": 3, "output_tokens": 5, "cache_read_input_tokens": 25613} ``` and a Claude Agent SDK session through the proxy reports `cacheReadInputTokens` correctly on its result records. Happy to open a PR with the above if useful.

signals.title: [Bug]: MCP auto-execute (require_approval "never") hijacks client-side tool_use from agentic clients like Claude Code, breaking all non-MCP tools with "Error executing tool"
signals.text: ## What happened? A model configured with an MCP tool reference using `require_approval: "never"` (so the proxy auto-executes it server-side) is deployed behind an agentic client that sends its own tools in the same request, such as Claude Code sending Read/Bash/Edit. The auto-execute loop takes over the entire tool_use turn and tries to execute every tool_use block the model emits, including the client's own non-MCP tools. Those tools are not in the MCP server map, so the proxy raises a KeyError that gets swallowed into `Error executing tool: '<tool_name>'` and fed back to the model. The model retries, fails again, and eventually gives up. From the client's perspective all of its native tools (Read, Bash, etc.) are broken for any request routed to that model What I expected: when `require_approval: "never"` is set, the proxy should auto-execute only the MCP tools it injected. A tool_use whose name does not resolve to a known MCP server should be passed through to the client unchanged so the client can execute it locally, the way a normal tool_use turn works when no MCP tool is present ## User Flow Before a fix 1. A user creates a virtual key and a team in the LiteLLM proxy UI, then registers an HTTP MCP server (say `image_understand`) and grants the team access to it 2. The user attaches the MCP tool to a model via the model's LiteLLM Params, e.g. `{"tools": [{"type": "mcp", "server_url": "litellm_proxy/mcp/image_understand", "require_approval": "never"}]}` 3. The user points an agentic client (Claude Code) at `POST /v1/messages` on the proxy, using that model and that virtual key. The client sends its own tools (Read, Bash, Edit, ...) alongside whatever the proxy injects 4. The model decides to call Read on a local file. The proxy's auto-execute loop intercepts that tool_use, fails with `Error executing tool: 'Read'`, and returns the error text to the model instead of handing the tool_use back to the client 5. The model retries with Bash, gets `Error executing tool: 'Bash'`, and eventually stops with a message saying the tools are unavailable. The user sees tool call failures and the client's native tooling is dead for that model After a fix 1. Same setup as above: MCP server registered, team granted access, MCP tool attached to the model with `require_approval: "never"` 2. The user points Claude Code at `POST /v1/messages` with that model and key, sending its own tools 3. The model calls Read on a local file. The proxy recognizes Read is not one of its MCP tools, returns the tool_use block to the client in the response, and lets the client execute it locally 4. When the model calls the injected MCP tool (`image_understand`), the proxy auto-executes it server-side as before and feeds the result back 5. Both the client's native tools and the injected MCP tool work in the same turn ## Proof the bug occurs I verified the root cause by reading the current main branch (v1.98.0-dev.2). I was not able to capture a full Claude Code trace against my own proxy in time for this report, so the proof below is the code path plus the user-visible symptom. I can add a full end-to-end curl reproduction if the maintainers want one Config / setup: a model with an MCP tool attached via LiteLLM Params ```json {"tools": [{"type": "mcp", "server_url": "litellm_proxy/mcp/image_understand", "require_approval": "never"}]} ``` Version or commit: v1.98.0-dev.2 on main Commands and their full output The auto-execute loop in `litellm/llms/anthropic/experimental_pass_through/messages/mcp_handler.py` extracts every tool_use block without checking whether it belongs to an MCP server ``` # line 38-40 def _extract_tool_use_blocks(response): return tuple(block for block in _get_response_content(response) if block.get("type") == "tool_use") # line 139-158 (abridged) for _ in range(MAX_MCP_TOOL_USE_ITERATIONS): if _get_stop_reason(response) != "tool_use": break tool_use_blocks = _extract_tool_use_blocks(response) if not tool_use_blocks: break tool_results = await LiteLLM_Proxy_MCP_Handler._execute_tool_calls( tool_server_map=tool_server_map, tool_calls=list(tool_use_blocks), ... ) ``` `tool_server_map` is built only from the injected MCP tools (in `_process_mcp_tools_without_openai_transform`). When `_execute_tool_calls` looks up a client-side tool name that is not in that map, it throws KeyError ``` # litellm/responses/mcp/litellm_proxy_mcp_handler.py line 675 server_name = tool_server_map[tool_name] ``` That KeyError is caught by the broad except at line 891-905 and turned into the user-visible error string ``` # line 891-905 (abridged) except Exception as e: ... tool_results.append({ "tool_call_id": tool_call_id, "result": f"Error executing tool: {e}", "name": tool_name, }) ``` So a model emitting `tool_use` for `Read` produces `Error executing tool: 'Read'`, which matches what I observed in the proxy spend logs and what Claude Code surfaced as "tool call failed" The symptom from the agentic client side (Claude Code talking to the proxy over `/v1/messages`): the model attempts Read on a file that exists, gets `Error executing tool: 'Read'` back, tries Bash, gets `Error executing tool: 'Bash'`, then tells the user it cannot read files or run commands. A plain curl client that sends no tools of its own works perfectly against the same model, because then every tool_use resolves to an MCP tool. This is why the bug is specific to agentic clients that bring their own tools ## What part of LiteLLM is this about? Proxy ## What LiteLLM version are you on ? v1.98.0-dev.2 ## Twitter / LinkedIn details _No response_

signals.title: [Bug]: PUT /v1/mcp/server silently nulls authorization_url, token_url, oauth2_flow when delegate_auth_to_upstream=true
signals.text: ### What happened? When an MCP server is configured with `auth_type: oauth2`, `oauth2_flow: authorization_code`, and `delegate_auth_to_upstream: true`, any subsequent update via `PUT /v1/mcp/server` silently discards `authorization_url`, `token_url`, and `oauth2_flow` — even when those exact fields are explicitly present with non-null values in the request body. The response (and the persisted record, confirmed via a follow-up `GET /v1/mcp/server`) always comes back with these three fields set to `null`. This breaks the Admin UI's own "Authorize & Fetch Token" convenience button (used to fetch a test token for a server's Tools tab), since that feature depends on `authorization_url`/`token_url` being present. It fails with: \`\`\` {"detail":"MCP server authorization url is not configured. OAuth endpoint discovery against the configured server url did not resolve it; the url may be misconfigured. Check the proxy logs for 'MCP OAuth' warnings from server load, verify the server url, or set Authorization URL and Token URL manually, or set Issuer to discover them from the identity provider (RFC 8414)."} \`\`\` Setting `issuer` instead (for RFC 8414 discovery) does not help either — discovery does not appear to run on-demand, and `authorization_url`/`token_url` remain `null` regardless. Importantly, this only affects the UI test button. The actual delegated/passthrough OAuth flow works correctly for real traffic: a client that authenticates against the upstream IdP directly and passes its own bearer token via `x-mcp-<server_name>-authorization`, alongside a valid LiteLLM virtual key in `Authorization`, successfully reaches the upstream MCP server and receives a real tool list. So the runtime behavior of `delegate_auth_to_upstream` is sound — only the persisted config for `authorization_url`/`token_url`/`oauth2_flow` is being wiped on save. ### Steps to reproduce 1. Create/register an MCP server with `auth_type: oauth2`, `oauth2_flow: authorization_code`, `authorization_url`, `token_url`, and `delegate_auth_to_upstream: true`. 2. Send a `PUT /v1/mcp/server` with the full server object, explicitly including `authorization_url`, `token_url`, and `oauth2_flow: "authorization_code"` (and `issuer` cleared to `""`): \`\`\`bash curl -X PUT 'https://your-litellm-proxy.example.com/v1/mcp/server' \ -H 'authorization: Bearer <admin-key>' \ -H 'content-type: application/json' \ --data-raw '{ "server_id": "<server_id>", "server_name": "example_mcp_server", "url": "https://your-mcp-server.example.com/mcp", "transport": "http", "auth_type": "oauth2", "oauth2_flow": "authorization_code", "issuer": "", "authorization_url": "https://your-idp.example.com/realms/your-realm/protocol/openid-connect/auth", "token_url": "https://your-idp.example.com/realms/your-realm/protocol/openid-connect/token", "delegate_auth_to_upstream": true, "oauth_passthrough": false, "dcr_bridge": false }' \`\`\` 3. Inspect the response, or immediately follow up with `GET /v1/mcp/server` and find the same `server_id`. ### Expected behavior `authorization_url` and `token_url` should be persisted exactly as submitted, and `oauth2_flow` should remain `"authorization_code"`. ### Actual behavior The response (and subsequent GET) shows: \`\`\`json { "issuer": "", "authorization_url": null, "token_url": null, "oauth2_flow": null, "delegate_auth_to_upstream": true } \`\`\` All three fields are nulled despite being explicitly sent as non-null in the request. ### Relevant log output N/A on our end — we don't have access to the proxy's server-side logs in this deployment, only client-observable request/response pairs (above). ### Are you a ML Ops Team? No ### What LiteLLM version are you on? v1.97.0 ### Twitter / LinkedIn details _No response_

signals.title: [Bug]: provider_budget_config reports budget_reset_at ~57 years in the future without Redis
signals.text: ### What happened? With `provider_budget_config` and **no Redis configured**, `GET /provider/budgets` reports a `budget_reset_at` roughly 57 years in the future, so a monthly budget effectively never resets. Config: ```yaml router_settings: provider_budget_config: openrouter: budget_limit: 5 time_period: 30d ``` Response: ```json {"providers":{"openrouter":{"budget_limit":5.0,"time_period":"30d", "spend":4.8888e-06,"budget_reset_at":"2083-05-04T16:04:00.635943+00:00"}}} ``` Same result with `time_period: 1mo` (`2083-05-05T15:39:32`), so it is not specific to the period format. Today's date when this was captured: 2026-08-18. ### Root cause `async_get_ttl` means different things in the two cache backends, and `_get_current_provider_budget_reset_at` assumes the Redis meaning: - `RedisCache.async_get_ttl()` returns **remaining seconds** (Redis `TTL`). - `InMemoryCache.async_get_ttl()` returns `self.ttl_dict.get(key)` — and `ttl_dict` stores an **absolute expiry timestamp**: `self.ttl_dict[key] = time.time() + float(kwargs["ttl"])` (`litellm/caching/in_memory_cache.py`). `litellm/router_strategy/budget_limiter.py`: ```python if self.dual_cache.redis_cache: ttl_seconds = await self.dual_cache.redis_cache.async_get_ttl(spend_key) else: ttl_seconds = await self.dual_cache.async_get_ttl(spend_key) if ttl_seconds is None: return None return (datetime.now(timezone.utc) + timedelta(seconds=ttl_seconds)).isoformat() ``` Without Redis, `ttl_seconds` is an absolute unix timestamp (~1.79e9), so the result is `now + ~56.7 years` — which matches the observed 2083. The budget limit itself works; only the reported reset time (and therefore the reset window for in-memory deployments) is wrong. ### Suggested fix Either make `InMemoryCache.async_get_ttl` return remaining seconds like the Redis backend does, or convert at the call site: ```python ttl_seconds = await self.dual_cache.async_get_ttl(spend_key) ttl_seconds = ttl_seconds - time.time() # in-memory stores absolute expiry ``` The first option is preferable — `async_get_ttl` returning different units per backend is a trap for any other caller. ### Relevant log output ``` LiteLLM.LoggingError: [Non-Blocking] Exception occurred while success logging File ".../litellm/router_strategy/budget_limiter.py", line 412, in async_log_success_event raise ValueError("custom_llm_provider is required") ValueError: custom_llm_provider is required ``` Separate but related observation while testing the same feature: every request through a `pass_through_endpoints` route raises the above in `budget_limiter.async_log_success_event`, so pass-through traffic is not counted toward provider budgets at all. Happy to file that separately if useful. ### Are you a ML Ops Team? No ### What LiteLLM version are you on? v1.97.0 ### Twitter / LinkedIn details _No response_

signals.title: Claude Code Max subscription: all proxied requests return 429 rate_limit_error while direct requests succeed
signals.text: ### What happened Following the [Using Claude Code Max Subscription](https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/tutorials/claude_code_max_subscription) tutorial, every request routed through LiteLLM is rejected by Anthropic with `429 rate_limit_error`, while identical requests sent directly to `api.anthropic.com` from the same machine, same account, minutes apart, succeed normally. Auth itself works — the OAuth token is forwarded and accepted. The failure is specifically a rate limit on the first request. ### Config ```yaml model_list: - model_name: "*" litellm_params: model: "anthropic/*" api_key: os.environ/ANTHROPIC_API_KEY # placeholder; OAuth is forwarded general_settings: forward_client_headers_to_llm_api: true master_key: os.environ/LITELLM_MASTER_KEY database_url: os.environ/DATABASE_URL ``` Client: ``` ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://localhost:4000 ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_HEADERS="x-litellm-api-key: Bearer sk-..." ``` ### Error ``` litellm.llms.base_llm.chat.transformation.BaseLLMException: {"type":"error","error":{"type":"rate_limit_error","message":"Error"},"request_id":"req_011CeAopz1M8JRveuCG44Dyt"} INFO: "POST /v1/messages?beta=true HTTP/1.1" 429 Too Many Requests ``` ### What I ruled out **Not an account usage limit.** With the proxied session returning 429, launching Claude Code directly (`ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=https://api.anthropic.com`) and sending a message returned a normal response. Same account, same machine, minutes apart. **Not request transformation.** Reproduced identically two ways: 1. The provider path above (`anthropic_response()` → parses and re-serializes). 2. A raw relay that does not reinterpret the request: ```yaml pass_through_endpoints: - path: "/raw/v1/messages" target: "https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages" forward_headers: true ``` Both return `429 rate_limit_error`. **Not stripped client headers.** I pointed the `pass_through_endpoint` target at a local echo server to inspect what actually reaches upstream. All client-identity headers forward intact: ``` PATH /v1/messages?beta=true authorization: Bearer sk-... anthropic-version: 2023-06-01 anthropic-beta: oauth-2025-04-20,claude-code-20250219 user-agent: claude-cli/2.1.231 (external, cli) x-app: cli x-stainless-lang: js x-stainless-package-version: 0.60.0 x-stainless-runtime: node ``` One difference from a direct request: LiteLLM also forwards `x-litellm-api-key` upstream, which the Anthropic API would not otherwise receive. I have not been able to test whether stripping it changes anything. ### Secondary finding: `/anthropic` passthrough ignores `forward_client_headers_to_llm_api` Independent of the above, the built-in `/anthropic` passthrough route does not forward the client's OAuth `Authorization` header — it substitutes the configured `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` as `x-api-key`, even with `forward_client_headers_to_llm_api: true` set. Probing with a deliberately invalid token distinguishes the two paths cleanly: | Route | Response to invalid token | | --- | --- | | `/v1/messages` (provider) | `"OAuth access token is invalid."` | | `/anthropic/v1/messages` | `"API key is invalid."` | | `/raw/v1/messages` (pass_through, `forward_headers: true`) | `"OAuth access token is invalid."` | So the `/anthropic` route is unusable for Max-subscription auth as documented. The explicit `pass_through_endpoints` form works correctly. ### Environment - `ghcr.io/berriai/litellm:main-stable`, pulled 2026-08-18 - Postgres 16 (docker compose), DB connected, `/health/readiness` healthy - Claude Code 2.1.231 - macOS (Darwin 25.5.0), Apple Silicon - Docker 29.5.3 ### Question Is routing Claude Code Max subscription traffic through LiteLLM still expected to work? If the 429 is Anthropic distinguishing proxied subscription traffic below the HTTP layer, that would make the tutorial unachievable as written, and it would be worth saying so in the docs. Happy to run further diagnostics.

signals.title: [Bug]: Responses API `reasoning: {"summary": ...}` crashes ollama_chat with `TypeError: unhashable type: 'dict'`
signals.text: ## What happened? Calling `/v1/responses` against an `ollama_chat/*` model with a `reasoning` object that contains a `summary` key fails with `litellm.APIConnectionError: unhashable type: 'dict'`. This makes **Codex CLI (`wire_api = "responses"`) unusable against a LiteLLM proxy backed by Ollama** — Codex sends `reasoning: {"summary": "auto"}` on every request, so every call fails and the client falls into a reconnect loop (`ERROR: Reconnecting... 1/5 … 5/5`). ## Root cause Two pieces of code disagree about the type of `reasoning_effort`. **1. The Responses→Chat bridge deliberately keeps the whole dict when `summary` is present** (`litellm/responses/litellm_completion_transformation/transformation.py`, ~L259-274): ```python if isinstance(reasoning_param, dict): # reasoning can be {"effort": "low|medium|high", "summary": "detailed"} # Keep the full dict when summary is set so the responses API bridge can # forward it; otherwise use the effort string for chat completion (e.g. Gemini). if "summary" in reasoning_param: reasoning_effort = reasoning_param # <-- dict elif "effort" in reasoning_param: reasoning_effort = reasoning_param.get("effort") # <-- str ``` **2. `OllamaChatConfig.map_openai_params` assumes it is always a string** (`litellm/llms/ollama/chat/transformation.py`, ~L172-176): ```python if param == "reasoning_effort" and value is not None: if model.startswith("gpt-oss"): optional_params["think"] = value else: optional_params["think"] = value in {"low", "medium", "high"} # <-- set membership ``` `value in {...}` hashes `value`. When `value` is the preserved dict, this raises `TypeError: unhashable type: 'dict'`. Note this is **not** the same as #15059 / PR #15465 (which corrected *which* `think` value is produced for a valid effort string). Those touch the same lines but assume `value` is a string; this report is about `value` being a `dict` at all. PR #15465's mapping would hit the identical crash. ## Reproduction Minimal matrix against an `ollama_chat/*` model. Only the presence of `summary` matters — `tools`, `stream`, `store`, `include`, and `text` are all irrelevant. | Request body (`/v1/responses`) | Result | |---|---| | `{"model": M, "input": "say OK"}` | OK | | `{"model": M, "input": "say OK", "reasoning": {"effort": "medium"}}` | OK | | `{"model": M, "input": "say OK", "reasoning": {"summary": "auto"}}` | **`unhashable type: 'dict'`** | | `{"model": M, "input": "say OK", "reasoning": {"effort": "medium", "summary": "auto"}}` | **`unhashable type: 'dict'`** | ```bash curl -s -X POST http://<proxy>/v1/responses \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"model":"my-ollama-alias","input":"say OK","reasoning":{"summary":"auto"}}' ``` `config.yaml`: ```yaml model_list: - model_name: my-ollama-alias litellm_params: model: ollama_chat/<any-model> api_base: http://127.0.0.1:11434 ``` ## Relevant log output ``` litellm.proxy.proxy_server._handle_llm_api_exception(): Exception occured - litellm.APIConnectionError: unhashable type: 'dict' Traceback (most recent call last): File "/app/.venv/lib/python3.13/site-packages/litellm/main.py", line 5314, in completion optional_params = get_optional_params(**optional_param_args, **non_default_params) File "/app/.venv/lib/python3.13/site-packages/litellm/utils.py", line 4146, in get_optional_params optional_params = litellm.OllamaChatConfig().map_openai_params( File "/app/.venv/lib/python3.13/site-packages/litellm/llms/ollama/chat/transformation.py", line 176, in map_openai_params optional_params["think"] = value in {"low", "medium", "high"} ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ TypeError: unhashable type: 'dict' ``` ## Suggested fix Guard the dict case in `OllamaChatConfig.map_openai_params` — pull `effort` out when a dict arrives, and treat a summary-only object as "no explicit effort": ```python if param == "reasoning_effort" and value is not None: if isinstance(value, dict): value = value.get("effort") if value is None: pass elif model.startswith("gpt-oss"): optional_params["think"] = value else: optional_params["think"] = value in {"low", "medium", "high"} ``` Other providers that read `reasoning_effort` off the Responses bridge likely need the same guard, since the bridge can hand any of them a dict. ## Workaround Drop the parameter before it reaches the mapper, per model: ```yaml - model_name: my-ollama-alias litellm_params: model: ollama_chat/<any-model> api_base: http://127.0.0.1:11434 additional_drop_params: ["reasoning_effort"] ``` This runs before `map_openai_params`, so the crash site is never reached. Downside: callers lose `reasoning_effort` entirely for that alias (thinking reverts to the model default, and for Qwen3 the thinking text then leaks into `content` — we pair it with `think: false`). ## Are you a ML Ops Team? No. ## What LiteLLM version are you on? `ghcr.io/berriai/litellm:main-stable` (image `468c25f35f3e`, pulled 2026-08-19). Both code paths quoted above are unchanged on `main` at time of filing. Backend: Ollama 0.32.14, model `Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF:UD-Q4_K_XL`. Client: Codex CLI 0.148 with `wire_api = "responses"`.
