signal.title: feat(rust): route /chat/completions through the Rust core for anthropic and bedrock
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - `rust: true` covers no `/chat/completions` deployment today - The Rust core has no chat completions route at all - The opt-in never even reached the chat completions handlers How it solves it: - New `chat_completions` route module in `litellm-core` - Anthropic Messages and Bedrock Converse provider transforms - Requests outside the covered subset fall back to Python ## User Flow Before: an operator who sets `rust: true` on a chat completions deployment gets nothing, with no way to tell 1. They add `rust: true` to a `claude-sonnet-4-5` deployment and restart the proxy 2. They send POST http://localhost:4000/v1/chat/completions with that model 3. The answer comes back correctly, and the response headers carry no `x-litellm-rust` 4. They repeat it against a `bedrock/us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6` deployment and see the same, so the flag reads as broken rather than as unsupported After: the same flag serves the request through the Rust core, and says so on the response 1. They add `rust: true` to the same two deployments and restart the proxy 2. They send POST http://localhost:4000/v1/chat/completions with the Anthropic model 3. The answer comes back with `x-litellm-rust: true` in the response headers, and the same content and token counts as the deployment without the flag 4. The Bedrock deployment behaves identically 5. They send a request carrying tools, an image, or `"stream": true`, get a correct answer with no `x-litellm-rust` header, and can tell from the header alone which requests the Rust path is serving ## Relevant issues ## Linear ticket Resolves LIT-5698 ## Pre-Submission checklist **Please complete all items before asking a LiteLLM maintainer to review your PR** - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] My PR passes all CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, format, unit tests) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [x] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review (Greptile reviews automatically once the PR is opened; only comment `@greptileai` to re-request a review after pushing changes) ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix Shared setup. The same config serves both legs, with each provider deployed twice so the only difference between an A and a B request is the flag: ```yaml title="config.yaml" model_list: - model_name: claude-rust litellm_params: model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5 api_key: os.environ/ANTHROPIC_API_KEY rust: true - model_name: claude-python litellm_params: model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5 api_key: os.environ/ANTHROPIC_API_KEY - model_name: bedrock-rust litellm_params: model: bedrock/us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6 aws_region_name: us-west-2 rust: true - model_name: bedrock-python litellm_params: model: bedrock/us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6 aws_region_name: us-west-2 general_settings: master_key: sk-lit5698 ``` Both legs run against the real Anthropic API and real AWS Bedrock, on the same machine, minutes apart. `LITELLM_RUST` is exported empty on both so only the per-model flag is in play. The system prompt is chosen so the answer itself shows whether it reached the provider. ### Before (5277dab4f2) #### anthropic, `rust: true` vs no flag 1. Start the proxy at the merge base and send the flagged deployment: ```bash curl -i -s http://localhost:4598/v1/chat/completions \ -H 'Authorization: Bearer sk-lit5698' -H 'content-type: application/json' \ -d '{"model":"claude-rust","max_tokens":32,"messages":[{"role":"system","content":"Ignore the question. Reply with exactly one word: PONG"},{"role":"user","content":"What is the capital of France?"}]}' ``` ``` HTTP/1.1 200 OK x-litellm-rust: (absent) content : 'PONG' finish_reason : stop prompt_tokens : 28 completion_tokens: 6 total: 34 ``` 2. The unflagged deployment answers identically, so the flag changed nothing: ``` HTTP/1.1 200 OK x-litellm-rust: (absent) content : 'PONG' prompt_tokens : 28 completion_tokens: 6 total: 34 ``` #### bedrock converse, `rust: true` vs no flag 1. Send the flagged Bedrock deployment: ``` HTTP/1.1 200 OK x-litellm-rust: (absent) content : 'PONG' finish_reason : stop prompt_tokens : 29 completion_tokens: 6 total: 35 ``` 2. The unflagged one is again indistinguishable: ``` HTTP/1.1 200 OK x-litellm-rust: (absent) content : 'PONG' prompt_tokens : 29 completion_tokens: 6 total: 35 ``` #### requests outside the covered subset 1. Tools, a multimodal image, and `"stream": true` all answer correctly and all carry no `x-litellm-rust` header, exactly like every other request on this leg ### After (5017c83484) #### anthropic, `rust: true` vs no flag 1. Send the flagged deployment: ```bash curl -i -s http://localhost:4598/v1/chat/completions \ -H 'Authorization: Bearer sk-lit5698' -H 'content-type: application/json' \ -d '{"model":"claude-rust","max_tokens":32,"messages":[{"role":"system","content":"Ignore the question. Reply with exactly one word: PONG"},{"role":"user","content":"What is the capital of France?"}]}' ``` ``` HTTP/1.1 200 OK x-litellm-rust: true content : 'PONG' finish_reason : stop prompt_tokens : 28 completion_tokens: 6 total: 34 ``` 2. The unflagged deployment stays on Python and returns the same content and the same token counts: ```bash curl -i -s http://localhost:4598/v1/chat/completions \ -H 'Authorization: Bearer sk-lit5698' -H 'content-type: application/json' \ -d '{"model":"claude-python","max_tokens":32,"messages":[{"role":"system","content":"Ignore the question. Reply with exactly one word: PONG"},{"role":"user","content":"What is the capital of France?"}]}' ``` ``` HTTP/1.1 200 OK x-litellm-rust: (absent) content : 'PONG' finish_reason : stop prompt_tokens : 28 completion_tokens: 6 total: 34 ``` The equal `prompt_tokens` on the two legs is the parity check: a dropped system prompt would show up as a smaller count on the Rust side, and `PONG` shows the system prompt was obeyed on both. #### bedrock converse, `rust: true` vs no flag 1. Send the flagged Bedrock deployment: ```bash curl -i -s http://localhost:4598/v1/chat/completions \ -H 'Authorization: Bearer sk-lit5698' -H 'content-type: application/json' \ -d '{"model":"bedrock-rust","max_tokens":32,"messages":[{"role":"system","content":"Ignore the question. Reply with exactly one word: PONG"},{"role":"user","content":"What is the capital of France?"}]}' ``` ``` HTTP/1.1 200 OK x-litellm-rust: true content : 'PONG' finish_reason : stop prompt_tokens : 29 completion_tokens: 6 total: 35 ``` 2. The unflagged one matches it exactly: ``` HTTP/1.1 200 OK x-litellm-rust: (absent) content : 'PONG' finish_reason : stop prompt_tokens : 29 completion_tokens: 6 total: 35 ``` 3. A multi-turn conversation on the Rust path keeps its history: ```bash curl -i -s http://localhost:4598/v1/chat/completions \ -H 'Authorization: Bearer sk-lit5698' -H 'content-type: application/json' \ -d '{"model":"claude-rust","max_tokens":32,"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"My name is Ada."},{"role":"assistant","content":"Nice to meet you, Ada."},{"role":"user","content":"What is my name? One word."}]}' ``` ``` HTTP/1.1 200 OK x-litellm-rust: true content : 'Ada' prompt_tokens : 33 completion_tokens: 4 total: 37 ``` #### requests outside the covered subset 1. Tools on a flagged Anthropic deployment fall back and still return a tool call: ```bash curl -i -s http://localhost:4598/v1/chat/completions \ -H 'Authorization: Bearer sk-lit5698' -H 'content-type: application/json' \ -d '{"model":"claude-rust","max_tokens":64,"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"What is the weather in Paris?"}],"tools":[{"type":"function","function":{"name":"get_weather","parameters":{"type":"object","properties":{"city":{"type":"string"}},"required":["city"]}}}]}' ``` ``` HTTP/1.1 200 OK x-litellm-rust: (absent) content : None finish_reason : tool_calls prompt_tokens : 553 completion_tokens: 53 total: 606 ``` 2. An image on a flagged Bedrock deployment falls back and still describes the image: ``` HTTP/1.1 200 OK x-litellm-rust: (absent) content : 'The image shows a very small, dark shape ...' finish_reason : length ``` 3. `"stream": true` on a flagged deployment falls back and still streams: ```bash curl -s -N http://localhost:4598/v1/chat/completions \ -H 'Authorization: Bearer sk-lit5698' -H 'content-type: application/json' \ -d '{"model":"claude-rust","max_tokens":32,"stream":true,"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"count to three"}]}' ``` ``` data: {"id":"chatcmpl-...","object":"chat.completion.chunk","choices":[{"index":0,"delta":{"role":"assistant","content":"1, 2, 3"}}]} data: {"id":"chatcmpl-...","object":"chat.completion.chunk","choices":[{"index":0,"delta":{},"finish_reason":"stop"}]} ``` ### Round 7: a request Python serves that `rust: true` made fail (54d00707e6) An OpenAI-shaped `{"role": "user", "content": []}` cleared the capability gate, because an empty parts list fails no per-part check. Python drops such a message and sends a valid request; the Rust path sent the empty `content` array on to the provider. Same config as above, both deployments on the real Anthropic API, `LITELLM_RUST` exported empty. ```bash curl -s -D - http://localhost:4791/v1/chat/completions \ -H 'Authorization: Bearer sk-lit5698e' -H 'content-type: application/json' \ -d '{"model":"claude-rust","max_tokens":32,"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"My name is Ada. What is my name? Answer with one word."},{"role":"assistant","content":"Your name is"},{"role":"user","content":[]}]}' ``` Before, on the previous head: ``` HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request x-litellm-rust: (absent) error : litellm.APIError: litellm rust chat completions: 400: {"type":"error","error":{"type":"invalid_request_error", "message":"messages.2: user messages must have non-empty content"}} ``` After: ``` HTTP/1.1 200 OK x-litellm-rust: (absent) content : ' Ada.' finish_reason : stop prompt_tokens : 25 completion_tokens: 5 ``` Two controls ran in the same window on both legs. The unflagged `claude-python` deployment answered that identical body with `' Ada.'` at 25 and 5 tokens on both legs, which is what the flagged deployment now matches exactly. A plain text request on `claude-rust` returned `x-litellm-rust: true` and `'PONG'` on both legs, so the Rust path was live throughout and the fix narrows the gate rather than turning it off. ## Type 🆕 New Feature ## Caveats - Non-streaming only; streaming falls back to Python - Text conversations only; tools and images fall back - Bedrock covers the `converse` route, not `invoke` - Rust pre-call logging records the request before translation - Rust `post_call` carries the core's normalized response, not the provider's wire body - `rust` is a deployment setting, refused in a proxy request body - Follow-ups: tools LIT-5715, streaming LIT-5716 - Docs: BerriAI/litellm-docs#923, merge that after this ## Review notes Scope of the Rust path, and why it is drawn there. Acceptance is an allowlist rather than a denylist, so a parameter or message shape the core has never seen declines by construction instead of being translated wrong. `chat_completions_decline_reason` answers that question with no credential resolution and no I/O, which is what lets the caller emit its pre-call logging exactly once on whichever path is about to run. Covered today: system, user and assistant turns whose content is a string or all-text parts, plus the sampling parameters each provider maps. Everything else declines, including tool calls, tool results, images, extended thinking, `response_format`, prompt caching, and `topK` on Bedrock, which Python routes by base model through the model catalog the core cannot read. Parity is pinned rather than asserted. The shared conversation builder mirrors Python's `anthropic_messages_pt` for the surface it accepts: consecutive same-role turns merge, the final assistant turn is right-stripped, and empty text becomes the same placeholder Python substitutes. Converse diverges on both of those, so the Bedrock config declines blank text and any conversation that opens or closes on an assistant turn, which makes both divergences unreachable rather than papered over. `usage` folds cache tokens into `prompt_tokens` and reports the same `prompt_tokens_details` split Python does, so cost tracking agrees either way. The response deliberately carries no `id`, so the `chatcmpl-` id LiteLLM already minted survives. Bedrock signs with the credentials the Python handler already resolved, handed down through `optional_params`, rather than re-deriving them. Without that, an unrelated `AWS_ROLE_NAME` or `AWS_PROFILE_NAME` in the environment outranks explicit keys during classification and the two paths would sign as different principals. The Converse URL Python built is passed through untouched for the same reason, since Python encodes the model id itself. Two plumbing fixes were needed for the flag to work at all, both found on a live proxy rather than by reading. `rust` was absent from the key set `completion()` forwards into `get_litellm_params`, so the opt-in never reached the chat completions handlers and the gate was never consulted. Registering it as a litellm param elsewhere keeps it out of the provider body; this keeps it in `litellm_params`, where the handlers read it. Review round 1 found that a Rust failure re-entered the Python path after pre-call logging had already run, so callbacks fired twice for one request. The fix went at the root rather than at the symptom, because the same re-entry also re-issued the provider call and billed the customer twice for work already done. The bridge now separates the two cases: anything raised before the request goes out declines and the host serves it on Python, while a failure after it is surfaced as an `APIError` carrying the upstream status, which LiteLLM's exception mapping already understands. Since a decline is the same attempt continuing rather than a second one, the fallback no longer re-logs pre_call, so exactly one fires per request either way. Review round 2 caught the hole that fix left: a config reports the same error variants on either side of the provider call, so a response the core could not normalize (`MissingField`, or an unsupported content block) was being classed as a pre-send decline and retried. The handler now re-tags every error raised while normalizing a response the provider already answered, so the retryable set can only contain failures raised before the request went out. Round-trip tests drive a stub upstream and assert exactly that: a body missing `usage`, a body carrying a `tool_use` block, and a 429 all come back as errors the host will not retry, while a well-formed body round-trips. The route-owned `client.rs` was also flagged, and it is kept deliberately. It is part of the documented route template: `litellm-rust/ADDING_A_PROVIDER.md` and `crates/core/CLAUDE.md` both list `client.rs` as one of a route module's files, and `crates/core/src/messages/client.rs` is the reference implementation this mirrors. The core cannot reach LiteLLM's Python HTTP handler, which lives in the host; `core/CLAUDE.md` puts serving and transport concerns outside the core on purpose. It follows the workspace's Network I/O rules: one client behind a `OnceLock` rather than one per request, with both a connect and a full-request timeout, and rustls. Round 3 found the same lifecycle defect on the synchronous Anthropic path, which the earlier fix had only closed for the async one. It is closed the same way and pinned by three mutation checks, including one that the ordinary path still logs, so the suppression cannot swallow a log it was never meant to. Every invariant above is pinned by a mutation check: 31 mutants, 31 killed. Round 4 took the veria finding that the opt-in was request-controlled. `rust` is a litellm param, `route_llm_request` splats a proxy request body straight into the router, and the gate reads the merged `litellm_params`, so an authenticated caller could send `rust: true` and pick a transport and a callback surface the deployment never chose. A spy on the gate settled it rather than reading: driven with the kwarg it saw `litellm_params["rust"] is True`, and the control without it saw the key absent. The flag now sits in `_BANNED_REQUEST_BODY_PARAMS`, so it is a deployment decision again, liftable only by the same admin opt-in as the rest of that list, and covered under `extra_body` for free. The check runs in `pre_db_read_auth_checks`, so it also closes the same caller-controlled path on `/v1/messages`, where `_maybe_rust_anthropic_messages` has read this flag since before this PR: the same spy, driven through `litellm.anthropic_messages`, saw the caller's `rust=True` arrive there too. The responses-websocket route is not affected in either direction, since it builds its request body server-side and no caller field ever reached its gate. Deleting the entry fails three of the five new tests. One knock-on is worth naming rather than leaving to be found. `_config_base_for_health_check` reads the same list, and treats any banned param in a connection-test body as "this request describes its own connection", so it drops the configured credentials. A `/health/test_connection` body that echoes a Rust deployment's `litellm_params` verbatim now probes without them. No dashboard flow sends the field, and the Add Model wizard has no config base to drop from, so this reaches a hand-written caller only. Narrowing that set is the surgical fix if it ever bites; weakening the ban is not. The LIT002 count is resolved rather than argued, so `lint` is green. It counted twelve new dict literals. Ten of them the bridge JSON-encodes or logging callbacks consume as dicts, and `MappingProxyType` breaks both at runtime (`json.dumps` rejects a mappingproxy, and the response converter rewrites the dict it is handed), so those carry a `# mutable-ok` naming the reason: nine comments, since one line holds a nested literal. The last two went for real, by deleting the `rust_kwargs` bundles and passing the nine arguments by keyword instead. `**dict` unpacking is unchecked, so writing them out also drops twenty basedpyright errors across the three files. Round 5 is the same lifecycle defect once more, on the synchronous Bedrock path. Round 3 closed it for Anthropic by capturing the gate's answer and guarding the Python-path `pre_call` with it; Bedrock still called the gate inline, so nothing downstream could tell that the request had already been logged, and a synchronous call that the gate accepted and the core then declined logged twice. It is closed the same way, with the same comment explaining why the async branch does not need it. Two mutation checks, run separately: removing the guard fails the decline test, and inverting it also fails the control that an ordinary request with no opt-in still logs exactly once, so the suppression cannot swallow a log it was never meant to. Round 6 closed the second half of veria's original sentence, which the ban did not touch: the Rust path emitted no `post_call` at all. That is not conditional on who set the flag, so an operator's own `rust: true` lost it too, since `post_call` is raised inside the provider transform the core replaces. Measured rather than read: a `CustomLogger` on a Router deployment with `rust: true` and no request kwarg observed `['pre_api_call', 'success']` and no `post_api_call`, with the other two events as the positive control that the logger was wired and reachable. So `original_response` was unset on every Rust-served request, which OTel, Arize and two guardrail hooks read. The bridge now takes a `ResponseObserver` and calls it on success only, from both `chat_completions` and `achat_completions`, so the two paths cannot drift the way the pre_call suppression twice did. `response_logger` builds the observer, so the handlers share one implementation rather than each growing a closure, and hoisting it out of `completion` is also what keeps that function under the C901 ceiling. A decline never calls it, because the Python path that serves the request raises its own. Each hook site was mutated separately rather than both at once: dropping the synchronous one fails the two synchronous tests, dropping the asynchronous one fails only the asynchronous test, and the decline tests hold either way. The payload is the core's normalized response rather than the provider's wire body, which is the closest thing that crosses the bridge; the `/v1/messages` Rust route still has this gap and is out of scope here. Round 7 took the empty-content-parts finding, which is the one open bot finding that is a real defect. `unsupported_message` checked every part and therefore accepted a message with no parts at all, and Bedrock's blank-text scan skipped it for the same reason, so a request that Python serves fine came back 400 once the deployment carried the flag. The guard goes in the shared gate, so both providers get it from one place, and each provider's test file pins its own side with a positive control that a one-part text message still accepts. Removing the guard fails both tests. The other two open findings are answered rather than taken. The redundant-documentation one is partly right: the route's module header duplicated what `Unsupported`'s own doc comment in `transformation.rs` says, so that paragraph is deleted and only the entrypoint description remains, which is what `messages/mod.rs` carries for the reference route. The route-owned `client.rs` stays, and the honest version of that argument is not a claim about tunability. The two core clients hold identical values today, `MESSAGES_TIMEOUT_SECS` and `CHAT_COMPLETIONS_TIMEOUT_SECS` both 600 with both connect timeouts at 10, so folding them would be behavior-neutral right now and would collapse four constants into two. The reason not to is that `constants.rs` documents each pair as mirroring its own Python default, so one constant would then serve two parity contracts and have to be unpicked the day those defaults diverge, and `crates/core/CLAUDE.md` lists `client.rs` among a route module's six files with `src/messages` as the reference, so deleting it is a change to the documented template rather than to this route alone. The workspace already carries five independently configured production clients and they are not one shape: `ai-gateway/src/client.rs` sets no connect timeout, the OCR document fetch builds one per call with `redirect::Policy::none()`, and the log shipper sets no bounds at all. What this route copies is the one the docs point at. The shared-helper work the finding reaches for is in this PR already, since `core/src/http_utils.rs` is new and `messages/common_utils.rs` gave up 42 lines consuming it. None of that changes the last point, which is that Python's `HTTPHandler` lives in the host and is unreachable from the core crate by design. The Bedrock synchronous double `pre_call` finding was filed against `90f4bd0e6c` and fixed in `296fa843dd`, one commit later. `converse_handler.py` guards the Python-path `pre_call` with `if not serves_via_rust`, the same shape Anthropic uses. <!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY --> --- > [!NOTE] > <sup>[Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) is generating a summary for commit 90f4bd0e6c4e1b8d78cab1434cd4f850a2850d4c. Configure [here](https://www.cursor.com/dashboard/bugbot).</sup> <!-- /CURSOR_SUMMARY -->

signal.title: fix: propagate budget_duration when creating new budget in /customer/update
signal.text: ## Summary When calling `/customer/update` with `budget_duration` and `max_budget`, the `budget_duration` was not being propagated to the newly created budget. This meant the budget reset schedule was never set. This PR fixes the issue by: 1. Adding `budget_duration` field to `UpdateCustomerRequest` in `_types.py` 2. Computing `budget_reset_at` from `budget_duration` when creating a new budget in `customer_endpoints.py` 3. Also recomputing `budget_reset_at` when updating an existing budget with a new `budget_duration` Fixes #33941 --- **Note:** This is a replacement for #33982 (which was accidentally closed during a rebase attempt). The branch needs a local rebase onto latest `main` before merging due to annotation style changes (`Optional[str]` to `str | None`) that occurred in the files this PR modifies.

signal.title: fix(zai): add provider and current model catalog
signal.text: ## TLDR Fixes the Z.AI dashboard onboarding path and brings the bundled Z.AI catalog up to the current documented models. - Adds Z.AI to the Add Model provider catalog. - Lets provider search match the LiteLLM slug `zai` as well as the display name. - Adds the six current Z.AI models missing from the model cost map: `glm-5.3`, `glm-5.2`, `glm-5-turbo`, `glm-5v-turbo`, `glm-4.7-flashx`, and `glm-4.6v`. - Keeps `model_prices_and_context_window.json` and the bundled backup map in sync. The Z.AI provider uses the OpenAI-compatible base URL `https://api.z.ai/api/paas/v4`. ## User Flow Before: 1. A proxy admin opens Add Model and searches for `zai` or `z.ai`. 2. The provider dropdown returns no result, so no Z.AI credentials or model choices can be configured. After: 1. The same admin searches for `zai` or `z.ai` and selects Z.AI. 2. The form shows the API key field and default Z.AI API base. 3. The model selector includes the current Z.AI models, including GLM-5.3, GLM-5.2, GLM-5-Turbo, GLM-5V-Turbo, GLM-4.7-FlashX, and GLM-4.6V. ## Root Cause LiteLLM supported the `zai` provider in the SDK and had existing Z.AI metadata, but the dashboard provider-creation catalog omitted it. The catalog also lagged the current Z.AI model list. ## Relevant Issues Fixes #25482 Supersedes the stale unmerged implementation in #25485. The existing provider-name mapping from #26419 is retained. ## Validation - `python3 -m json.tool model_prices_and_context_window.json` - Verified the canonical and bundled backup maps are byte-identical. - Added `tests/test_litellm/test_zai_model_metadata.py`, which asserts the documented 15-model Z.AI subset and exact metadata for the six newly catalogued models. - `npm run test -- --run src/components/add_model/AddModelForm.test.tsx` passes: 13 tests. - In a local Admin UI running against the proposed bundled catalog, `GET /public/litellm_model_cost_map` exposes all six new model IDs and the Add Model selector shows all six, including search results for `zai/glm-4.7-flashx` and `zai/glm-4.6v`. ## CI Note The earlier `misc` failure in run 32214763016 is unrelated to this PR's original changes. It failed `tests/test_litellm/batches/test_batch_utils.py::test_handle_completed_vertex_batch_computes_cost_usage_and_models`, where a Vertex batch cost expectation was double the observed value. This PR did not change batch code, Vertex code, or the model cost map in that run. The new push should receive a fresh CI result. ## Pre-Submission Checklist - [x] I have added meaningful tests. - [x] My PR passes all CI/CD checks. - [x] My PR's scope is isolated to Z.AI dashboard onboarding and catalog metadata. - [x] I have received a Greptile Confidence Score of at least 4/5 before requesting maintainer review. ## Type Bug Fix ## Caveats - The focused Python test requires the full LiteLLM Python dependency set, which is unavailable in this local worktree. The JSON, bundled-map consistency, runtime API, and UI flows were verified locally; GitHub CI will run the Python test. - A full local Docker image build requires the Docker buildx plugin. ### Final Attestation - [x] The tests check the right things, including edge cases and real-world customer regressions.

signal.title: fix(ci): run the full dashboard suite when a change reaches outside src/
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - `vitest related` selects no tests for non-`src/` files - `--passWithNoTests` then turns that empty selection green - dashboard dependency bumps merge having run zero unit tests - the breakage only surfaces later, on staging's full run How it solves it: - one changed file outside `src/` now runs the full suite - `related` still covers the common `src/`-only pull request - the decision is a script, so it is testable ## User Flow Before: a maintainer bumping a dashboard dependency gets a green UI Unit Tests check that ran nothing, and finds out on staging 1. They open a pull request that changes only `ui/litellm-dashboard/package.json` and `package-lock.json` 2. The UI Unit Tests check reports success in about a minute 3. Opening the check's "Run UI unit tests (Vitest)" step shows `No test files found, exiting with code 0` 4. They merge, and the full run on the push to `litellm_internal_staging` fails on components the bumped package broke 5. Staging is now red for everyone until someone bisects the merge queue back to that bump After: the same pull request runs every dashboard test before anyone can merge it 1. They open the same pull request changing only `ui/litellm-dashboard/package.json` and `package-lock.json` 2. The UI Unit Tests check now reports `1 changed UI files reach outside src/, so related would miss their dependents; running the full suite` 3. The step runs the whole dashboard suite and fails on the pull request itself if the bump broke anything 4. They see the breakage on their own check instead of on staging 5. A pull request that only touches files under `ui/litellm-dashboard/src/` keeps the fast `related` path and its short runtime ## Relevant issues ## Linear ticket ## Pre-Submission checklist **Please complete all items before asking a LiteLLM maintainer to review your PR** - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] The handful of test files covering my change pass locally, e.g. `uv run pytest tests/test_litellm/<your_test_file>.py -v`. Leave the suites (`make test-unit-*`, `make test-unit`) to CI: it finishes in ~15 minutes where a laptop takes an hour or more - [x] My PR passes all required CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, schema.d.ts sync check, etc.) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [ ] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review (Greptile reviews automatically once the PR is opened; only comment `@greptileai` to re-request a review after pushing changes) ## Delays in PR merge? If you're seeing a delay in your PR being merged, ping the LiteLLM Team on [Slack (#pr-review)](https://join.slack.com/t/litellmossslack/shared_invite/zt-3o7nkuyfr-p_kbNJj8taRfXGgQI1~YyA). ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix The behaviour under test is a GitHub Actions step, so the runs below are live UI Unit Tests runs on this pull request, not local ones. Each side was captured by pushing a throwaway commit that gives the step a specific changed-file set, then reverting it, so Before and After see byte-identical input. Before runs the step exactly as it stands on `litellm_internal_staging` today, After runs the step as this pull request leaves it Shared setup, identical on both sides: - case 1 adds `ui/litellm-dashboard/CI_SCOPE_PROOF.md`, a file no test imports, standing in for `package-lock.json` - case 2 adds `ui/litellm-dashboard/src/ciScopeProof.ts` and its `src/ciScopeProof.test.ts` ### Before (969b461ae663e5f34a43ef9f13471fd4ef40c836 and 049a9f40976e676d3a625bddf61932ac74687a3a) #### case 1: the only dashboard change is outside src/ 1. Run https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/actions/runs/32322485020, step "Run UI unit tests (Vitest)" 2. Observed: ``` Pull request: running tests related to 1 changed UI files > litellm-dashboard@0.1.0 test > vitest related CI_SCOPE_PROOF.md --run --passWithNoTests --pool forks --poolOptions.forks.maxForks=14 RUN v3.2.6 /home/runner/work/litellm/litellm/ui/litellm-dashboard No test files found, exiting with code 0 ``` 3. The check reports success having executed 0 of the dashboard's 8539 unit tests #### case 2: every dashboard change is under src/ 1. Run https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/actions/runs/32323246162, step "Run UI unit tests (Vitest)" 2. Observed: ``` Pull request: running tests related to 2 changed UI files > vitest related src/ciScopeProof.test.ts src/ciScopeProof.ts --run --passWithNoTests --pool forks --poolOptions.forks.maxForks=14 Test Files 1 passed (1) Tests 1 passed (1) Duration 9.21s ``` ### After (def1e0394bef75144f81ef70c857e4be6d69b714 and 2036b0802f5190361b6b8ff7d8965b742f24598e) #### case 1: the only dashboard change is outside src/ 1. Run https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/actions/runs/32322033309, step "Run UI unit tests (Vitest)" 2. Observed: ``` Pull request: 1 changed UI files reach outside src/, so related would miss their dependents; running the full suite > litellm-dashboard@0.1.0 test > vitest --run --pool forks --poolOptions.forks.maxForks=14 Test Files 741 passed (741) Tests 8539 passed (8539) Duration 284.81s ``` 3. The same input that used to run nothing now runs every dashboard test before the pull request can merge #### case 2: every dashboard change is under src/ 1. Run https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/actions/runs/32323138176, step "Run UI unit tests (Vitest)" 2. Observed: ``` Pull request: running tests related to 2 changed UI files > vitest related src/ciScopeProof.test.ts src/ciScopeProof.ts --run --passWithNoTests --pool forks --poolOptions.forks.maxForks=14 Test Files 1 passed (1) Tests 1 passed (1) Duration 7.43s ``` 3. Unchanged from Before, so the fast path a normal dashboard pull request takes still costs seconds ## Type 🐛 Bug Fix 🚄 Infrastructure ## Caveats (if any) - `src/`-only pull requests keep the old blind spot for non-imported files ### Final Attestation - [x] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR

signal.title: feat(ptu): accrue flat cost for PTU deployments declared in config.yaml
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - A PTU deployment in config.yaml accrues no flat cost - The rollup only reads the database model table - Its traffic is billed per token instead How it solves it: - The rollup also reads config-declared deployments off the router - Registering one zeroes its pricing, since capacity is prepaid - Both halves apply the same rules from one module ## User Flow Before: a team on reserved capacity is billed for its tokens and never for the capacity 1. An admin declares a provisioned-throughput deployment in `config.yaml` with `team_id`, `ptu_count`, `cost_per_ptu_per_hour` and `ptu_effective_from`, then starts the proxy with `LITELLM_ENABLE_PTU_COST_ATTRIBUTION=True` 2. Someone on that team sends POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions and gets a normal answer 3. https://litellm-domain/ui/?page=logs shows that request charged at the provider's per-token rate 4. The nightly attribution job runs at 00:15 UTC and writes nothing for that deployment 5. https://litellm-domain/ui/?page=usage shows the team's token spend and no reserved-capacity cost, so the hourly charge the provider is invoicing appears nowhere After: the same team is billed for the capacity it reserved, and not again for the traffic that capacity serves 1. The admin declares the same deployment and starts the same proxy 2. Someone on that team sends the same POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions and gets the same answer 3. https://litellm-domain/ui/?page=logs shows that request at $0, because the reservation already paid for it 4. The nightly job runs and attributes the reservation to the team 5. https://litellm-domain/ui/?page=usage shows the team's reserved-capacity cost for the day, charted separately from request cost An admin who wants the deployment billed per token instead removes `ptu_count` and `cost_per_ptu_per_hour`, exactly as on the API path ## Relevant issues ## Linear ticket Resolves LIT-5809 ## Pre-Submission checklist **Please complete all items before asking a LiteLLM maintainer to review your PR** - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] My PR passes all CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, format, unit tests) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [ ] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review (Greptile reviews automatically once the PR is opened; only comment `@greptileai` to re-request a review after pushing changes) ## Delays in PR merge? If you're seeing a delay in your PR being merged, ping the LiteLLM Team on [Slack (#pr-review)](https://join.slack.com/t/litellmossslack/shared_invite/zt-3o7nkuyfr-p_kbNJj8taRfXGgQI1~YyA). ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix Real Postgres, real Gemini traffic, a proxy booted from the config below on each side, no mocks. Gemini stands in for Azure because PTU capacity cannot be provisioned here; the fields the feature reads are provider-agnostic, and what is being proven is the cost path. The only thing not exercised is the cron trigger itself, since the job has no on-demand entry point, so each side calls the same scheduled function directly against its own database. ```yaml model_list: - model_name: gpt-4o-ptu litellm_params: model: gemini/gemini-2.5-flash api_key: os.environ/GEMINI_API_KEY input_cost_per_token: 0.000005 output_cost_per_token: 0.000015 model_info: team_id: ptu-team-0001 ptu_count: 100 cost_per_ptu_per_hour: 0.02 ptu_effective_from: "2026-01-01T00:00:00Z" general_settings: master_key: sk-lit5809 ``` ```bash export LITELLM_ENABLE_PTU_COST_ATTRIBUTION=True python -m litellm.proxy.proxy_cli --config ptu.yaml --port KEY=$(curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:/key/generate -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-lit5809" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"team_id":"ptu-team-0001","models":["gpt-4o-ptu"]}' | jq -r .key) ``` ### Before (eecb226762) #### a real request through the config.yaml PTU deployment 1. Send it ```bash curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:4811/v1/chat/completions -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"model":"gpt-4o-ptu","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Say hi."}],"max_tokens":25}' ``` ``` tokens: 4 / 21 ``` 2. The deployment is priced at what the operator declared ``` router pricing: input=5e-06 output=1.5e-05 ``` #### the nightly attribution job 1. Run it for that day ``` rollup: RollupResult(day=2026-08-18, models_processed=0, rows_written=0, rows_failed=0, lapsed=()) flat-cost rows: [] ``` 2. Read the team's day back out of Postgres ``` api_key | model_group | spend | prompt_tokens | completion_tokens | ptu_flat_cost ------------------------------------------------------------------+-------------+----------+---------------+-------------------+--------------- 291e0dcf9ff6ecfbb84b5306a9cd6fb2575ca8a2fa992d859ad81593d58ba670 | gpt-4o-ptu | 0.000335 | 4 | 21 | 0 ``` The tokens are billed at 4 x 5e-06 plus 21 x 1.5e-05, and the reservation the provider is invoicing hourly is recorded nowhere ### After (286bbc97b8) #### a real request through the config.yaml PTU deployment 1. Send the same request ```bash curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:4812/v1/chat/completions -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"model":"gpt-4o-ptu","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Say hi."}],"max_tokens":25}' ``` ``` tokens: 4 / 21 ``` 2. The deployment carries no per-token rate ``` router pricing: input=0.0 output=0.0 ``` #### the nightly attribution job 1. Run it for that day ``` rollup: RollupResult(day=2026-08-18, models_processed=1, rows_written=1, rows_failed=0, lapsed=()) flat-cost rows: [('ptu-team-0001', 'gpt-4o-ptu', 48.0)] ``` 2. Read the team's day back out of Postgres ``` api_key | model_group | spend | prompt_tokens | completion_tokens | ptu_flat_cost ------------------------------------------------------------------+-------------+-------+---------------+-------------------+--------------- 8d808bffd673ab86d6f0e3a2addf8f5933ed7f26fd5a6b9d2666ed5aa52c0864 | gpt-4o-ptu | 0 | 4 | 21 | 0 __ptu_flat_cost__ | gpt-4o-ptu | 0 | 0 | 0 | 48 ``` 100 units at $0.02 an hour over a full day is $48, the same request records 4 and 21 real tokens at no per-token charge, and the deployment id is unchanged from the before run, so cooldowns, deployment budgets and existing spend rows all still key on it Re-run at the current tip, exit code checked and the log grepped for a traceback, after an earlier capture turned out to be a partially completed run ## Type 🆕 New Feature ## Changes The rollup reads the router's deployments alongside the table, keeping the ones no database row owns and dropping the per-request credential clones, which carry `original_model_id` and would otherwise bill one reservation once per distinct caller key. Registering such a deployment zeroes its pricing. The rules for what accrues and what that zeroes live in `litellm/litellm_core_utils/ptu_pricing.py`, which the write endpoints now import as well, because a deployment the rollup declines to charge and the router prices at zero would serve its traffic for free. `tiered_pricing` is emptied rather than zeroed, since its tiers outrank the rates beside them; the search context table is written zeroed because an absent one means the provider's default rather than free; and any further rate the deployment declares is zeroed alongside the standing set. The prune is bounded to the deployments a run scanned, but only for a run that priced a config-declared deployment, so a database-only proxy sweeps exactly as it does today. The nightly catch-up shares that loader, so a config-declared reservation is priced for its elapsed days too. Verified live: a reservation started five days ago writes five days at $240, one started two hundred days ago writes 91 days at $4,368, and a second run of either writes nothing further. ## QA runbook ## Caveats (if any) - A zeroed deployment wins QualityRouter's cost tiebreak where an unset rate lost it - Attribution needs every replica booted from the same config.yaml - Outside its window a PTU deployment bills nothing, matching the database path - Enabling this prices up to 91 elapsed days on the first nightly run ### Final Attestation - [x] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR ---

signal.title: fix(proxy): include litellm_call_id in LLM API exception logs
signal.text:
## TLDR Problem this solves: - Proxy error logs had no request id - Concurrent failures can't be traced to a request How it solves it: - Log `litellm_call_id` alongside the exception - Also emit it as a JSON log field ## User Flow Before: a developer running the proxy hits a provider timeout and can't tell which of their concurrent requests failed 1. Their app sends many concurrent `POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions`, each response carrying an `x-litellm-call-id` header 2. One request times out and comes back `408` with a `litellm.Timeout` message 3. They open the proxy's application logs and find an ERROR line with the exception text and traceback, a timestamp, and nothing tying it to a request 4. They cannot match that line to the `x-litellm-call-id` their app received, or to the row on `https://litellm-domain/ui/?page=logs`, so they can't tell which call failed After: the same failure logs the id the client already has, so the request is identifiable 1. Their app sends many concurrent `POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions`, each response carrying an `x-litellm-call-id` header 2. One request times out and comes back `408` with a `litellm.Timeout` message 3. The ERROR line now reads `Exception occured - litellm_call_id=<id> - litellm.Timeout: ...` and, with `JSON_LOGS=1`, carries a top level `litellm_call_id` field 4. They match that id to the `x-litellm-call-id` their app received and to the row on `https://litellm-domain/ui/?page=logs`, and investigate the exact failed request ## Relevant issues Fixes #37532 ## Linear ticket Resolves LIT-5856 ## Pre-Submission checklist **Please complete all items before asking a LiteLLM maintainer to review your PR** - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] The handful of test files covering my change pass locally, e.g. `uv run pytest tests/test_litellm/<your_test_file>.py -v`. Leave the suites (`make test-unit-*`, `make test-unit`) to CI: it finishes in ~15 minutes where a laptop takes an hour or more - [x] My PR passes all required CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, schema.d.ts sync check, etc.) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [ ] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review (Greptile reviews automatically once the PR is opened; only comment `@greptileai` to re-request a review after pushing changes) ## Delays in PR merge? If you're seeing a delay in your PR being merged, ping the LiteLLM Team on [Slack (#pr-review)](https://join.slack.com/t/litellmossslack/shared_invite/zt-3o7nkuyfr-p_kbNJj8taRfXGgQI1~YyA). ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix Shared setup, a deployment whose upstream never answers within the timeout, so every call fails the way the reporter's did. The proxy is run with `JSON_LOGS=1 LITELLM_LOG=INFO litellm --config config.yaml --port 4000` ```yaml model_list: - model_name: slow-model litellm_params: model: openai/gpt-4o api_key: fake-key api_base: http://127.0.0.1:8899 # server that accepts the request and never replies timeout: 5 litellm_settings: num_retries: 0 ``` ### Before (a6163e0146) 1. Send the request that will time out ``` $ curl -sS -i -m 30 http://localhost:4000/v1/chat/completions -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-1234" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d @body.json HTTP/1.1 408 Request Timeout x-litellm-call-id: 8e99b19e-1634-4415-affd-bf76bc2334d9 {"error":{"message":"litellm.Timeout: APITimeoutError - Request timed out. Error_str: Request timed out. - timeout value=5.0, time taken=5.3 seconds ..."}} ``` 2. Look at the ERROR line the proxy logged for it, no call id anywhere (stacktrace elided) ``` {"message": "litellm.proxy.proxy_server._handle_llm_api_exception(): Exception occured - litellm.Timeout: APITimeoutError - Request timed out. Error_str: Request timed out. - timeout value=5.0, time taken=5.3 seconds

Deployment Info: request_timeout: None
timeout: 5.0. Received Model Group=slow-model
Available Model Group Fallbacks=None", "level": "ERROR", "timestamp": "2026-08-20T01:06:18.206077", "component": "LiteLLM Proxy", "logger": "common_request_processing.py:1331", "stacktrace": "..."} ``` 3. Grep the log for the id the client received, nothing matches ``` $ grep -c 8e99b19e proxy.log 0 ``` ### After (c44e3598dd) 1. Send the same request ``` $ curl -sS -i -m 30 http://localhost:4000/v1/chat/completions -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-1234" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d @body.json HTTP/1.1 408 Request Timeout x-litellm-call-id: 64e235a8-9fec-450e-8b37-c6a6f1abfaad x-litellm-timeout: 5.0 {"error":{"message":"litellm.Timeout: APITimeoutError - Request timed out. Error_str: Request timed out. - timeout value=5.0, time taken=5.0 seconds ..."}} ``` 2. The ERROR line now names that exact call id, both in the message and as a JSON field (stacktrace elided) ``` {"message": "litellm.proxy.proxy_server._handle_llm_api_exception(): Exception occured - litellm_call_id=64e235a8-9fec-450e-8b37-c6a6f1abfaad - litellm.Timeout: APITimeoutError - Request timed out. Error_str: Request timed out. - timeout value=5.0, time taken=5.0 seconds

Deployment Info: request_timeout: None
timeout: 5.0. Received Model Group=slow-model
Available Model Group Fallbacks=None", "level": "ERROR", "timestamp": "2026-08-20T01:15:01.753171", "litellm_call_id": "64e235a8-9fec-450e-8b37-c6a6f1abfaad", "component": "LiteLLM Proxy", "logger": "common_request_processing.py:1332", "stacktrace": "..."} ``` ## Type 🐛 Bug Fix ## Caveats (if any) - The upstream here is a local never-answering server, no provider spend applies to a timeout - Only the proxy's LLM exception funnel is covered, other log lines unchanged ### Final Attestation - [x] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR Link to Devin session: https://app.devin.ai/sessions/9c16527a525743449636d1f8b6b8aad3

signal.title: feat(e2e): move record/replay to the provider edge (LIT-5745)
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - e2e replay stubbed the whole proxy, not just the providers - a replay pass proved nothing about auth, routing, cost, or spend - replay even passed with the proxy process fully stopped How it solves it: - record/replay now scopes to the proxy's provider-bound traffic only - an in-process provider edge server fronts the real providers - edge-wired tests register deployments whose api_base points at the edge - record forwards to the real provider and stores each exchange - replay answers provider calls from the bundle, zero provider spend - proxy and database stay live, so proxy regressions turn replay red - drift fails loudly with HTTP 599 instead of silently going live ## User Flow Before: a contributor replays an e2e suite and gets a green run that never touched the proxy, so it certifies nothing the proxy does 1. They start the proxy and confirm GET http://localhost:4000/health/liveliness returns "I'm alive!" 2. They record a spend test with `E2E_FIXTURE_MODE=record uv run pytest tests/e2e/quota_management/spend_tracking/ -v`; it passes against the real provider and writes a fixture bundle 3. They rerun it with `E2E_FIXTURE_MODE=replay`; it passes, but the proxy saw zero requests during the run: every response, key mint included, came from the bundle 4. They stop the proxy entirely and replay again; still green, so a replay pass says nothing about key auth, routing, cost calculation, or spend-log writes After: the same replay drives the live proxy end to end and only the provider is answered from the recording 1. They start the proxy and confirm GET http://localhost:4000/health/liveliness returns "I'm alive!" 2. They record with `E2E_FIXTURE_MODE=record uv run pytest tests/e2e/quota_management/spend_tracking/test_provider_edge_spend_e2e.py -v`; the test registers its model via POST http://localhost:4000/model/new with an api_base pointing at a local edge address, and the real provider's answer lands in the bundle 3. They replay with `OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-fake` on both the proxy and the run; POST http://localhost:4000/key/generate mints a real key, POST http://localhost:4000/v1/chat/completions returns the recorded completion, GET http://localhost:4000/spend/logs shows a non-zero spend row, and the run passes with zero provider calls 4. They stop the proxy and replay again; the run now goes red at setup with "No live proxy", because replay needs the proxy 5. They break the proxy instead (disable spend logging, or corrupt key generation); replay goes red with "no SpendLogs row" or a 401, catching the regression ## Relevant issues ## Linear ticket Resolves LIT-5745 ## Pre-Submission checklist **Please complete all items before asking a LiteLLM maintainer to review your PR** - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] The handful of test files covering my change pass locally, e.g. `uv run pytest tests/test_litellm/<your_test_file>.py -v`. Leave the suites (`make test-unit-*`, `make test-unit`) to CI: it finishes in ~15 minutes where a laptop takes an hour or more - [ ] My PR passes all required CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, schema.d.ts sync check, etc.) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [ ] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review (Greptile reviews automatically once the PR is opened; only comment `@greptileai` to re-request a review after pushing changes) ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix Shared setup: a scratch database `lit5745_qa`, and this proxy config ```yaml model_list: - model_name: bootstrap-noop litellm_params: model: openai/gpt-5.5 api_key: os.environ/OPENAI_API_KEY general_settings: master_key: os.environ/LITELLM_MASTER_KEY store_model_in_db: true proxy_batch_write_at: 5 ``` Proxy boot (per checkout, port checked free first with `lsof -nP -iTCP:<port> -sTCP:LISTEN`): ```bash set -a && source .env && set +a export DATABASE_URL="postgresql://...:.../lit5745_qa" uv run python litellm/proxy/proxy_cli.py --config lit5745_qa_config.yaml --port <port> --use_v2_migration_resolver curl -fs http://localhost:<port>/health/liveliness # "I'm alive!" ``` ### Before (629d7683f2) #### record 1. Boot the merge-base proxy on port 28353 and record one spend test against the real provider: ```bash E2E_FIXTURE_MODE=record E2E_RESET_SPEND_LOGS=1 LITELLM_PROXY_URL=http://localhost:28353 \ uv run pytest "tests/e2e/quota_management/spend_tracking/test_spend_tracking_e2e.py::test_chat_completion_writes_nonzero_spend_row" -v ``` ``` tests/e2e/quota_management/spend_tracking/test_spend_tracking_e2e.py::test_chat_completion_writes_nonzero_spend_row PASSED [100%] ========================= 1 passed in 66.49s (0:01:06) ========================= ``` #### replay with zero provider calls 1. Stop the proxy and confirm nothing listens: ```bash kill <proxy pid>; lsof -nP -iTCP:28353 -sTCP:LISTEN # proxy DOWN ``` 2. Replay the same test with the proxy down and a fake provider key: ```bash E2E_FIXTURE_MODE=replay LITELLM_PROXY_URL=http://localhost:28353 OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-fake \ uv run pytest "tests/e2e/quota_management/spend_tracking/test_spend_tracking_e2e.py::test_chat_completion_writes_nonzero_spend_row" -v ``` ``` tests/e2e/quota_management/spend_tracking/test_spend_tracking_e2e.py::test_chat_completion_writes_nonzero_spend_row PASSED [100%] ========================= 1 passed in 65.06s (0:01:05) ========================= ``` Green with no proxy process running at all: the run certified key auth, cost calculation, and spend writes that never executed #### replay against a broken proxy 1. No separate run can go red: the replay above already passed with the proxy stopped, the most broken proxy possible, so no proxy regression can ever turn a Before replay red ### After (367dd537b9) #### record 1. Boot the PR-tip proxy on port 28141 with real keys and record the edge-wired spend test (one real OpenAI call): ```bash E2E_FIXTURE_MODE=record E2E_RESET_SPEND_LOGS=1 LITELLM_PROXY_URL=http://localhost:28141 \ uv run pytest tests/e2e/quota_management/spend_tracking/test_provider_edge_spend_e2e.py -v ``` ``` tests/e2e/quota_management/spend_tracking/test_provider_edge_spend_e2e.py::test_edge_wired_chat_writes_nonzero_spend_row PASSED [100%] ========================= 1 passed in 83.98s (0:01:23) ========================= ``` #### replay with zero provider calls 1. Reboot the proxy with `OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-fake ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-fake` in its env, then replay with the same fake keys on the pytest side: ```bash E2E_FIXTURE_MODE=replay E2E_RESET_SPEND_LOGS=1 LITELLM_PROXY_URL=http://localhost:28141 \ OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-fake ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-fake \ uv run pytest tests/e2e/quota_management/spend_tracking/test_provider_edge_spend_e2e.py -v ``` ``` tests/e2e/quota_management/spend_tracking/test_provider_edge_spend_e2e.py::test_edge_wired_chat_writes_nonzero_spend_row PASSED [100%] ========================= 1 passed in 80.88s (0:01:20) ========================= ``` Neither side holds a real provider key, so a single leaked provider call would 401 and fail the run; the key mint, chat routing, cost calculation, and the non-zero spend row all executed against the live proxy and database #### replay against a broken proxy 1. Break spend writes: add `disable_spend_logs: true` to the config, reboot, replay again: ``` > assert matching, f"no SpendLogs row for request_id {chat.id}; saw {len(rows)} row(s)" E AssertionError: no SpendLogs row for request_id chatcmpl-EEmBI8wmtyO8weuLkSiCiobRa30zC; saw 0 row(s) ======================== 1 failed in 197.13s (0:03:17) ========================= ``` 2. Revert that, then break key generation with a temporary one-line patch that persists the hash of a corrupted token (`{**key_data, "token": f"{key_data['token']}-broken"}` at the DB insert), reboot, replay again: ``` E AssertionError: kind='unauthorized' body='{"error":{"message":"Authentication Error, Invalid proxy server token passed. Received API Key = sk-...8xKQ, Key Hash (Token) =db63ec69e77741b877decb60ed70824cc9b1d0c3f0cf21f1f9be524686cd9e56. Unable to find token in cache or `LiteLLM_VerificationTokenTable`","type":"token_not_found_in_db","param":"key","code":"401"}}' ======================== 1 failed in 75.69s (0:01:15) ========================= ``` 3. Revert the patch (`git checkout -- litellm/`), reboot clean, and replay goes green again: ``` tests/e2e/quota_management/spend_tracking/test_provider_edge_spend_e2e.py::test_edge_wired_chat_writes_nonzero_spend_row PASSED [100%] ========================= 1 passed in 80.76s (0:01:20) ========================= ``` ## Type 🧹 Refactoring ✅ Test ## Caveats (if any) - streaming records as one buffered body for now (LIT-5742) - CI wiring for record/replay is LIT-5748 - Bedrock cannot be edge-mounted: SigV4 signs the Host header - multipart bodies miss on replay: per-run random boundaries - only `/model/new` deployments can be edge-wired, not config-baked ones - replaying over a record run's DB rows dedupes spend writes (same response id is the SpendLogs primary key); run both modes with `E2E_RESET_SPEND_LOGS=1` or replay against a fresh DB ## QA runbook - tests/e2e/quota_management/spend_tracking/test_provider_edge_spend_e2e.py::test_edge_wired_chat_writes_nonzero_spend_row - an edge-wired chat billed through the live proxy writes a non-zero spend row, in live, record, and replay modes alike (needs `OPENAI_API_KEY` for live/record, `store_model_in_db: true`, and `DATABASE_URL` plus `E2E_RESET_SPEND_LOGS=1` in the pytest env so consecutive record/replay sessions do not dedupe each other's spend rows) - [ ] Run it once with `E2E_FIXTURE_MODE=record`; it registers a model via POST /model/new whose api_base points at the local provider edge, sends one real chat, and writes `tests/e2e/.fixtures` - [ ] Restart the proxy with `OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-fake` and rerun with `E2E_FIXTURE_MODE=replay`; expect green with zero provider calls - [ ] To reproduce by hand against the same proxy: POST /key/generate with the master key, POST /v1/chat/completions with that key and the registered model, then GET /spend/logs?api_key=<hashed key> and expect a row whose request_id matches the completion id with spend > 0 - [ ] Sanity check: this test makes sense to add and is not hand-wavey (e.g., assert actual expected spend instead of just spend > 0) or potentially flaky ### Final Attestation - [x] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR CHECKED: live-pr-risk at 367dd537b9. Harness-only change: no references to the reworked modules outside tests/e2e (repo and docs greps), full e2e suite collects clean on the head (685 tests, 0 errors), basedpyright over tests/e2e reports 0 errors, and record/replay plus three broken-proxy red runs were driven live on a real proxy, database, and provider

signal.title: feat(complexity_router): add business classification rubric preset
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - Built-in rubrics only cover chat and agentic coding traffic - Business/sales prompts over-route with engineering-flavored tier criteria How it solves it: - Adds a `business` classification rubric preset to the dropdown - The preset swaps in business tier definitions and business calibration examples - Keeps the same four tiers, so escalation and tier renames still work ## User Flow Before: an admin routing sales and support traffic has no business preset, so routine drafting over-routes to expensive tiers 1. They open http://localhost:4000/ui/?page=llm-playground, Add Model, Auto Router tab, and expand Complexity Router settings 2. The Classification Rubric dropdown offers only Legacy, Chat, and Agentic 3. They pick Chat, save, and send POST http://localhost:4000/v1/chat/completions with "draft a cold outreach email for a VP of Engineering at a fintech" 4. The classifier routes it to the COMPLEX tier model, and http://localhost:4000/ui/?page=logs shows the expensive deployment served it After: the same admin picks the Business preset and routine business drafting stays on the mid tier 1. They open the same Auto Router form and expand Complexity Router settings 2. The Classification Rubric dropdown now also offers Business, described as suited to sales, support, and go-to-market traffic 3. They pick Business, save, and send the same POST http://localhost:4000/v1/chat/completions with the same outreach-email prompt 4. signal.title: feat(observability): expose Prisma connection pool saturation metrics
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - During recent scalability incidents operators could see latency and database CPU symptoms but had no way to tell whether the proxy had simply run out of database connections, because nothing exposed the Prisma pool - There was also no way to separate time a query spent queued for a connection from time it spent executing, so "the database is slow" and "we are out of connections" looked identical on a dashboard - Pool exhaustion (prisma `P2024`) was neither counted nor surfaced anywhere How it solves it: - Ten bounded-cardinality metrics bridge the query engine's own pool counters into Prometheus, with pool wait and query execution kept as separate signals - `litellm_db_pool_timeouts_total` counts `P2024` at the error site, so exhaustion is recorded on the request path rather than by an exporter that has stopped running - The configured maximum is derived from the engine as `busy + idle` instead of being parsed out of `DATABASE_URL`, so no credential is read on this path ## User Flow Operators already running the prometheus callback get the new series on the existing `/metrics` endpoint with no configuration change. Nothing is emitted for deployments that do not enable prometheus. | Metric | Type | Meaning | |---|---|---| | `litellm_db_pool_connections_max` | Gauge | Configured pool size, summed across live workers | | `litellm_db_pool_connections_busy` | Gauge | Connections currently checked out | | `litellm_db_pool_connections_idle` | Gauge | Capacity not currently checked out | | `litellm_db_pool_connections_open` | Gauge | Connections actually opened to the database | | `litellm_db_pool_pending_acquirers` | Gauge | Queries queued for a free connection | | `litellm_db_pool_acquire_wait_seconds_total` | Counter | Cumulative seconds waiting for a slot, excluding execution | | `litellm_db_pool_acquire_total` | Counter | Acquisitions, for the mean-wait ratio | | `litellm_db_query_duration_seconds_total` | Counter | Cumulative seconds executing, excluding pool wait | | `litellm_db_query_total` | Counter | Queries executed | | `litellm_db_pool_timeouts_total` | Counter | Acquisitions that gave up waiting (`P2024`) | Saturation reads as `busy` at `max` with `pending_acquirers` above zero. Mean acquire latency is `rate(litellm_db_pool_acquire_wait_seconds_total[5m]) / rate(litellm_db_pool_acquire_total[5m])`, and the same ratio over the query pair gives execution time, which is the comparison that separates a slow database from an exhausted pool. ## Relevant issues ## Linear ticket Refs LIT-5435 This covers the database-pool section of the ticket only. The scheduled-job and per-pod request-pressure sections are separate PRs, so this one says Refs rather than Resolves. ## Pre-Submission checklist - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] My PR passes all CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, format, unit tests) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [ ] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix Real proxy, real Postgres 16, real Gemini API, no mocks. ### Before ``` $ curl -sSL http://127.0.0.1:20435/metrics -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-1234" \ | grep -E "^# HELP" | grep -iE "pool|connection|acquire|prisma" ``` No output. 119 metric families exposed, none of them about the connection pool. ### After, healthy pool at `database_connection_pool_limit: 3` ``` $ curl -sSL http://127.0.0.1:20435/metrics -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-1234" | grep -E "^litellm_db_(pool|query)" | grep -v _created litellm_db_pool_connections_max 3.0 litellm_db_pool_connections_busy 0.0 litellm_db_pool_connections_idle 3.0 litellm_db_pool_connections_open 3.0 litellm_db_pool_pending_acquirers 0.0 litellm_db_pool_acquire_wait_seconds_total 3.620699999999985e-05 litellm_db_pool_acquire_total 17.0 litellm_db_query_duration_seconds_total 0.182499623 litellm_db_query_total 37.0 litellm_db_pool_timeouts_total 0.0 ``` `max` reports the configured 3, derived from the engine rather than from the connection string. ### Under contention, 40 concurrent cold-cache auth lookups ``` 40 200 litellm_db_pool_acquire_wait_seconds_total 0.483372629 (was 3.6e-05) litellm_db_pool_acquire_total 165.0 litellm_db_query_duration_seconds_total 0.7769011680000002 litellm_db_query_total 416.0 ``` Pool wait rose four orders of magnitude while query execution stayed flat, which is the distinction this PR exists to provide. ### Saturated, pool of 1, sampled during a 45-request burst ``` litellm_db_pool_connections_busy 1.0 litellm_db_pool_pending_acquirers 12.0 ``` ### Exhausted, database stalled with `pool_timeout=1s` ``` 25 503 litellm_db_pool_connections_max 1.0 litellm_db_pool_timeouts_total 61.0 ``` ### Recovery ``` recovered request: 200 litellm_db_pool_pending_acquirers 0.0 litellm_db_pool_connections_busy 0.0 litellm_db_pool_timeouts_total 61.0 ``` Gauges track back to healthy and the counter holds. ## Type 🆕 New Feature ## Caveats (if any) The query engine decrements its waiter gauge when a waiter acquires a connection but not when one times out, so every `P2024` latches it one higher for the life of the process. Reproduced directly at `connection_limit=2, pool_timeout=1`, where a fully drained pool still reported seven waiters after two bursts. Free capacity is proof that nothing is queued, so a reading taken while a connection is idle is exactly the accumulated latch; the sampler subtracts that baseline and re-arms it on every idle sample. Verified after driving 46 real timeouts, with `pending_acquirers` correctly back to 0. `litellm_db_pool_acquire_wait_seconds_total` records only waits that ended in an acquisition, because the engine's histogram excludes timed-out waits. It therefore understates mean acquire latency during exhaustion, which is why the help text pairs it with the timeout counter. Sampling rides on database work, so a proxy whose auth cache is entirely warm samples less often. That is the intended coupling: the sampler is liveliest exactly when the database is busiest, and it cannot be silenced by a stalled scheduler. It is what the ticket asks for, a failure-resilient path rather than a periodic exporter. The cost of that choice, measured rather than estimated: one sample is a 383us call to the query engine's local HTTP server, taken at most once per 10 seconds per worker, which is 0.0038 percent of wall clock. It is dispatched as a task and never awaited, so it adds no latency to the database call it rides on and opens no cancellation window. It also does not consume a pool connection, confirmed by sampling successfully while the pool was fully checked out: ``` sampled while pool fully busy: busy=2 idle=0 -> answered OK ``` That last property is what makes the design work at all, since a sampler that needed a connection would be the first thing to fail during the exhaustion it exists to report. The counters are fed by differencing the engine's cumulative totals, so the first sample after startup establishes a baseline and the counters begin moving from the second sample. With `DATABASE_URL_READ_REPLICA` configured the reader has its own separate pool that these metrics do not cover. `RoutingPrismaWrapper.get_pool_sample` samples the writer, which is the pool that background jobs and spend writes contend for. Reader coverage needs a `pool` label and is left to a follow-up. `EXCEPTION_LABELS` in `litellm/types/integrations/prometheus.py` changes from a list to a tuple. It has no reader anywhere in the repo; freezing it offsets the one mutable-collection violation this diff adds, so no suppression was needed. ### Review follow-ups, both reproduced live before fixing `PrometheusLogger.get_instance` searched only `litellm.callbacks`. With the equally supported `litellm_settings.success_callback: ["prometheus"]` the metrics registered and then sat at zero forever, confirmed on a live proxy: ``` # success_callback registration, before litellm_db_pool_connections_max 0.0 litellm_db_pool_acquire_total 0.0 # same config, after litellm_db_pool_connections_max 3.0 litellm_db_pool_acquire_total 17.0 litellm_db_query_total 39.0 ``` It now resolves through `logging_callback_manager`, which covers all five callback lists, so the enterprise batch-cost metrics that use the same accessor benefit too. Separately, decorated database helpers nest: `get_object_permission` is called from inside `get_key_object` and both carry `@log_db_metrics`, so a single P2024 was counted once per enclosing `except`. The exception is now marked the first time it is counted. The exhaustion counter is per failed database operation, and a request performs several, so a 20-request burst against a stalled database records 48 timeouts rather than 20. ## QA runbook 1. Start Postgres and a proxy with `general_settings.database_connection_pool_limit: 3` and `litellm_settings.callbacks: ["prometheus"]` 2. Mint a virtual key with `POST /key/generate`, then send a chat completion with that key. A virtual key is required, since the master key path does no database lookup and so triggers no sample 3. `curl -sSL localhost:4000/metrics -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-1234" | grep litellm_db_` and confirm `litellm_db_pool_connections_max` equals the configured limit 4. Mint 40 keys and fire them concurrently with `xargs -P 40`, polling `/metrics` throughout. `litellm_db_pool_pending_acquirers` should rise above zero while `busy` sits at `max` 5. To force exhaustion, restart with `database_connection_pool_limit: 1` and `database_connection_timeout: 1`, `docker pause` the Postgres container, then fire the burst. `litellm_db_pool_timeouts_total` should climb and the requests should surface as 503 6. `docker unpause`, send one more request, and confirm `pending_acquirers` returns to 0 while the timeout counter holds ### Final Attestation - [x] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR ### Review follow-ups `get_instance` missed a string registration. `success_callback: ["prometheus"]` builds the logger lazily into `_in_memory_loggers` and never adds it to a callback list, so the lookup returned `None` for the life of such a proxy and every pool metric here would have sat at zero. It now falls back to that cache, with a test that drives the string form and the lazy construction. I refuted this on an earlier round citing 103 metric families on a live proxy; that measurement covered litellm's own metrics, which the logging path records on the instance directly rather than through this lookup, so it did not cover the claim. The report was right. On the review point that sampling adds a query-engine request to the database path, re-measured against a saturated pool on the current head: ``` pool at sample time: busy=5.0 idle=0.0 pending=5.0 get_metrics() returned in 2572us WHILE the pool was saturated ``` Five callers were already queued for a connection. A read that needed one would have joined that queue and blocked for seconds rather than returning in 2.6ms, so this takes no pool connection: it is an HTTP GET to the query-engine process. It is also dispatched with `create_task` rather than awaited, and throttled to once per 10s per worker, so it cannot extend a request or fail a query that succeeded. <!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY --> --- > [!NOTE] > **Medium Risk** > Touches the shared DB success/failure path and exception handling, but metrics failures are fully isolated so they cannot fail or delay database calls. Observability-only; no auth or data-mutation changes. > > **Overview** > Exposes **Prisma connection-pool saturation** as Prometheus metrics so operators can tell pool exhaustion apart from slow database queries. > > Adds ten unlabelled series (gauges for busy/idle/open/pending/max, counters for acquire wait, query duration, and `P2024` timeouts). Sampling rides the existing `@log_db_metrics` DB path—throttled to once per 10s, dispatched not awaited—so it stays alive under event-loop saturation and never adds latency or fails a successful query. Pool max is derived as `busy + idle` from the engine rather than from `DATABASE_URL`. > > Also fixes `PrometheusLogger.get_instance` to resolve via `logging_callback_manager` (covering `success_callback: ["prometheus"]`), and deduplicates timeout counting across nested decorated DB helpers. > > <sup>Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit 88cc6d7aa9767eb64c8bcb6f7552463cdf7b7c25. Bugbot is set up for automated code reviews on this repo. Configure [here](https://www.cursor.com/dashboard/bugbot).</sup> <!-- /CURSOR_SUMMARY -->

signal.title: feat(router): allow per-tier litellm_params in complexity autorouter config
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - autorouter tiers only accepted bare model names - varying reasoning effort per tier needed duplicate model_list entries How it solves it: - tier entries may now carry litellm_params - chosen entry's params merge into the routed request - applied params land in the routing decision log, with credential-shaped values masked ## User Flow Before: an operator who wants their reasoning tier to run opus with xhigh thinking, while the complex tier runs plain opus, cannot express that in the router config 1. They put `tiers: {COMPLEX: opus, REASONING: opus}` in `complexity_router_config` and restart the proxy 2. They POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions with `"model": "smart-router"` and a prompt that reads as reasoning work 3. The reply comes back from opus with no extended thinking, identical to the complex tier 4. To get thinking they have to add a second `opus-xhigh` entry to `model_list` duplicating the same deployment, then point the tier at it After: the reasoning level lives in the tier itself, no duplicate deployment needed 1. They write the reasoning tier as an entry with the model name plus `litellm_params: {reasoning_effort: xhigh}`, keeping `COMPLEX: opus`, and restart the proxy 2. They POST the same request to https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions with `"model": "smart-router"` 3. The reply now comes back with thinking content and a much larger completion, while the complex tier still answers without it 4. A caller that sends its own `"reasoning_effort": "low"` still gets the tier's xhigh, since the operator set it in the routing config on purpose 5. https://litellm-domain/ui/?page=logs shows the request with the applied parameters recorded on the routing decision ## Relevant issues ## Linear ticket ## Pre-Submission checklist - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] My PR passes all CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, format, unit tests) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [ ] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review (Greptile reviews automatically once the PR is opened; only comment `@greptileai` to re-request a review after pushing changes) ## Delays in PR merge? If you're seeing a delay in your PR being merged, ping the LiteLLM Team on [Slack (#pr-review)](https://join.slack.com/t/litellmossslack/shared_invite/zt-3o7nkuyfr-p_kbNJj8taRfXGgQI1~YyA). ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix Captured at commit `9c87dfc39f`, live proxy on localhost:4000 against real Anthropic and OpenAI APIs Config used: ```yaml model_list: - model_name: opus litellm_params: model: anthropic/claude-opus-4-8 api_key: os.environ/ANTHROPIC_API_KEY - model_name: gpt litellm_params: model: openai/gpt-5.6 api_key: os.environ/OPENAI_API_KEY - model_name: smart-router litellm_params: model: auto_router/complexity_router complexity_router_config: tiers: SIMPLE: gpt MEDIUM: gpt COMPLEX: opus REASONING: - model_name: opus litellm_params: reasoning_effort: xhigh default_model: gpt - model_name: smart-router-openai litellm_params: model: auto_router/complexity_router complexity_router_config: tiers: SIMPLE: gpt REASONING: - model_name: gpt litellm_params: reasoning_effort: high default_model: gpt ``` ```bash python litellm/proxy/proxy_cli.py --config tier_params_config.yaml --detailed_debug --port 4000 ``` 1. Anthropic tier, caller asks for `low`, tier says `xhigh` ```bash curl -s http://localhost:4000/v1/chat/completions -H 'content-type: application/json' \ -H 'Authorization: Bearer sk-1234' \ -d '{"model":"smart-router","reasoning_effort":"low","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Think through step by step and reason through this: prove every group of order 255 is cyclic."}]}' ``` ``` model: smart-router message.thinking_blocks: ['thinking'] usage: {'completion_tokens': 10247, 'prompt_tokens': 33, 'total_tokens': 10280, ...} ``` Proxy log for the same request, showing the tier params applied and recorded: ``` ComplexityRouter: ... tier=REASONING 'tier_litellm_params': {'reasoning_effort': 'xhigh'} ``` 2. OpenAI tier, caller asks for `minimal`, tier says `high` ```bash curl -s http://localhost:4000/v1/chat/completions -H 'content-type: application/json' \ -H 'Authorization: Bearer sk-1234' \ -d '{"model":"smart-router-openai","reasoning_effort":"minimal","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Think through step by step and reason through this: prove every group of order 255 is cyclic."}]}' ``` ``` model: smart-router-openai usage.completion_tokens_details: {'reasoning_tokens': 1024, ...} ``` Proxy log for the same request, showing the outgoing call carried the tier value rather than the caller's: ``` 'reasoning_effort': 'high' ``` 3. Same router, a simple prompt still routes to the plain tier with no thinking ```bash curl -s http://localhost:4000/v1/chat/completions -H 'content-type: application/json' \ -H 'Authorization: Bearer sk-1234' \ -d '{"model":"smart-router","reasoning_effort":"low","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Prove that every group of order 255 is cyclic. Work through the Sylow analysis rigorously."}]}' ``` ``` model: smart-router (served by gpt-5.6-sol, tier=SIMPLE) message.thinking_blocks: [] ``` ## Type 🆕 New Feature ## Caveats (if any) - tier params override the same key sent by the caller - object entries still need a matching model_list deployment - duplicate model_name inside one tier is rejected - Admin UI tier editor still writes plain model names - logged tier params are masked, so a secret set in a tier stays out of spend logs ### Final Attestation - [x] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR Link to Devin session: https://app.devin.ai/sessions/cdf8ee24d7f7481092e012da8495cfef Requested by: @krrish-berri-2
