signal.title: fix(user_update): stop premium metadata fields reaching the user table as columns
signal.text: ## Title fix(user_update): stop premium metadata fields reaching the user table as columns ## Relevant issues None filed. Found by comparing `/user/update` against its two siblings, `/key/update` and `/team/update`. ## Pre-Submission checklist - [x] I have Added testing in the `tests/litellm/` directory: `tests/test_litellm/proxy/management_endpoints/test_internal_user_endpoints.py` - [x] I have added the test output below - [x] My PR passes the touched test file with no new failures (control run below) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible: one added condition plus one new test ## Type 🐛 Bug Fix ## Changes `POST /user/update` (and the bulk variant, which shares the same helper) with `guardrails` or `prompts` in the body builds a prisma payload carrying them as **top-level keys**. Neither is a column on `LiteLLM_UserTable`, so `prisma_client.update_data(..., table_name="user")` hands them to the upsert and the write fails instead of storing the value. `_update_internal_user_params` filters the payload against only one of the two management-metadata name lists: ```python elif ( v is not None and v not in ([], {}) and k not in LiteLLM_ManagementEndpoint_MetadataFields ): non_default_values[k] = v ``` `LiteLLM_ManagementEndpoint_MetadataFields_Premium` (which holds `guardrails`, `policies`, `prompts`, `tags`, `logging`, ...) is never consulted, so those keys survive. `prepare_metadata_fields()` runs afterwards and **does** copy them into `non_default_values["metadata"]`, but it never pops the top-level key, so each one is written twice: once correctly into metadata, once as a phantom column. The two sibling routes get this right. `prepare_key_update_data` skips both lists: ```python if k in LiteLLM_ManagementEndpoint_MetadataFields or k in LiteLLM_ManagementEndpoint_MetadataFields_Premium: continue ``` `/team/update` does the same, and `/user/new` is unaffected because `generate_key_helper_fn` puts these into metadata and never into `user_data`. Only `/user/update` leaks them. What makes this an omission of one list rather than a deliberate design: the **non**-premium fields reachable on this request model (`model_rpm_limit`, `model_tpm_limit`, `mcp_rpm_limit`, `tag_rpm_limit`) are already dropped correctly today. Same class of field, same destination, opposite handling. The fix mirrors the sibling key path by filtering the premium list too. `LiteLLM_ManagementEndpoint_MetadataFields_Premium` is already in scope through the module's `from litellm.proxy._types import *`, so there is no new import. Nothing is lost: `prepare_metadata_fields` already persists all of these into metadata, which is where the request path reads them from (`litellm_pre_call_utils.py` reads `policies` and `guardrails` out of key / team / project **metadata**, never out of a user column). ### One nuance worth a maintainer's call `policies` **is** a real column on `LiteLLM_UserTable`, so today `/user/update` writes it to both the column and metadata. After this change it goes to metadata only, which matches `/user/new`, `/key/update` and `/team/update`. I checked for readers of the column before including it: a repo-wide search finds no code that reads `policies` off a user row (the one nearby hit is `team_repository.py`, a different table). If you would rather keep that vestigial column write, say so and I will drop `policies` from the exclusion; the `guardrails` / `prompts` half is the part that actually errors. ## Testing New test in the existing file, next to the other `_update_internal_user_params` tests. No database needed. ``` $ pytest tests/test_litellm/proxy/management_endpoints/test_internal_user_endpoints.py \ -k keeps_premium_metadata_out_of_columns # before the fix E AssertionError: guardrails must not be sent as a user column E assert 'guardrails' not in {'user_id': 'test_user_id', 'guardrails': ['my-guardrail'], E 'policies': ['my-policy'], 'prompts': ['my-prompt']} 1 failed # after the fix 1 passed ``` The test also asserts the values still arrive in `metadata` after `prepare_metadata_fields`, so it pins that the fix drops the phantom column without dropping the value. Direct before/after on the helper: ``` before: _update_internal_user_params(...) -> ['guardrails', 'policies', 'prompts', 'user_id'] after: _update_internal_user_params(...) -> ['user_id'] metadata -> {'model_rpm_limit': {'gpt-4': 5}, 'guardrails': ['my-guardrail'], 'policies': ['my-policy'], 'prompts': ['my-prompt']} ``` Control on the whole touched test file, same environment, with and without the change: ``` before: 8 failed, 29 passed, 61 errors after: 8 failed, 30 passed, 61 errors ``` Exactly +1 test and +1 pass; the failing set is byte-identical (diffed, not just counted). Those pre-existing failures and errors are environment gaps in my local install, not related to this change. `ruff check` reports the same 91 pre-existing findings before and after, none on a touched line. `ruff format --check --config ruff.toml` reports the source file already formatted; the test file reports the same single pre-existing reformat (an unrelated assert) both before and after. Note on the proxy checklist: I do not have a live proxy with paid LLM credentials, so I have not exercised this through a running server. This is a management-endpoint payload-shaping change with no LLM call in the path, and the function-level before/after above is the direct evidence.

signal.title: fix(management): boot proxy under a fastapi that dropped get_flat_dependant
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - Fresh `pip install litellm[proxy]` crashes the proxy on startup - Current fastapi removed the `get_flat_dependant` we import How it solves it: - Flatten the route's query params ourselves - Works across the whole `fastapi>=0.136.3,<1.0` range ## Relevant issues ## Linear ticket ## Pre-Submission checklist - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] My PR passes all CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, format, unit tests) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [ ] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix `litellm/proxy/management_endpoints/management_v1/common.py` imports `get_flat_dependant` from `fastapi.dependencies.utils`. That helper was removed in recent fastapi (gone in 0.141.1, the current PyPI release), so importing the management_v1 package, and therefore booting the proxy at all, raises `ImportError`. This is masked inside the repo because `uv.lock` pins fastapi to 0.136.3, which still has the symbol, so `make`, CI, and a dev proxy launched from a frozen sync all boot fine. Our published constraint is only `fastapi>=0.136.3,<1.0`, so a fresh `pip install 'litellm[proxy]'` (which does not see our lock) resolves fastapi to 0.141.1 and the proxy dies on startup before serving a single request. Reproduced by installing the fastapi a fresh install resolves to (0.141.1) and booting the proxy. Before, on `litellm_internal_staging` (`440b1bcf65`) with fastapi 0.141.1: ``` File ".../litellm/proxy/management_endpoints/management_v1/common.py", line 6, in <module> from fastapi.dependencies.utils import get_flat_dependant ImportError: cannot import name 'get_flat_dependant' from 'fastapi.dependencies.utils' (.../fastapi/dependencies/utils.py). Did you mean: 'get_dependant'? ``` After, on this branch (`c668067f4a`), same fastapi 0.141.1: ``` LiteLLM: Proxy initialized with Config, Set models: bedrock-sonnet-4-6 GET /health/readiness HTTP/1.1" 200 OK {"status":"healthy","db":"Not connected"} ``` The helper is also present in the locked 0.136.3, so the replacement is exercised by CI too. ## Type 🐛 Bug Fix ## Changes `_declared_query_params` needs the set of query-param aliases the matched route declares, including those contributed by nested dependencies, so `reject_unknown_query_params` can 400 on anything unrecognized. It reconstructed that set from `get_flat_dependant(dependant, skip_repeats=True).query_params`. Since that helper is gone, this walks the route `Dependant` directly and collects `query_params` aliases across the dependency tree ``` def _flat_query_params(dependant): return ( *(field.alias for field in dependant.query_params), *(alias for dep in dependant.dependencies for alias in _flat_query_params(dep)), ) ``` FastAPI dependant graphs are acyclic and shallow, and duplicates collapse in the returned `frozenset`, so no repeat-visit bookkeeping is needed. The caller now narrows `route.dependant` with `isinstance(..., Dependant)` instead of a bare `is None` check, which both guards the walk and drops a `reportAny` ## QA runbook - tests/test_litellm/proxy/management_endpoints/management_v1/test_common.py::test_accepts_query_params_declared_on_the_route_and_nested_dependencies - a query param declared only on a nested dependency is still accepted, proving the flatten recurses - [ ] Build a FastAPI route with `dependencies=[Depends(reject_unknown_query_params)]`, a `page` query param on the route, and a `team_id` query param on a nested `Depends` - [ ] GET `/things?page=2&team_id=t1` and expect 200 - [ ] Sanity check: a shallow scan of only the route's own params would 400 on `team_id`, so the test fails if the recursion regresses - tests/test_litellm/proxy/management_endpoints/management_v1/test_common.py::test_rejects_unknown_param_and_reports_nested_declared_params_as_allowed - an unrecognized query param is rejected and the reported allow-list includes nested params - [ ] GET `/things?bogus=1` and expect 400 with `bogus` named in `detail` - [ ] Expect `allowed` to be a superset of `{"page", "team_id"}` - [ ] Sanity check: this test makes sense to add and is not hand-wavey or potentially flaky ### Final Attestation - [x] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR </body> Link to Devin session: https://app.devin.ai/sessions/177117598f214818bc610155fb711c6a Requested by: @mateo-berri

signal.title: [Bug]: inflation/drift in /tag/daily/activity for custom-header tag metrics
signal.text: ### Check for existing issues - [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate. ### What happened? Custom-header tag metrics from /tag/daily/activity show inflation/drift. For the same filters and date range, totals can change between repeated reads, especially across paginated calls. We confirmed this is not fully mitigated by client-side fixes alone ### User Flow Requests are logged into LiteLLM_SpendLogs with request_tags/custom-header tags. LiteLLM asynchronously rolls up data into LiteLLM_DailyTagSpend. Dashboard/service reads /tag/daily/activity (which reads DailyTagSpend). While async rollup is in progress, paginated reads can return shifting totals, causing temporary inflation/drift. ### Proof the bug occurs Re-running /tag/daily/activity with same params produced different totals/pages within close time windows. Totals stabilize only after rollup catches up, showing timing-dependent inconsistency. Related upstream issues report similar behavior: https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/28979 https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/30164 ### What part of LiteLLM is this about? Other ### What LiteLLM version are you on ? v1.83.7-stable ### Twitter / LinkedIn details _No response_

signal.title: fix(router): keep acreate_file fallbacks inside the requested model group
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - Files uploaded for one model group could silently land on another provider via router fallbacks - The returned unified file id then fails every batch create with a permanent 429 How it solves it: - File creation now reuses the fallback pin that already protects batch and fine-tuning calls - Cross-group fallbacks are skipped for uploads, so the real provider error surfaces instead ## User Flow Before: a developer uploading a batch file for their azure model group gets HTTP 200, but every batch create against the returned id fails forever 1. During transient Azure trouble they send POST https://litellm-domain/v1/files with form fields `purpose=batch`, `target_model_names=azure-gpt`, and their JSONL file 2. They get HTTP 200 with `"status": "uploaded"` and a scrambled file id, so they believe the file is ready for azure-gpt 3. They send POST https://litellm-domain/v1/batches with that file id and get HTTP 429 "No deployments available for selected model, Try again in 5 seconds" 4. They wait and retry the batch create, and it returns the same 429 every time, because the file actually landed under the account of the fallback group's provider After: the upload fails loudly while Azure is down, and a retried upload once Azure is back produces a working batch 1. During the same transient Azure trouble they send the same POST https://litellm-domain/v1/files with `purpose=batch` and `target_model_names=azure-gpt` 2. They get HTTP 500 carrying the real connection error, so they know the upload did not go through and nothing was stored anywhere 3. Once Azure is reachable they retry the upload, get HTTP 200, and POST https://litellm-domain/v1/batches with the returned id succeeds ## Relevant issues Related to #35371 and #36181, which pinned the batch and fine-tuning side of the same fallback walk ## Linear ticket Resolves LIT-5788 ## Pre-Submission checklist **Please complete all items before asking a LiteLLM maintainer to review your PR** - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] My PR passes all CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, format, unit tests) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [x] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review (Greptile reviews automatically once the PR is opened; only comment `@greptileai` to re-request a review after pushing changes) - [x] b7f4f531b3f88f58ffbed3d3adbcafa4614d5fa0 passes /live-pr-risk ## Delays in PR merge? If you're seeing a delay in your PR being merged, ping the LiteLLM Team on [Slack (#pr-review)](https://join.slack.com/t/litellmossslack/shared_invite/zt-3o7nkuyfr-p_kbNJj8taRfXGgQI1~YyA). ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix Shared setup: proxy booted from the worktree with a fresh Postgres DB and the master key from .env, on random free ports: 30362 for the before leg, then 45817 and (after OpenAI finished the batch) 38571 for the after leg, both boots of the same tip commit. Config has an unreachable azure group, a healthy openai group, and a fallback between them: ```yaml model_list: - model_name: azure-gpt litellm_params: model: azure/my-azure-deployment api_base: http://127.0.0.1:9 api_key: dummy-key api_version: "2024-06-01" - model_name: openai-gpt litellm_params: model: openai/gpt-4.1-mini api_key: os.environ/OPENAI_API_KEY router_settings: fallbacks: - azure-gpt: - openai-gpt num_retries: 1 general_settings: master_key: os.environ/LITELLM_MASTER_KEY database_url: os.environ/LIT5788_DATABASE_URL ``` `batch_input.jsonl`: ```json {"custom_id": "req-1", "method": "POST", "url": "/v1/chat/completions", "body": {"model": "azure-gpt", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "say hi"}], "max_tokens": 5}} ``` ### Before (ec6f1c1a56345350f669377f14ec8586bd43329e) #### Upload for azure-gpt during the outage, then batch create 1. `curl -sS -i http://localhost:30362/v1/files -H "Authorization: Bearer $MASTER_KEY" -F purpose=batch -F target_model_names="azure-gpt" -F file=@batch_input.jsonl` 2. HTTP 200 with `"status":"uploaded"` and a unified id, even though azure-gpt is unreachable: ``` HTTP/1.1 200 OK {"id":"","bytes":176,"created_at":1787106179,"filename":"modified_file.jsonl","object":"file","purpose":"batch","status":"uploaded",...} ``` 3. The id base64-decodes to `target_model_names,azure-gpt` next to an OpenAI-format `llm_output_file_id,file-9LPo6PjRrhgCtkhQ3M1Ryc`, and the file physically exists on the provider the caller never named: `curl -sS https://api.openai.com/v1/files/file-9LPo6PjRrhgCtkhQ3M1Ryc -H "Authorization: Bearer $OPENAI_API_KEY"` returns `"status": "processed"` 4. `curl -sS -i http://localhost:30362/v1/batches -H "Authorization: Bearer $MASTER_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d "{\"input_file_id\": \"$UF\", \"endpoint\": \"/v1/chat/completions\", \"completion_window\": \"24h\", \"model\": \"azure-gpt\"}"` 5. Permanent failure inviting infinite retries (a retry 8 seconds later returned the same thing): ``` HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests {"error":{"message":"No deployments available for selected model, Try again in 5 seconds. Passed model=azure-gpt. pre-call-checks=False, cooldown_list=[]","type":"internal_server_error","param":"None","code":"429"}} ``` #### Control: upload and batch on the healthy openai-gpt group 1. `curl -sS -i http://localhost:30362/v1/files -H "Authorization: Bearer $MASTER_KEY" -F purpose=batch -F target_model_names="openai-gpt" -F file=@batch_input.jsonl` 2. HTTP 200 and the decoded id consistently pairs `target_model_names,openai-gpt` with the openai deployment, so the harness itself is sound ### After (b7f4f531b3f88f58ffbed3d3adbcafa4614d5fa0) #### Upload for azure-gpt during the outage 1. `curl -sS -i http://localhost:38571/v1/files -H "Authorization: Bearer $MASTER_KEY" -F purpose=batch -F target_model_names="azure-gpt" -F file=@batch_input.jsonl` 2. The upload now surfaces the real provider error instead of silently succeeding, and there is no unified id to orphan: ``` HTTP/1.1 500 Internal Server Error {"error":{"message":"Connection error.. Received Model Group=azure-gpt\nAvailable Model Group Fallbacks=['openai-gpt']\nError doing the fallback: Connection error.","type":null,"param":null,"code":"500"}} ``` 3. Proxy log shows the pin doing its job: `LiteLLM Router:INFO: fallback_event_handlers.py:354 - Skipping fallback to model_group = openai-gpt: request is pinned to model_group = azure-gpt by its uploaded file` 4. signal.title: fix(model_prices): set prompt_cache_min_tokens=4096 for Gemini 3.5/3.6/3.7 Flash and 3.1 Pro Preview
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - Gemini 3.5/3.6/3.7 Flash entries lack `prompt_cache_min_tokens` - LiteLLM assumes the default 1024-token caching minimum for them - Google requires 4,096 tokens minimum, so small prompts hit a 400 How it solves it: - Adds `prompt_cache_min_tokens: 4096` to those models (all provider variants) - Also adds it to `gemini-3.1-pro-preview`, listed at 4,096 in the same Google table ## User Flow Before: a developer using prompt caching with a small prompt gets a hard 400 from Vertex 1. They send POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions to model group `gemini-3.5-flash` with `cache_control` on a ~3,300-token prompt 2. The request fails with `400: The cached content is of 3334 tokens. The minimum token count to start explicit caching is 4096.` After: the same request is handled knowing the real 4,096-token minimum 1. They send the same POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions to `gemini-3.5-flash` 2. LiteLLM's prompt-caching checks resolve the model's minimum as 4,096, so sub-minimum prompts are no longer treated as cacheable and routed into the failing explicit-caching path ## Relevant issues Source: https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/caching#implicit-caching — "Gemini 3.7 Flash 4,096 / Gemini 3.6 Flash 4,096 / Gemini 3.5 Flash 4,096 / Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview 4,096" (verified against the raw page HTML on 2026-08-19). signal.title: fix(proxy): log spend for OpenAI passthrough embeddings with unmapped models
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - OpenAI passthrough embeddings with unmapped models return 200 but never get billed - Cost lookup failure crashed the logging task, dropping the spend log row How it solves it: - Embeddings cost failures now log spend at cost 0 instead of crashing - Errors on non-chat bodies no longer hit the chat-shaped fallback ## User Flow Before: a developer calls embeddings through the OpenAI passthrough with their Azure deployment name, gets a normal 200, and the proxy admin never sees the request billed 1. The proxy admin exposes the OpenAI passthrough by setting the upstream base URL and key, then hands the developer a virtual key 2. The developer sends `POST https://litellm-domain/openai_passthrough/v1/embeddings` with `{"model": "my-embeddings-deployment", "input": ["hello"]}`, a deployment name LiteLLM has no pricing for 3. They get back 200 with a normal embeddings body: `object: "list"`, the vector in `data`, and real token usage 4. The admin opens https://litellm-domain/ui/?page=logs and the request is nowhere in the list; `GET https://litellm-domain/spend/logs` shows no row for it either 5. The key's spend at `GET https://litellm-domain/key/info` never moves, so the request is served but invisible and unbilled forever After: the same request shows up in the spend logs with its token counts, priced at $0 until a mapped price exists 1. The proxy admin exposes the OpenAI passthrough by setting the upstream base URL and key, then hands the developer a virtual key 2. The developer sends `POST https://litellm-domain/openai_passthrough/v1/embeddings` with `{"model": "my-embeddings-deployment", "input": ["hello"]}`, a deployment name LiteLLM has no pricing for 3. They get back 200 with a normal embeddings body: `object: "list"`, the vector in `data`, and real token usage 4. The admin opens https://litellm-domain/ui/?page=logs and the request is there; `GET https://litellm-domain/spend/logs?request_id=<id>` returns the row with the deployment name, its real prompt token count, and `"spend": 0.0` 5. Requests with models LiteLLM does have pricing for keep billing at their real cost, exactly as before ## Relevant issues Embeddings residual of #36646 (the chat completions side was fixed in #36660) ## Linear ticket Resolves LIT-5787 ## Pre-Submission checklist **Please complete all items before asking a LiteLLM maintainer to review your PR** - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] My PR passes all CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, format, unit tests) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [x] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review (Greptile reviews automatically once the PR is opened; only comment `@greptileai` to re-request a review after pushing changes) ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix Shared setup: live proxy from the worktree against a real Azure OpenAI upstream (real API calls, real $) ```bash export OPENAI_API_BASE="https://e2e-claude-foundry.openai.azure.com/openai" export OPENAI_API_KEY="<azure key>" .venv/bin/python litellm/proxy/proxy_cli.py --config litellm/proxy/dev_config.yaml --detailed_debug --port <port> ``` `lit5787-embed-qa2` is an Azure deployment name with no entry in the pricing map; `text-embedding-3-small` is mapped ### Before (ec6f1c1a56) #### Unmapped deployment name 1. Request served fine: ```bash curl -sS http://localhost:43217/openai_passthrough/v1/embeddings \ -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-1234" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"model": "lit5787-embed-qa2", "input": ["spend attribution probe LIT-5787"]}' ``` Returns 200 with a normal embeddings body (`object: "list"`, vector in `data`, real `usage`), and the proxy log shows `"POST /openai_passthrough/v1/embeddings HTTP/1.1" 200 OK` 2. The logging task dies before writing anything: ```text 19:27:50 - LiteLLM:ERROR: logging_worker.py:104 - LoggingWorker error: litellm.APIError: LiteLLM: provider returned a response with no 'choices'. Raw keys: ['id', 'object', 'data', 'model', 'usage'] ... ValueError: This model isn't mapped yet. Add it here - https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/main/model_prices_and_context_window.json ``` 3. The next spend flush has nothing for the request, and no spend log row is ever written: ```text 19:27:51 - spend_update_queue.py:37 - Aggregating updates by entity type: [] 19:27:51 - db_spend_update_writer.py:1225 - User Spend transactions: {} 19:27:51 - db_spend_update_writer.py:1267 - KEY Spend transactions: {} ``` #### Mapped model (control) 1. Same curl with `{"model": "text-embedding-3-small", "input": "spend attribution probe LIT-5787 control"}` returns 200 2. Spend row written as expected: `SpendTable: created payload - request_id: d0d17210-..., model: text-embedding-3-small, spend: 2e-07` ### After (81914ebc31) #### Unmapped deployment name 1. Same request against the fixed tip: ```bash curl -sS http://localhost:24886/openai_passthrough/v1/embeddings \ -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-1234" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"model": "lit5787-embed-qa2", "input": ["spend attribution probe LIT-5787 tip"]}' ``` Returns the same 200 embeddings body 2. The logging task now survives and writes the spend row (zero LoggingWorker errors in the whole run): ```text 19:48:32 - openai_passthrough_logging_handler.py:246 - Error calculating embeddings cost for model lit5787-embed-qa2, logging spend with cost 0: This model isn't mapped yet. ... 19:48:32 - spend_tracking_utils.py:441 - SpendTable: created payload - request_id: cacdffd2-40ed-4baa-9fda-4e2fc2686324, model: lit5787-embed-qa2, spend: 0.0 19:48:32 - db_spend_update_writer.py:816 - Writing spend log to db - request_id: cacdffd2-40ed-4baa-9fda-4e2fc2686324, spend: 0.0 ``` 3. The row is visible where the admin looks: ```bash curl -sS "http://localhost:24886/spend/logs?request_id=cacdffd2-40ed-4baa-9fda-4e2fc2686324" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-1234" ``` Returns the row: `request_id: cacdffd2-40ed-4baa-9fda-4e2fc2686324`, `model: lit5787-embed-qa2`, `custom_llm_provider: openai`, `spend: 0.0`, `prompt_tokens: 11`, `completion_tokens: 0`, `call_type: pass_through_endpoint` #### Mapped model (control) 1. Same curl with `{"model": "text-embedding-3-small", "input": "spend attribution probe LIT-5787 control tip"}` returns 200 2. Real cost still billed: `SpendTable: created payload - request_id: be84855d-014b-4e2f-b972-ea6ed18e627d, model: text-embedding-3-small, spend: 2.2e-07` ## Type 🐛 Bug Fix ## Caveats (if any) - Unmapped models bill at $0 until pricing is added to the map ### Final Attestation - [x] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR live-pr-risk CHECKED at 81914ebc31: PASS. Only dispatch site (success_handler) A/B verified on a live proxy at base and tip with real Azure calls; no subclasses, no wire/config/DB/UI surface. Error paths on image and responses routes previously always crashed the chat-shaped fallback (body has no choices), so returning the pre-existing result-None contract removes no working behavior

signal.title: feat(otel): attribute Prisma database spans to PostgreSQL instead of localhost
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - Database work shows up in APM as `litellm-server -> localhost`. Prisma's Python client talks to a local Rust query engine over loopback HTTP, so anything instrumenting the transport (ddtrace's httpx patching, an httpx OTEL instrumentor) names the peer `localhost`, and litellm's own `postgres` span carried nothing better: `service=postgres`, `call_type=get_data`, and no `db.*` at all - An operator staring at a slow auth or budget lookup could not tell it was PostgreSQL time, and had no server address to correlate the window against the database's own metrics How it solves it: - Datastore service spans (`postgres`, `batch_write_to_db`, `redis`) now carry `db.system.name`, `db.system` and `db.operation.name`, and are emitted as `CLIENT` spans instead of `INTERNAL`, so a backend that types spans from kind plus `db.system` renders them as database calls - PostgreSQL spans also carry `server.address`, `server.port` and `db.namespace` parsed from `DATABASE_URL`. Only host, port, database and schema are read; the user, password, IAM token and every other query parameter are never touched, so no credential can reach an exporter, and no SQL text or bind value is ever attached - Both OTel paths are covered: the default v1 integration and the opt-in v2 logger share one resolver, so v2's existing `db.system.name` mapping is no longer a second copy of the same table `db.system` is dual-emitted alongside the semconv-current `db.system.name` because Datadog's OTLP intake still infers a span's database type from the older key. `db.namespace` follows the PostgreSQL semconv `{database}|{schema}` shape, with Prisma's literal default `public` schema left implicit. The match is case-sensitive: Prisma quotes the schema name, so `?schema=PUBLIC` provisions a second schema alongside `public` with its own tables, and folding the two into one namespace would report two different schemas as the same database. A DSN whose password carries an unencoded `/`, `#` or `?` truncates the URL authority, which makes `urlparse` report the username as the host and the credential tail as the path, query or fragment. Postgres drivers reject such a string outright (`P1013`, so the proxy cannot start on it), and the parser refuses it rather than deriving an endpoint from a mis-split authority: it rejects a raw database segment holding `@` or `/`, and any DSN whose userinfo `@` fell outside the netloc, which is what the `#` and `?` spellings look like. A hostless `postgresql:///litellm`, which Prisma does accept as a local-socket DSN, yields `db.namespace` with no server address instead of nothing. ## User Flow Nothing to configure. A deployment already exporting OTel spans through the generic `otel` callback, or through `arize_phoenix`, `weave_otel`, `agentops`, `levo`, `logfire` or `langtrace`, gets the attributes on its next restart. The `arize` and `langfuse_otel` callbacks deliberately no-op both service hooks (`arize.py:113`, `langfuse_otel.py:427`), so they never received DB spans and still do not. Before: an on-call engineer chasing p99 latency on the gateway sees the wait blamed on `localhost` and cannot tell it is database time 1. They send POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions and watch the request in their tracing backend 2. Inside the request they find a span named `postgres`, tagged only `service=postgres`, `call_type=get_data`, `table_name=combined_view`, typed as internal work 3. Their backend's service map shows the gateway talking to `localhost`, the loopback peer of the local query engine, so filtering the request by database calls returns nothing 4. They cannot line the slow window up against their database's own metrics, because no span names a database host or port After: the same span identifies PostgreSQL and the exact server, so it shows up as a database call and correlates with the database's metrics 1. The admin restarts the proxy with the same config, nothing new to set 2. They send the same POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions and open the same request 3. The `postgres` span is now typed as an outbound client call and carries `db.system.name=postgresql`, `db.operation.name=get_data`, `server.address` and `server.port` of the real database and `db.namespace` of the database it reads, with the old `service`, `call_type` and `table_name` tags still there 4. Filtering the trace by database calls returns the `postgres` and `batch_write_to_db` spans, and the address on them matches the host in their database dashboard, so the slow window can be lined up against it 5. No DSN username or password appears on any span, and cache spans still say `db.system=redis` with no database address borrowed from the Postgres DSN ## Relevant issues ## Linear ticket Refs LIT-5436 ## Pre-Submission checklist **Please complete all items before asking a LiteLLM maintainer to review your PR** - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] My PR passes all CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, format, unit tests) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [ ] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review (Greptile reviews automatically once the PR is opened; only comment `@greptileai` to re-request a review after pushing changes) ## Delays in PR merge? If you're seeing a delay in your PR being merged, ping the LiteLLM Team on [Slack (#pr-review)](https://join.slack.com/t/litellmossslack/shared_invite/zt-3o7nkuyfr-p_kbNJj8taRfXGgQI1~YyA). ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix Live proxy on a real Postgres, real Gemini calls, spans exported over OTLP to Langfuse Cloud and read back through Langfuse's own API. Base and head legs ran the same requests against the same database; the launcher printed `litellm.__file__` and a fix-symbol probe on each leg so the tree under test is not in doubt. Rig: ```bash docker run -d --name litfix-pg-5436 -p 15436:5432 \ -e POSTGRES_DB=litellm -e POSTGRES_USER=llmproxy -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=dbpassword9090 postgres:16 export DATABASE_URL="postgresql://llmproxy:dbpassword9090@192.168.1.244:15436/litellm?schema=public" export OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT="https://cloud.langfuse.com/api/public/otel" export OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS="Authorization=Basic <langfuse pk:sk>" export OTEL_SERVICE_NAME="litellm-server" python -m litellm.proxy.proxy_cli --config rig/config.yaml --port 20436 --use_prisma_db_push curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:20436/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"model":"gemini-flash","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"hello"}]}' ``` Before, the `postgres` span as Langfuse stored it. Nothing identifies PostgreSQL and there is no server to correlate against, so the only host in the trace is the query engine's loopback address: ```json { "call_type": "get_data", "service": "postgres", "table_name": "combined_view" } ``` After, the same span from the same request shape: ```json { "call_type": "get_data", "db.namespace": "litellm", "db.operation.name": "get_data", "db.system": "postgresql", "db.system.name": "postgresql", "server.address": "192.168.1.244", "server.port": "15436", "service": "postgres", "table_name": "combined_view" } ``` `?schema=public` is in the DSN and correctly does not appear in `db.namespace`. The port is the database's, not the query engine's ephemeral loopback port. Read back with: ```bash curl -s -u "$LANGFUSE_PUBLIC_KEY:$LANGFUSE_SECRET_KEY" \ "$LANGFUSE_HOST/api/public/observations?limit=25" \ | jq '.data[] | select(.name=="postgres") | .metadata.attributes' ``` Span kinds and the negative cases, captured from the raw OTLP export on the same run: ``` postgres kind=CLIENT db.system=postgresql server.address=192.168.1.244 server.port=15436 db.namespace=litellm batch_write_to_db kind=CLIENT db.system=postgresql server.address=192.168.1.244 server.port=15436 db.namespace=litellm auth kind=INTERNAL (no db.* attributes) router kind=INTERNAL (no db.* attributes) ``` With `DATABASE_URL_READ_REPLICA` set, the proxy logged `read-replica routing enabled via DATABASE_URL_READ_REPLICA` and the endpoint attributes correctly dropped out while the system and operation stayed: ``` postgres kind=CLIENT {"call_type": "get_data", "db.operation.name": "get_data", "db.system": "postgresql", "db.system.name": "postgresql", "service": "postgres", "table_name": "combined_view"} ``` No credential from the DSN appeared anywhere in the exported payload on any leg, checked by substring search over the full protobuf-decoded export. To view the two traces in the Langfuse UI (same project, before then after): 1. https://cloud.langfuse.com/project/cmrmn6k7s00d0ad0dz7kyag1e/traces/e22670fc344a189b7c45a328e831f361 2. https://cloud.langfuse.com/project/cmrmn6k7s00d0ad0dz7kyag1e/traces/ba93049c4ea11c1ecd449e1aff43ed4f Open the `postgres` observation in each and compare the metadata attributes panel. Re-verified on a second rig, this time exporting to a local Jaeger so the spans can be read straight off the collector. Base leg at `0b82b087fd` (litellm_internal_staging), head leg at `e2980c7753`, same Postgres, same request shape, real Anthropic calls, both legs into one Jaeger instance: ``` base postgres kind=internal {call_type, service, table_name} base batch_write_to_db kind=internal {call_type, service} head postgres kind=client db.system=postgresql db.system.name=postgresql db.operation.name=get_data server.address=172.16.18.2 server.port=15436 db.namespace=litellm (call_type, service, table_name still present, span name still "postgres") head batch_write_to_db kind=client same endpoint attributes, db.operation.name=_PROXY_track_cost_callback head redis kind=client db.system=redis, no server.address (it does not borrow the Postgres DSN) head auth/router/self/proxy_pre_call/litellm_request kind=internal, no db.* or server.* ``` With `LITELLM_OTEL_V2=True` the v2 logger produced the same endpoint attributes on `postgres get_data`, `postgres get_key_object` and `batch_write_to_db _PROXY_track_cost_callback`, alongside the `litellm.service.*` keys it already emitted. With `DATABASE_URL_READ_REPLICA` set, the endpoint attributes dropped out and only the system and operation stayed. Grepping the Jaeger API export for the DSN user and password returned zero hits on every leg ## Type 🆕 New Feature ## Caveats (if any) Behavior changes worth calling out: - `postgres`, `batch_write_to_db` and `redis` service spans change span kind from `INTERNAL` to `CLIENT`. That is what lets a backend classify them as database calls; a dashboard filtering those spans by kind would need updating. Span names are unchanged on the v1 path, deliberately, so anything keyed on the name `postgres` keeps working - Three to five attributes are added per datastore span. Nothing in the repo asserts an exact attribute set on a service span, and no span-attribute limit is configured, so this is additive - `db.system` is a superseded semconv key. It is emitted for Datadog compatibility during the migration window, not as the primary The endpoint is resolved from the environment on every span rather than cached, because `DATABASE_URL` is not static: the RDS IAM refresh rebuilds it from `DATABASE_HOST` and friends on every rotation, and the DB-backed `environment_variables` overlay can rewrite those keys after startup with no blocklist covering them. One residual gap remains, and it is the inverse: that overlay changes `os.environ` without reconnecting the live Prisma client, so between the rewrite and the next reconnect a span names the newly configured server while queries still reach the old one. Naming the live connection instead of the environment would need this module to reach into the proxy's Prisma client, which is the wrong direction for a layer the SDK imports, so the window is documented rather than closed. It self-corrects at the next reconnect What this does not cover, and why the Linear reference is `Refs` rather than `Resolves`: - The ticket asks that a backend be able to separate local Prisma transport time from downstream query time. litellm's span is a single duration covering pool acquisition, the loopback hop and the query, because the query engine does not report that split back to the Python client. Making it separable needs a span around the engine call itself, which is a hot-path change I did not want to fold in here. The docs section explains how to bound it today using the APM's own transport span plus the database's query timing - When a read replica is configured, litellm names no endpoint at all rather than naming the writer. `RoutingPrismaWrapper` picks reader or writer per Prisma call, underneath the span, so naming the primary would pin replica read latency onto the wrong instance. Per-call reader/writer attribution is the follow-up - Datadog was not exercised directly; no account is available on this machine. The `db.system` and `CLIENT`-kind decisions come from Datadog's published OTLP mapping rather than from an observed Datadog trace ## QA runbook Docs PR: BerriAI/litellm-docs#869. signal.title: [Bug]: A single malformed tool_calls[].function.arguments DoSes a proxy replica — pre-network transformation error is mapped to retryable APIConnectionError, and the cyclic fallback graph is walked without cycle detection (79,858 attempts against num_retries=2, ~2.3 GB of logs in ~7 min, event loop starved, pod killed with exit 137)
signal.text: ### Check for existing issues - [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate. ### What happened? > **Title (paste into the GitHub issue title field):** > > `[Bug]: A single malformed tool_calls[].function.arguments DoSes a proxy replica — pre-network transformation error is mapped to retryable APIConnectionError, and the cyclic fallback graph is walked without cycle detection (79,858 attempts against num_retries=2, ~2.3 GB of logs in ~7 min, event loop starved, pod killed with exit 137)` > > Suggested labels: `bug`, `bedrock`, `router`, `availability` --- ## What happened? A client replayed a conversation history in which one assistant message contained a **truncated** `tool_calls[].function.arguments` JSON string. LiteLLM's Bedrock Converse transformation tried to `json.loads()` that string, failed, and raised a **bare `Exception`**. `exception_mapping_utils.exception_type()` classified it as **`litellm.APIConnectionError`** — a *retryable* class. Because the failure occurs inside `_async_transform_request()`, i.e. **before any network I/O**, each retry costs ~0.56 ms of pure CPU. The router's retry + fallback machinery therefore degenerated into a **CPU-speed busy loop**. Each iteration wrote a ~30-line, ~3 KB chained traceback synchronously to stdout, on the **same thread that runs the asyncio event loop**. Measured result for **one single client request**: - **79,858** transformation failures in **45.05 s** (≈ **1,773 failures/s**, one every **0.56 ms**) - …against a configured budget of `num_retries: 2`, i.e. **at most ~9 attempts** for the model group involved. The observed count overshoots the configured bound by **≈8,900×**, because the `fallbacks` graph contains a 4-node **cycle** that the router walks without cycle detection (§5.10) - the configured `retry_after: 2.0` was **not applied** — measured interval between attempts was **0.564 ms**, not 2 s - **53,202 log lines/s**, ≈ **5.5 MB/s** to stdout, **~2.3 GB** of logs for the ~7-minute event - **4 container-log rotations in 50 seconds** - one CPU core saturated, **asyncio event loop starved** - Redis client reads started timing out (the Redis *server* was provably idle and healthy) - `/health/readiness` and `/health/liveliness` stopped answering within their timeouts - **12 consecutive liveness failures → kubelet killed the container → SIGTERM (8 s grace, the frozen process could not handle it) → SIGKILL → `exitCode: 137`, `reason: Error`** So: **an unprivileged client can take down a LiteLLM proxy replica with one HTTP request**, without any large payload, high request rate, or misconfiguration on the operator's side. This is why I'm filing it as an availability issue and not only as a transformation bug. This is not a hypothetical — it happened in production on 2026-07-30 and it is reproducible from the request body alone. ## Impact / severity | Dimension | Assessment | | --- | --- | | Trigger cost to attacker | One HTTP request, a few hundred bytes, any valid API key | | Effect | Replica becomes unresponsive on **all** endpoints (health, other tenants' traffic) for minutes, then is killed by the orchestrator | | Blast radius | Not limited to the offending request: the event loop is shared, so every in-flight request on that replica is affected and lost on SIGKILL | | Self-amplifying | Killing the replica pushes its traffic to peers; after restart the same client retried and the fresh container was starved again within 65 s (see §5.9) | | Secondary | ~2.3 GB of logs per incident — real risk of filling the node disk and of blowing up log-ingest cost | | Detectability | Very poor: `exitCode 137` with `reason: Error` looks exactly like an OOM kill, but `memory.events oom_kill` is `0`. Node-level CPU/memory metrics look completely healthy (see §5.7) | ## Environment | Item | Value | | --- | --- | | LiteLLM version | **v1.93.0** | | Image | `ghcr.io/berriai/litellm-database:1.93.0` | | Deployment | `litellm-helm` chart 1.93.0, 6 replicas, namespace `ai-gateway` | | Python | 3.13 (`/app/.venv/lib/python3.13/site-packages/litellm/...`) | | Provider | AWS Bedrock **Converse**, streaming (`converse_handler.py::async_streaming`), `ap-southeast-1` | | Platform | Amazon EKS, Amazon Linux 2023, kernel `6.12.92-122.166.amzn2023.x86_64`, 16 vCPU / 63 GB nodes | | Container limits | 8 CPU / 16 Gi | | Backing services | PostgreSQL (Bitnami) and Redis (Bitnami), both off-pod, both healthy throughout | | Are you an ML Ops team? | Yes | Relevant configuration (managed through the Admin UI, therefore stored in the `LiteLLM_Config` table; secrets removed): ```yaml # router_settings num_retries: 2 retry_after: 2.0 allowed_fails: 3 cooldown_time: 60.0 timeout: 300.0 routing_strategy: simple-shuffle model_group_alias: {} fallbacks: [ 11 entries — full graph in §5.10 ] # litellm_settings num_retries: 2 request_timeout: 600 drop_params: true modify_params: true cache: true cache_params: { type: redis, ttl: 300, supported_call_types: [acompletion, completion] } success_callback: [langfuse] failure_callback: [langfuse] callbacks: [custom_callbacks.proxy_handler_instance, prometheus] store_audit_logs: true # general_settings store_model_in_db: true store_prompts_in_spend_logs: true database_connection_pool_limit: 10 database_connection_timeout: 60 health_check_interval: 300 maximum_spend_logs_retention_period: 7d maximum_spend_logs_retention_interval: 1h ``` Note `drop_params: true` and `modify_params: true` are both enabled — we have already opted into LiteLLM's message-fixup leniency, and it does not cover this case. Probe configuration at the time of the incident (already **relaxed** relative to the chart defaults, and still not enough): ```yaml livenessProbe: { path: /health/liveliness, periodSeconds: 30, timeoutSeconds: 10, failureThreshold: 12 } # ≈6 min tolerance readinessProbe: { path: /health/readiness, periodSeconds: 15, timeoutSeconds: 10, failureThreshold: 3 } startupProbe: { path: /health/readiness, periodSeconds: 10, timeoutSeconds: 5, failureThreshold: 30 } terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 8 ``` Note the replica was killed **despite a ~6-minute liveness tolerance**. The loop had been running for longer than that. ## Root cause: three separate defects ### Defect 1 — a client input error is raised as a bare `Exception` and mapped to a *retryable* class `litellm/litellm_core_utils/prompt_templates/factory.py::_convert_to_bedrock_tool_call_invoke` 1. line 3682 — `json.loads(function_arguments)` → `json.decoder.JSONDecodeError` 2. line 3695 — fallback `split_concatenated_json_objects()` (`common_utils.py:1711`) also fails, because it handles *concatenated* JSON but not *truncated* JSON 3. line 3731 — `raise Exception(f"Unable to convert openai tool calls={tool_calls} to bedrock tool calls. Received error={e}")` `litellm/litellm_core_utils/exception_mapping_utils.py:2482 / 2505` then wraps that bare `Exception` into `litellm.APIConnectionError`. `APIConnectionError` means "the network or the upstream provider hiccuped, try again". Here nothing has been sent anywhere — the request never reaches Bedrock. This is a **400-class client input error** and must be non-retryable. The `split_concatenated_json_objects` helper is itself evidence that upstream already added leniency for malformed model-emitted tool arguments; truncation was simply not covered. ### Defect 2 — the fallback graph is walked without cycle detection, so retries are effectively unbounded Frames observed in the traceback: ``` router.py:6235 async_function_with_fallbacks (log site) router.py:6286 async_function_with_fallbacks router.py:6387 async_function_with_retries router.py:6465 async_function_with_retries router.py:6532 async_function_with_retries router.py:6541 make_call router.py:2802 / 2753 _acompletion utils.py:1870 / 1689 wrapper_async main.py:696 / 643 acompletion ``` Retrying a *deterministic* failure can never succeed. Worse, because the failure is raised before any socket is opened, there is **no natural rate limit**: retry-after / backoff logic that keys off provider latency or `retry_after` headers has nothing to slow it down. The loop runs at CPU speed (measured 0.564 ms per attempt). **Our configured budget is small, and cannot account for what happened.** `num_retries: 2` (set in both `router_settings` and `litellm_settings`) means at most 3 attempts per model group; the group involved has 2 fallback groups, bounding the work at roughly **9 attempts**. We measured **79,858** — an overshoot of ≈8,900×. The reason is that our `fallbacks` graph contains a cycle (full graph and derivation in §5.10): ``` claude-sonnet-5 ⇄ claude-sonnet-4-6 claude-sonnet-4-6 → claude-haiku-4-5 → GLM-5.2 → claude-sonnet-4-6 ``` `{claude-sonnet-5, claude-sonnet-4-6, claude-haiku-4-5, GLM-5.2}` form a strongly connected component. Every group in it fails *identically* on this input, so the traversal never terminates. Nothing in the logs suggests the router noticed it was revisiting a model group it had already tried. I'd argue a cyclic fallback graph should not be able to hang the proxy regardless of whether the config is "correct" — it is trivially easy to create by accident (each of the 11 entries above looks locally reasonable), the UI accepts it without warning, and there is no startup validation or runtime guard. Two further mechanisms that should have stopped this did not fire. I'd like maintainers to confirm whether that is expected: - **`retry_after: 2.0` was not honoured.** Measured inter-attempt interval: 0.564 ms. Backoff appears not to apply to `APIConnectionError` on this path, which is what allows CPU-speed spinning. - **`allowed_fails: 3` + `cooldown_time: 60.0` never cooled anything out of the loop.** If cooldown bookkeeping is written to Redis, and Redis calls were themselves timing out because the loop was starved (§5.6), then the circuit breaker cannot engage precisely when it is most needed. That feedback loop deserves an explicit guard — cooldown state that depends on the resource being starved is not a circuit breaker. ### Defect 3 — the error path logs the entire message history, once per retry, synchronously Two problems in one: - The exception message embeds the **full `tool_calls` repr**, and the `verbose_logger.exception()` call emits a multi-level chained traceback. Measured: **exactly 30.0 log lines and 3,089 bytes per failure** (constant across three independently rotated log files — see §5.3). Multiply by the retry loop and you get GB-scale log volume. - The logger format string is **never interpolated**. The log contains the literal: ``` Unable to convert openai tool calls={} to bedrock tool calls. Received error={} ``` i.e. a `str.format`-style template passed to a `%`-style logger (or emitted without arguments), so the operator-facing log line carries **no information at all**. The useful text only appears in the exception message. Also worth noting: because the tool-call repr is logged, **user conversation content is written to stdout at ERROR level** — a data-handling concern independent of the volume issue. ## Evidence All commands below were run against the live cluster. Times are UTC unless suffixed "local" (local = UTC+8). ### 5.1 The traceback (verbatim frames, from `/var/log/pods/.../litellm/2.log.20260730-071804.gz`) ``` LiteLLM Router:ERROR: router.py:6235 - litellm.router.py::async_function_with_fallbacks() - Error occurred while trying to do fallbacks - litellm.APIConnectionError: litellm.APIConnectionError: Unable to convert openai tool calls=[{'id': 'tooluse_MAh2QLVjBRkvi5QJkLQ08V', 'type': 'function', 'function': {'name': 'replace_note_content', 'arguments': '{"note_id": "999af35c-4061-4ece-8581-7d43fc988ba4", "title": "WG-全站内容版图坐标表"'}}] to bedrock tool calls. Received error=Expecting ',' delimiter: line 1 column 76 (char 75) Traceback (most recent call last): File ".../litellm/litellm_core_utils/prompt_templates/factory.py", line 3682, in _convert_to_bedrock_tool_call_invoke File "/usr/lib/python3.13/json/__init__.py", line 352, in loads File "/usr/lib/python3.13/json/decoder.py", line 345, in decode File "/usr/lib/python3.13/json/decoder.py", line 361, in raw_decode json.decoder.JSONDecodeError: Expecting ',' delimiter: line 1 column 76 (char 75) During handling of the above exception, another exception occurred: File ".../litellm/litellm_core_utils/prompt_templates/factory.py", line 3695, in _convert_to_bedrock_tool_call_invoke File ".../litellm/litellm_core_utils/prompt_templates/common_utils.py", line 1711, in split_concatenated_json_objects File "/usr/lib/python3.13/json/decoder.py", line 361, in raw_decode json.decoder.JSONDecodeError: Expecting ',' delimiter: line 1 column 76 (char 75) During handling of the above exception, another exception occurred: File ".../litellm/main.py", line 643, in acompletion File ".../litellm/llms/bedrock/chat/converse_handler.py", line 105, in async_streaming File ".../litellm/llms/bedrock/chat/converse_transformation.py", line 1604, in _async_transform_request File ".../litellm/litellm_core_utils/prompt_templates/factory.py", line 4549, in _bedrock_converse_messages_pt_async File ".../litellm/litellm_core_utils/prompt_templates/factory.py", line 3731, in _convert_to_bedrock_tool_call_invoke Exception: Unable to convert openai tool calls={} to bedrock tool calls. Received error={} ^^^^ ^^^^ unformatted placeholders (Defect 3) File ".../litellm/router.py", line 6286, in async_function_with_fallbacks File ".../litellm/router.py", line 6532, in async_function_with_retries File ".../litellm/router.py", line 6465, in async_function_with_retries File ".../litellm/router.py", line 6541, in make_call File ".../litellm/router.py", line 2802, in _acompletion File ".../litellm/router.py", line 2753, in _acompletion File ".../litellm/utils.py", line 1870, in wrapper_async File ".../litellm/utils.py", line 1689, in wrapper_async File ".../litellm/main.py", line 696, in acompletion File ".../litellm/litellm_core_utils/exception_mapping_utils.py", line 2505, in exception_type File ".../litellm/litellm_core_utils/exception_mapping_utils.py", line 2482, in exception_type litellm.exceptions.APIConnectionError: litellm.APIConnectionError: Unable to convert openai tool calls=[...] ``` ### 5.2 The offending input ``` "arguments": "{\"note_id\": \"999af35c-4061-4ece-8581-7d43fc988ba4\", \"title\": \"WG-全站内容版图坐标表\"" ``` Exactly 75 characters long, with **no closing `}`** — `raw_decode` reports `Expecting ',' delimiter: line 1 column 76 (char 75)`, i.e. it ran off the end of the string right after the `title` value. A partially-streamed / truncated tool call that a client then replayed back into the message history. ### 5.3 Amplification measurements (three independently rotated log files) Counted with `zcat/wc -l` and `grep -c 'Unable to convert openai tool calls'`; the time span is the delta between the first and last `kubectl logs --timestamps` RFC3339 timestamps inside each file. | Log file | Bytes | Lines | `Unable to convert` count | Lines / failure | Bytes / failure | Timestamp span | Lines/s | Failures/s | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `2.log.20260730-071804.gz` | 17.6 MB gz (~247 MB raw) | 2,396,900 | 79,858 | **30.0** | — | `07:17:16.342308096Z` → `07:18:01.395021768Z` = **45.05 s** | **53,202** | **1,773** | | `2.log.20260730-071854` | 41,086,647 | 399,041 | 13,302 | **30.0** | **3,089** | 7.046 s | 56,634 | 1,888 | | `2.log` (current file at SIGKILL) | 61,634,348 | 598,651 | 19,954 | **30.0** | **3,089** | 0.845 s | — (buffer flush after SIGTERM, not a steady-state rate) | — | The three files independently agree on **30.0 log lines** and **3,089 bytes per failure** and **~103 bytes per line**, which is what makes the per-second figures trustworthy. Derived: `45.05 s / 79,858 = 0.564 ms` per retry iteration. Sustained stdout write rate `1,773 × 3,089 B ≈ 5.5 MB/s`. Over the ~7-minute event that is **~2.3 GB**. ### 5.4 Container log rotation — four times in fifty seconds ``` /var/log/pods/ai-gateway_<pod>_<uid>/litellm/ 2.log.20260730-071804.gz 2.log.20260730-071835.gz 2.log.20260730-071844.gz 2.log.20260730-071854 2.log ``` Rotations at `07:18:04`, `07:18:35`, `07:18:44`, `07:18:54`. Node-side confirmation from `sar -d -p` on the node running the pod (10-minute samples, 15:00 and 15:20 local): ``` nvme1n1 wkB/s 7478.35 %util 1.86 # 15:00 local nvme1n1 wkB/s 5582.55 %util 1.18 # 15:20 local ``` The sustained ~5.5–7.3 MB/s write rate matches the computed log volume — the flood was running *before* the pod froze, not only during the death throes. > **Operator warning worth adding to the docs:** `kubectl logs` only reads the *current* CRI log file. During this incident that made it look as though the process had emitted **zero** logs for 11 minutes, when in fact the opposite was true — the earlier content had been rotated away. I initially drew exactly the wrong conclusion from `kubectl logs --previous`. Anyone debugging this must look directly at `/var/log/pods/<ns>_<pod>_<uid>/<container>/`. ### 5.5 Proof that this is ONE request, not a client retry storm ```bash zcat 2.log.20260730-071804.gz | grep -o "tooluse_[A-Za-z0-9]*" | sort -u | wc -l # -> 1 zcat 2.log.20260730-071804.gz | grep -o '"note_id": "[^"]*"' | sort -u | wc -l # -> 1 ``` **Exactly one** distinct `tool_call.id` (`tooluse_MAh2QLVjBRkvi5QJkLQ08V`) and **one** distinct `note_id` across all **79,858** failures. The loop is entirely internal to LiteLLM. A client hammering the proxy would have produced many distinct tool-call ids. ### 5.6 Event loop starvation, shown by Redis client timeouts against a healthy Redis The pod logged `redis.exceptions.TimeoutError` (client-side read timeout) via `/usr/lib/python3.13/asyncio/timeouts.py:117 __aexit__`. Server side, at the same moment: | Redis metric | Value | | --- | --- | | `dbsize` | 470 keys | | `used_memory_human` | 2.40 MB | | largest key (`redis-cli --bigkeys`) | string, 10,779 bytes | | `slowlog get` | **empty** | | `latency history` | **empty** | | `blocked_clients` | 0 | | `evicted_keys` | 0 | | AOF status | `ok` | | `connected_clients` | 171 | | Redis node CPU idle | 97.4 – 97.5 % | | Redis node disk `%util` | < 2 %, `await` < 1.4 ms | A perfectly idle server plus a client-side read timeout inverts the usual reading: **LiteLLM's own event loop was too starved to drain the socket.** Redis is the victim here, not the cause. (Equally: the fact that `asyncio.timeout` fired at all proves the loop was still *cycling*, just hopelessly behind — this was CPU starvation, not a hard block.) ### 5.7 Every infrastructure explanation is excluded `sar` on the node running the pod, 10-minute samples at 15:10 / 15:20 local: | Metric | 15:10 | 15:20 | Verdict | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `%memused` | 17.24 % | 15.54 % | ~51 GB available (`free -m`: 49,105 MB) → not memory pressure | | `%user` (16 vCPU) | 6.91 % | 10.73 % | **one saturated core ≈ 6.25 %** → consistent with exactly one hot thread | | `%idle` | 91.5 % | 87.7 % | node looks perfectly healthy — this is the trap | | `%iowait` | 0.12 % | 0.10 % | not I/O bound | | `%steal` | 0 | 0 | no hypervisor contention | | `ldavg-1` | 0.97 | 2.06 | fine for 16 cores | | `runq-sz` / `blocked` | 4 / 0 | 1 / 0 | nothing blocked in D-state | Container cgroup v2: ``` /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.events -> oom 0 oom_kill 0 # NOT an OOM kill /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.stat -> nr_throttled 1 throttled_usec 303009 # 0.3 s total, irrelevant journalctl -k | grep -i oom -> (no output) ``` Network/kernel: ``` net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_count = 1760 net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max = 524288 journalctl -k | grep -Ei 'conntrack|neighbour|net_ratelimit' -> (no output) ``` PostgreSQL was not implicated: it runs off-pod, showed no slow queries or lock waits, and the only relevant proxy config was spend-log retention (`maximum_spend_logs_retention_period: 7d`, `store_audit_logs: true`). The one readiness `503` (15:18:21 local) is consistent with LiteLLM's *internal* DB health check timing out under loop starvation, not with PostgreSQL being unhealthy. **No debug logging was enabled.** Grepping the proxy ConfigMap for `verbose`/`debug`/`json_logs`/`log` returned only the two spend-log retention keys. The entire ~2.3 GB was error-path output at default log level. ### 5.8 Kill timeline (`journalctl -u kubelet -u containerd`) Local time = UTC+8; the klog `I0730 07:xx` stamps in the same lines are UTC. | Time (local) | Event | | --- | --- | | ≤ 15:10 | readiness probe already timing out; pod flaps Ready/NotReady (brief recoveries 15:11:27, 15:15:33) | | 15:12:00 | liveness probe begins failing, **every 30 s, 12 consecutive times** | | 15:17:30 | `Container litellm failed liveness probe, will be restarted` | | 15:18:21 | readiness probe returns `statuscode: 503` (process answers but self-check fails) | | 15:18:52.983 | containerd `StopContainer ... with timeout 8 (s)`; `signal terminated` (SIGTERM) | | 15:19:00.990 | `Kill container` (SIGKILL — the frozen process never handled SIGTERM) | | 15:19:01.179 | `exit_status:137` → this is where `exitCode 137 / reason: Error` comes from | | 15:19:02.309 | new container started, `attempt:3` | `137 = 128 + 9` (SIGKILL). Crucially `reason: Error`, **not** `OOMKilled` — but almost every operator, and much of the existing tooling, reads 137 as "out of memory". Combined with §5.7 this misdirection cost us a full day of investigation. ### 5.9 The restart does not help — the fresh container was re-starved in 65 seconds | Time (local) | Event | | --- | --- | | 15:19:30 | new container reports Ready | | 15:20:35 | readiness probe **already** timing out again | | 15:22:00 – 15:24:00 | liveness probe failing again | | after 15:24 | recovered on its own, without being killed | Two conclusions. First, this is not a slow resource leak — it is instantaneous re-poisoning by the same retried request. Second, **the liveness kill is net-negative here**: the process demonstrably recovers by itself, while the kill drops every in-flight request and shifts load onto peer replicas, spreading the failure. ### 5.10 The configured retry budget vs. the observed iteration count — and the fallback cycle Full `fallbacks` graph, verbatim from `LiteLLM_Config.router_settings`: ```yaml fallbacks: - gemini-3.1-flash-image: [gemini-3.1-flash-image-preview] - gpt-5.6-sol: [gpt-5.6-luna, gpt-5.6-terra] - gpt-5.5: [bedrock_mantle/gpt-5.5, bedrock_mantle/gpt-5.4, gpt-5.4, gpt-5.4-mini, gpt-5.4-nano] - gemini-3-pro-image: [gemini-3-pro-image-preview, gpt-image-2] - GLM-5.2: [claude-sonnet-4-6, bedrock/claude-sonnet-4-6, claude-sonnet-5] - claude-opus-4-8: [claude-opus-4-7, claude-opus-4-6] - claude-sonnet-5: [claude-sonnet-4-6, claude-haiku-4-5] - claude-opus-4-7: [claude-opus-4-6] - claude-opus-4-6: [claude-sonnet-5, claude-sonnet-4-6] - claude-sonnet-4-6: [claude-sonnet-5, claude-haiku-4-5] - claude-haiku-4-5: [gpt-5.5, GLM-5.2] ``` Cycles present: | Cycle | Length | | --- | --- | | `claude-sonnet-5 → claude-sonnet-4-6 → claude-sonnet-5` | 2 | | `claude-sonnet-4-6 → claude-haiku-4-5 → GLM-5.2 → claude-sonnet-4-6` | 3 | | `claude-sonnet-5 → claude-haiku-4-5 → GLM-5.2 → claude-sonnet-5` | 3 | Strongly connected component: `{claude-sonnet-5, claude-sonnet-4-6, claude-haiku-4-5, GLM-5.2}`. Additional entry points that funnel *into* the SCC without being part of it: `claude-opus-4-8 → claude-opus-4-7 → claude-opus-4-6 → claude-sonnet-5`. In other words, **six of our Claude/GLM model groups can all reach a non-terminating fallback walk.** Arithmetic: | Quantity | Value | | --- | --- | | `num_retries` | 2 → **3 attempts** per model group | | fallback groups for the group involved | 2 | | Expected upper bound if the graph were acyclic | 3 × (1 primary + 2 fallbacks) = **9 attempts** | | **Observed** | **79,858 attempts** | | Overshoot vs. configured bound | **≈8,873×** | | Measured interval between attempts | **0.564 ms** (configured `retry_after: 2.0` s) | | `allowed_fails` / `cooldown_time` | 3 / 60.0 s — no deployment observably cooled out of the loop | Side observation, possibly a separate usability bug: one fallback target, `bedrock/claude-sonnet-4-6`, looks like a deployment / `litellm_params.model` string rather than a model-group name. If that silently never resolves, a clear startup warning would help — as would rejecting (or at least warning about) a cyclic fallback graph at config-load time. ### 5.11 Secondary amplifiers — per-request side effects also ran ~80,000 times Because each retry re-enters the full call wrapper (`utils.py::wrapper_async` appears in every iteration of the traceback), the per-request side effects were multiplied by the loop as well. Flagging these as **mechanism inference** — they follow from our config plus the traceback frames, and maintainers are better placed to confirm which of them actually fire per attempt: | Setting | Value | Consequence at ~80,000 attempts | | --- | --- | --- | | `failure_callback` | `[langfuse]` | ~80,000 Langfuse failure events, each carrying the full request payload. We have separately had a single oversized Langfuse report block this event loop, so this path is known-sensitive in our deployment. | | `cache` / `cache_params` | `true`, redis, `supported_call_types: [acompletion, completion]` | a cache lookup per attempt → ~80,000 Redis round-trips issued *from the very loop that was starving*. This is plausibly the direct source of the `redis.exceptions.TimeoutError` in §5.6, and of the failure of `cooldown_time` to engage. | | `store_prompts_in_spend_logs` / `store_audit_logs` | `true` / `true` | error + spend rows per attempt, **including prompts**, against `database_connection_pool_limit: 10` — consistent with the single readiness `503` at 15:18:21 in §5.8. | | `callbacks` | `[..., prometheus]` | metric updates per attempt. | The general point: **an unbounded retry loop does not just burn CPU — it multiplies every observability and persistence side effect the operator has configured**, and several of those write to the exact dependencies (Redis, PostgreSQL) whose health the proxy reports on. ## Minimal reproduction Any model group backed by Bedrock Converse. The essential ingredient is an assistant message whose `tool_calls[].function.arguments` is a **truncated** JSON string. ```bash curl -sS http://<litellm-proxy>:4000/v1/chat/completions \ -H 'Authorization: Bearer sk-<key>' \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{ "model": "<any bedrock converse model group>", "stream": true, "messages": [ { "role": "user", "content": "rename that note" }, { "role": "assistant", "content": null, "tool_calls": [ { "id": "tooluse_MAh2QLVjBRkvi5QJkLQ08V", "type": "function", "function": { "name": "replace_note_content", "arguments": "{\"note_id\": \"999af35c-4061-4ece-8581-7d43fc988ba4\", \"title\": \"WG-example\"" } } ] }, { "role": "tool", "tool_call_id": "tooluse_MAh2QLVjBRkvi5QJkLQ08V", "content": "ok" } ] }' ``` Note the missing `}` at the end of the `arguments` string — that is the whole payload. **Observed:** `APIConnectionError`, then the router retries the transformation. With `num_retries: 2` alone you get ~9 attempts and a few hundred log lines. With a **cyclic** `fallbacks` graph the walk never terminates — in our case ~80,000 attempts, tens of thousands of log lines per second, and a starved event loop. **Expected:** HTTP `400` with a message identifying the offending message index and `tool_call_id`, no retry, one log line. To reproduce the full replica takedown, add a cycle to `fallbacks` — two lines is enough: ```yaml router_settings: num_retries: 2 fallbacks: - model-a: [model-b] - model-b: [model-a] # ← cycle; both groups must be Bedrock Converse ``` Then send the request above at `model-a` and watch log lines per second and `/health/liveliness` latency while it is in flight. Note that neither `retry_after` nor `allowed_fails`/`cooldown_time` stops it. ## Expected behaviour 1. Invalid `tool_calls[].function.arguments` is a **client input error** → `BadRequestError` / HTTP 400, **not** `APIConnectionError`. 2. Errors raised during request transformation (before any network I/O) must be **non-retryable** and must not enter the fallback chain. 3. A fallback walk must never revisit a model group it has already attempted for the same request, and a cyclic `fallbacks` graph should be rejected or warned about at config-load time. 4. Configured backoff (`retry_after`) should apply to every retryable class, so that a zero-latency failure cannot spin at CPU speed. 5. The error should be logged **once per request**, not once per retry attempt, and the log line must not contain the full message history at ERROR level. 6. Per-request side effects (`failure_callback`, cache lookups, spend/audit log writes) should fire once per request, not once per attempt. 7. Log format placeholders must actually be interpolated. ## Suggested fix **a) Raise a non-retryable, typed exception in the transformation layer** — `factory.py::_convert_to_bedrock_tool_call_invoke`, around line 3731: ```python except Exception as e: raise litellm.BadRequestError( # instead of: raise Exception(...) message=( f"Invalid tool_calls[{idx}].function.arguments: not valid JSON. " f"tool_call_id={tool_call.get('id')!r}, error={e}" ), model=model, llm_provider="bedrock", ) ``` This alone fixes most of the problem, because `BadRequestError` (400) is already excluded from the router's retry set — Defect 2 stops being reachable via this path. **b) Do not sweep bare transformation exceptions into `APIConnectionError`** — in `exception_mapping_utils.py::exception_type` (lines ~2482/2505), the "unknown exception → `APIConnectionError`" catch-all is what makes any future transformation bug retryable in the same way. Consider a distinct non-retryable class for errors raised before the HTTP request is issued. **c) Track visited model groups in the fallback walk** — this is the fix that would have prevented the outage even without (a) and (b). Carry a `visited: set[str]` through `async_function_with_fallbacks` and skip (or terminate on) any model group already attempted for this request. Additionally, validate the `fallbacks` graph when config is loaded and refuse/warn on cycles — the Admin UI currently accepts a cyclic graph silently, and each individual entry looks locally reasonable, so this is very easy to create by accident. **d) Guard the router against zero-latency failure loops** — even with (a)–(c), a deterministic pre-network failure should be structurally incapable of becoming a busy loop. Suggestions: enforce a minimum backoff floor (even a few ms) per retry and apply the configured `retry_after` to all retryable classes, not only rate limits; add a per-request wall-clock budget in addition to the retry count; break the loop when N consecutive attempts fail with an identical exception type *and* message hash. Also consider that cooldown state which lives in Redis cannot act as a circuit breaker when the loop being broken is what is starving the Redis client — a purely in-process failure counter would be more robust for this case. **e) Bound the error-path log volume and per-attempt side effects** — truncate the request/tool-call repr in exception messages (e.g. first 512 chars), demote the full repr to `verbose_logger.debug`, keep a short one-line summary at ERROR, and log the traceback only on the first attempt of a request rather than on every retry. The same applies to `failure_callback`, cache lookups and spend/audit-log writes (§5.11): firing them per *attempt* rather than per *request* multiplies the blast radius into Redis and PostgreSQL. **f) Fix the format string** so `Unable to convert openai tool calls={} to bedrock tool calls. Received error={}` actually interpolates its arguments. **g) Optionally, be lenient like `split_concatenated_json_objects` already is** — that helper exists because models emit malformed tool arguments in practice. Extending it to attempt recovery of *truncated* JSON (or to surface a clear 400) would close the original trigger. Leniency is optional; **non-retryability is not**. ## Workaround we deployed Since we cannot patch the image, we added a validation gate in a `CustomLogger.async_pre_call_hook`, which runs **before** the router and can therefore reject the request with a real 400 instead of letting it into the retry loop: ```python import json for i, msg in enumerate(data.get("messages") or []): if not isinstance(msg, dict): continue for tc in (msg.get("tool_calls") or []): args = ((tc or {}).get("function") or {}).get("arguments") if not isinstance(args, str) or not args.strip(): continue try: json.loads(args) except (ValueError, TypeError): raise HTTPException( status_code=400, detail={ "error": "malformed_tool_call_arguments", "message": "tool_calls[].function.arguments is not valid JSON " "(truncated tool call in message history)", "message_index": i, "tool_call_id": (tc or {}).get("id"), }, ) ``` For other operators hitting this before a fix lands, the mitigations that actually helped, in order of effect: (1) the pre-call validation hook above; (2) **break the cycles in `fallbacks`** — check your graph for strongly connected components; ours had a 4-node one and `num_retries: 2` was already as low as it usefully goes; (3) raise the log level of the router logger to `CRITICAL` in an emergency to stop the flood; (4) switch the liveness probe to `tcpSocket` (or raise `failureThreshold` a lot) so a temporarily starved-but-recovering replica is not killed; (5) set kubelet `containerLogMaxSize` / `containerLogMaxFiles` so a flood cannot fill the node disk. ## Questions for maintainers The configuration is included above (§Environment and §5.10), so the "is this just a huge `num_retries`?" question is settled: it is not — `num_retries: 2` bounds the work at ~9 attempts and we observed 79,858. What I cannot determine from outside the codebase: 1. **Is the fallback walk cycle-guarded at all?** If `async_function_with_fallbacks` re-enters itself for a fallback group that has its own `fallbacks` entry, a cyclic graph is unbounded by construction. Our data is consistent with that; please confirm. 2. **Should `retry_after: 2.0` have applied here?** Measured 0.564 ms between attempts. If backoff is deliberately limited to rate-limit errors, then any zero-latency retryable error can spin at CPU speed, which seems worth changing independently of this bug. 3. **Why did `allowed_fails: 3` / `cooldown_time: 60.0` not cool the deployments out of the loop?** Is cooldown state written to Redis on the request path — and if so, is it expected to fail open when Redis times out? 4. **Do `failure_callback`, cache lookups and spend/audit-log writes fire per attempt or per request?** (§5.11) If per attempt, the loop also generated ~80,000 Langfuse events and ~80,000 Redis and PostgreSQL operations, which changes the recommended mitigation. 5. **Is a cyclic `fallbacks` graph considered invalid configuration?** If so, validation at config-load time would turn a production outage into a startup error. If not, cycle-tracking during the walk becomes mandatory. Happy to provide on request: the first N lines of a rotated log file at full verbosity, the complete `kubectl describe pod`, the raw `journalctl` extracts, `sar` output for other windows, further Redis/PostgreSQL statistics, or a `grep -c` across the other five replicas to confirm blast radius. ## Checklist - [x] Reproduced on the latest version we run (v1.93.0) - [x] Searched existing issues for `_convert_to_bedrock_tool_call_invoke`, `split_concatenated_json_objects`, `Unable to convert openai tool calls` - [x] Included the full traceback with file/line references - [x] Included a minimal reproduction request body - [x] Included the full `router_settings` / `litellm_settings` / `general_settings` (secrets removed) - [x] Ruled out OOM, CPU throttling, node resource pressure, conntrack exhaustion, Redis, PostgreSQL, and network as causes ### Steps to Reproduce 1. 2. 3. ### Relevant log output ```shell ``` ### What part of LiteLLM is this about? Other ### What LiteLLM version are you on ? v1.93.0 ### Twitter / LinkedIn details _No response_

signal.title: fix(router): honor key-level tag filtering in pre-routing and pin auto-router e2e regressions
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - Auto-router fixes shipped to the customer had no e2e regression pins - Tag-split routing, alias pricing, heuristic scope, and Responses routing could silently regress How it solves it: - 13 live-proxy pins in tests/e2e/router covering tracker items R-01 through R-07 - Coverage registry cells for every pin; the Responses pin is proven fail-before-fix - Tracker inventory maps every item to a pin, delegation, or follow-up - Fixes a router gap the CI run surfaced: request-level enable_tag_filtering, which the proxy sets from key and team router_settings, now also gates pre-routing marker capture, so the suite scopes tag filtering to its own keys instead of flipping the shared proxy's config and breaking concurrent suites ## User Flow Before: a regression in tag-split auto-routing ships unnoticed and the gateway's users see it first 1. A platform admin registers a plain deployment and a tagged auto-router marker under one model name via POST /model/new and turns on tag filtering via POST /config/update 2. A routing regression like the Aug 12 one ships in a new proxy release; no automated check exercises this setup 3. A developer sends an untagged POST /v1/chat/completions to the shared name and gets 400 "Unmapped LLM provider auto_router" instead of an answer 4. A Codex user sends POST /v1/responses with an x-litellm-tags header and hits the same 400 5. The failures surface as production incidents and support tickets before the release can be rolled back After: the same regression now fails the e2e suite by name before a release reaches users 1. The suite itself registers the same setup via POST /model/new against a live proxy and mints its keys via POST /key/generate with `"router_settings": {"enable_tag_filtering": true}`, so filtering rides only its own requests 2. It sends tagged and untagged POST /v1/chat/completions, /v1/messages, and /v1/responses requests to the shared name and reads back from the spend logs which deployment served each one 3. A release carrying the regression turns the run red, naming the broken behavior, for example the semantic auto-router Responses pin failing with the exact 400 above 4. The regression is caught in CI and users keep getting answers from the deployment their tags select ## Coverage matrix Every Fixed or Delivered item in the customer issue tracker, with where its regression protection lives.
